📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this Thanksgiving, don’t overlook that side dish of green peas. Pilates babes, protein-maxxers, and anybody who is even a little bit wellness-obsessed are going in hard on the green legume, and for good reason.

According to recent reports, according to the Food and Drug Administration, a cup of unsalted green peas has around 9 grams of protein—but that’s just the beginning. It’s also filled with vitamin A (necessary for your immune system), K, and C, plus a lot of fiber.

It has been revealed that “It’s come to my attention that the hot girls are now eating peas,” Lainie Kates of Lainie Cooks says at the opening her video for the now-viral recipe for Tuscan Parmesan Peas. But it’s one particular add-in that made the recipe viral. “Lots of parmesan cheese,” she says while grating a block the size of her own head. “Three ounces of parmesan cheese is about 33 extra grams of protein.”.

Pilates instructor Raven Ross calls herself the queen of “pea propaganda” and is one of the reasons the vegetable is back into the conversation. “Whoever told you eating healthy is hard straight up lied to your face,” she says while sharing one of her pea-based bowls, which also has a bell pepper and chicken sausage inside to hit around 40 grams of protein and 20 grams of fiber in one meal.

Industry observers note that the beauty of green peas is that the legume is essentially as universal as cauliflower. A frozen bag from any supermarket (I have to say, the Trader Joe’s Petit Peas are my favorite, though perhaps it’s just a branding bias) can be whipped into a dip or added into almost any dish for a vegetarian source of both protein and fiber. It’s also a popular source for protein powder.

It seems that all of our childhood objections to the green vegetable were wrong—so this Thanksgiving, pass the peas, please.

#134849. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (395 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting.
  • Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.
  • More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Tech Report: Extra-Fluffy Cinnamon Rolls

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting.
  • Sources indicate that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.
  • In a recent development, the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

Sources indicate that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

In a recent development, the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

In a recent development, yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

This is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls.

In a recent development, save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

Whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

While the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

Industry observers note that butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

The Most Flattering Hairstyles for Women Over 50, From Bobs to Long Layers

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • In a recent development, the rules are relative when it comes to “age-appropriate hair.” No matter what decade you’re presently thriving in, the style you choose should make you feel good.
  • The most key thing is to choose for the hair you have now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In a recent development, the rules are relative when it comes to “age-appropriate hair.” No matter what decade you’re presently thriving in, the style you choose should make you feel good. That remarked, as hair texture, volume, and color change with age, some styles may feel and look better once you hit your 50s. The options are vast, but don’t think you have to go shorter as you mature or cover up sprouting grays. If anything, feel free to experiment. Worn short hair all your life? Try some extensions and waist-length waves. Or if you’ve had long hair for as long as you can remember, trim a few inches off into a happy medium lob. Experts share tips and ideas for choosing the best hairstyle if you’re over 50.

The most key thing is to choose for the hair you have now. “I tell my clients to think about things like fullness, movement, tone, and shape,” Elba Iris, John Frieda stylist and educator, tells ELLE. A good style, Elba adds, should make hair look healthy and as full as possible, have movement so it never looks stiff or set, and have shine with dimension. It’s also helpful to be realistic about your routine and consider how much daily effort and time you can commit to styling your hair.

Also, keep in mind that length is a personal choice. “One thing I really dislike is when women are told they need to cut their hair after a certain age,” indicates Rodger Azadganian, a hairstylist, salon owner, and founder of Äz Haircare. “I think that’s such an outdated idea. I care much more about the condition of the hair and whether the cut suits the person. If you love long hair, keep it long,” he encourages. Iris completely agrees, adding that shape, health, shine, and confidence are what make your hair look youthful.

Azadganian is a huge fan of a sharp bob, which he says always looks sophisticated. “I also love collarbone-length hair with a little movement around the face. And I think long, beautiful hair on a woman over 50 can be incredibly chic,” he adds.

Iris notes the styles that consistently flatter his over-50 clients are those with softness around the face, deep angles, and layers if the hair is longer. Like Azadganian, Iris also says a collarbone-length lob with long soft layers is the most versatile. “It keeps length, gives movement, and [can be] styled in various ways,” says Iris. He adds that a textured bob, worn a little undone rather than perfectly smooth, is chic at any age and makes fine hair look thicker because the ends are blunt and full.

If you have or prefer short hair, Iris says a soft pixie with a longer, swept fringe is beautiful and lifts the whole face. “Face-framing layers or a soft curtain fringe are my secret weapon—they draw the eye up, soften everything, and grow out gracefully between appointments.”.

Sources indicate that gray hair grows in with a different texture than you may be used to. It’s often wirier, drier, and more resistant to products and color, so styles may need more moisture and smoothing than before.

In a recent development, for those who dye their hair all one color and have started to, or are already fully gray, regrowth may pose an unflattering problem. “Solid color against graying regrowth creates a harsh line and can actually make thinning at the part more visible,” Iris cautions. Instead, both Iris and Azadganian recommend dimensional color over anything too flat or solid. Go for softer dimension—highlights, lowlights, or a blended “gray blending” approach. This technique diffuses the regrowth, adds the illusion of depth and fullness, and buys you more time between appointments.

If you’re embracing grey fully, love it. The key, though, according to Iris, is to keep it bright and conditioned. “Grey hair can yellow and look dull; a glossing treatment and the right purple shampoo, like John Frieda Violet Crush, keep it silver and striking instead of dusty. Color should work with your styling, never make it harder,” Iris recommends.

For fine hair, both Azadganian and Iris suggest keeping the ends blunt in order to make the hair look fuller. “A bob or lob with a strong perimeter makes hair look twice as dense, and I’d avoid heavy layering, which removes the fullness you can see. Fullness also has to be built at the styling,” Iris explains. He recommends the John Frieda Ultra Filler+ shampoo and conditioner for fine hair to plump each strand and to make hair look and feel thicker when styled. Use a thickening spray at the root before blow-drying for lasting lift.

For thick or coarse hair, go with longer layers to take out some weight and keep it from looking heavy and triangular. For curly and coily hair, Iris says shape is key. “A cut done on dry hair, in its natural state, with layers that let the curl sit where it lives, plus real moisture.”.

In a recent development, azadganian says a beautifully shaped curly bob is incredible. “I always want the haircut to work with the texture instead of forcing it into something else,” he notes.

In a recent development, wavy hair looks best in a mid-length cut with soft layers that enhance the natural bend of the texture without heat styling. As for length, Iris states short hair loves texture and a little messiness. “Mid-length, chin to collarbone, is the sweet spot for most women because it’s long enough to feel feminine and short enough to stay full,” says Iris. Long hair after 50 absolutely works, but as both stylists noted, only if the hair is kept healthy and styled.

Azadganian indicates one of the biggest mistakes with hair over age 50 is getting stuck with the same hairstyle for decades. “You don’t need to change everything, but even updating your layers, fringe, or part can make such a difference. I love seeing women experiment with their hair at every age,” says Azadganian.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

According to recent reports, to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

In a recent development, drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

Industry observers note that to a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

It has been revealed that place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

After Careful Review, These Are the Best Perfumes for Women

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that where does one even begin when narrowing down the best perfumes for women? It’s a daunting task, to say the least. With hundreds of thousands of women’s fragrances flooding the market (and that’s putting it mildly), finding your signature scent or building out a fragrance wardrobe can quickly lead to sensory overload.

First, there’s the matter of personality and preference: Everyone’s idea of “the best” is deeply personal and sometimes even polarizing. Are you drawn to hyper-femme blooms, or do you lean toward moody, spice-forward aromas? What about delicious gourmands, warm solar scents, or—conversely—earthy notes grounded in fresh greens and wood? Perhaps you are a no-fuss minimalist who sticks to subtle skin scents. Are you interested in something long-lasting or a light and airy eau de toilette? Maybe you’d rather layer a few different perfumes to create your own unique combination. The choices are quite literally endless.

It has been revealed that whether you prefer standout blends from legacy houses or niche scents from innovative alchemists—there’s something for everyone, with picks from experts and Vogue editors alike. Ahead, our definitive guide to the best perfumes for women, along with expert tips on finding the perfect scent that feels uniquely yours. Prepare for a sensory journey that balances tradition and innovation.

Industry observers note that if we haven’t driven the point home already: Fragrance is deeply personal. So what’s the secret to finding the best fragrances? Look no further than your reflection. “The most notable thing to consider when looking for a signature fragrance is choosing one that reflects who you are as a person,” says fragrance expert Nwasike, reminding us that scent should be an extension of self—intimate, expressive, and unmistakably you.

According to recent reports, on a more practical note? It’s all about testing, testing, and yes—more testing. Start by spritzing your top contenders on fragrance blotter strips. Once something sparks that visceral “yes,” only then should you see how it plays with your skin. This step is key, indicates Nwasike, to “understand the true nature of the fragrance” and how it will evolve with your body chemistry throughout the day.

Not one for snap decisions? No problem. Nwasike recommends trying samples or gift sets before committing to a full bottle. Consider it your scent’s trial period—a little like dating before marrying a signature scent.

According to recent reports, for those just beginning their fragrance journey, one of the first questions that often arises is: What’s the difference between eau de toilette and eau de parfum? The distinction lies in concentration—and, ultimately, longevity. “Eau de parfum (or EDP for short) generally contains between 15% and 20% fragrance oil,” explains fragrance expert Levy. As a result, it tends to last around four to five hours on the skin.

In a recent development, eau de toilette, on the other hand, is lighter and more fleeting. “The term comes from the French phrase faire sa toilette, meaning ‘to get ready,’” says Levy. Designed for a quick, refreshing burst of scent, eau de toilette typically lingers for two to three hours and contains between 5% and 15% fragrance oil.

In a recent development, craving serious staying power, maximum projection, and a swoon-worthy scent trail? Pick an extrait or absolut perfume—the most concentrated forms of fragrance. “Every perfumer works differently, so there is no single method for creating an extrait,” perfumer Aurélien Guichard of French label Matière Première previously told Vogue. What you can expect, though, is intensity, richness, and a scent that truly lingers.

How to Make Perfume Last Longer.

Industry observers note that making sure your fragrance lasts with you throughout the day is more than just a spritz-and-go experience. “To extend the longevity of a fragrance, your skin needs to be hydrated,” states Nwasike, who opts for applying a rich mositruizer before spraying her perfume. For more of a boost, you can even mix in a perfume oil with your body moisturizer for added layering. And while we’re spraying, don’t just opt for skin contact. “Always spray your fragrance on your clothing, because fragrance on fabric slows the evaporation process," says Nwasike.

Last but certainly not least, where you store your fragrance matters just as much as how you wear it. Nwasike advises storing your perfume in a cool, dark, and dry place, as direct sunlight can break down fragrance molecules.

In curating this edit, we considered the elements that make a fragrance truly unforgettable. First and foremost: captivating notes designed to turn heads. Our selection spans iconic blends from storied fragrance houses to fresh, modern offerings from emerging perfumers shaking up the scene. Yes, there are the universally adored staples—Carolina Herrera Good Girl, Marc Jacobs Daisy, Viktor & Rolf Flowerbomb, Versace Bright Crystal, Gucci Bloom, and Miss Dior. All icons no doubt. But our goal? To guide you toward something a little less expected—something not already dominating your TikTok FYP.

With insights from industry experts and Vogue editors alike—who shared the scents that draw the most compliments—we’ve crafted a tightly edited list that celebrates the art of standing out subtly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

In a recent development, to a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

It has been revealed that scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

Meghan Markle may have traded the sunny climes of Montecito for the British countryside, but her penchant for a thoughtful tablescape, a homemade preserve, and a well-appointed guest room remains. As the Duchess of Sussex prepares to celebrate her first Thanksgiving since relocating to the UK, she’s imparting some of her festive hosting wisdom.

In the forthcoming winter matter of Bon Appétit, Meghan shares her approach to holiday entertaining, alongside conversations spanning family, favorite restaurants, and the duchess’s Netflix series, With Love, Meghan.

It has been revealed that long before she had her own lifestyle brand (or, indeed, her own wine), Meghan was a college student looking to impress her dinner guests with a little help from Rachael Ray. An avid viewer of 30 Minute Meals, she recalls making a rather sophisticated grilled cheese sandwich in her first apartment, layering fontina, apple slices, and thyme, pressing it all together on her George Foreman grill, and finishing it with olive oil and Maldon sea salt. The wine pairing was Trader Joe’s famously inexpensive Two Buck Chuck. “Early 2000s at its finest,” she recalls.

While Meghan’s taste in wine has evolved somewhat (last summer saw the launch of her own Napa Valley rosé), her approach to entertaining hasn’t changed all that much. “I still believe little touches are all you need to make something ordinary feel special, especially when you're having loved ones over,” she tells the magazine. “It doesn't have to be over the top.”.

So, what does a stay at the Sussexes’ entail? She likes to lay the table a day in advance, freeing herself up to actually enjoy the company of her guests when they arrive. For those staying overnight, she programs the coffee machine to brew before they wake up, stocks the kitchen with breakfast provisions (think bagels, berries, yogurt, smoked salmon, and capers), and leaves a handwritten note inviting them to help themselves.

And when Meghan is the guest rather than the hostess? She favors something edible and homemade, like a batch of honey-roasted spiced nuts or a blackberry pound cake that can double as breakfast the following morning. Presentation is part of the pleasure too, and she advises using a little kitchen twine, a length of ribbon, or a sprig of rosemary to make things feel more considered. (Both recipes feature in the newly introduced glitch.).

Recent findings suggest that those who tuned into last year’s festive instalment of With Love, Meghan will be familiar with the duchess’s enthusiasm for the holidays. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished.
  • In a recent development, the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder.
  • It has been revealed that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman claims. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

In a recent development, the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, indicates of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

It has been revealed that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the latest podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman states this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

In a recent development, whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman claims. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

It has been revealed that at Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she states.

Recent findings suggest that the vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she notes. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up quickly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Recent findings suggest that alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

According to recent reports, this recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

1 hour (plus 1 hour for marinating).

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Recent findings suggest that heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

Sources indicate that to a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

Sources indicate that in a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

According to recent reports, add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

According to recent reports, remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

We look at how comfortably they cut, whether they pull or miss hairs, and how easy they are to handle and clean. Extra attachments need to be useful, and we consider battery life and charging alongside performance.

Recent findings suggest that the guide draws on Adam Hurly’s years of grooming reviews and Ian Burke’s experience of living with the Zorami trimmer long after receiving it as a joke gift. My additions bring in testing for British GQ, alongside Owen Gough’s assessment of the MultiShape system. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation. What is the best nose hair trimmer?

The best men’s nose hair trimmer is Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer 5000 Series, according to GQ. The powerful device offers dual trimming options (for internal and peripheral nostril hairs) and also functions as a facial hair, eyebrow, and ear hair trimmer.

Can a nose hair trimmer cut you?

It has been revealed that whether you are using a rotary head or a linear head, nose hair trimmers are built with a protective guard, which ensures the blade doesn’t come in direct contact with the skin. The protective guard also helps you get a clean cut so the device doesn’t pull or pluck at your nose hairs. Generally speaking, nose hair trimmers do not hurt.

Sources indicate that not only can nose hair trimmers be washed, but it is important to disinfect them between use, first by flushing out stray hair clippings. Let them dry before storing, too, to avoid rust and bacterial proliferation between each use. It’s a good idea to clean the device again before using it, since it is going into your nose, after all.

Do you need a nose hair trimmer, and how often should you use it?

Sources indicate that if visible nose hairs bother you, a trimmer is a simple way to keep them tidy. There’s no fixed schedule to follow – a quick trim when hairs start showing is usually all that’s needed. Concentrate on those visible hairs around the nostril opening, rather than trying to remove everything inside. Ear hair and eyebrows can be tidied as needed, using the appropriate attachment and comb.

How do you use a nose hair trimmer?

Sources indicate that to trim your nose hair, simply stick the trimming tip of the device in your nostril and apply a gentle circular motion. Here are a few more tips to keep in mind, according to Simone:.

How do I clean my nose hair trimmer?

The cleaning systems for nose hair trimmers vary. “Some nose hair trimmers are waterproof, so it’s easy to just rinse under water, if you are the sole user, and just let it air dry,” notes Simone. If you share the device with somebody else, then it’s going to be all the more notable that you disinfect between uses (ideally before and after each trim). “Make sure you have tapped out the hair trapped inside to avoid clogging,” adds Simone. “For a disinfectant, I would use a sterilizing alcohol pad or barber’s disinfectant, and just wipe the tool gently dry.”.

It has been revealed that the newcomers are the Rudolph, Bumble, and Sam the Snowman Doughnuts. Rudolph starts with an Original Glazed doughnut dipped in icing, then gets a glittery Christmas garland sprinkle blend, vanilla-flavored frosting, and a Rudolph wreath decoration.

Finally, the Sam the Snowman Doughnut starts with an Original Glazed dipped in vanilla icing and covered in white chocolate curls, then gets a buttercreme Christmas tree and Sam the Snowman fondant piece.

“We love giving fans latest ways to enjoy the traditions they grew up with, and this collection is all about bringing people together over something fun, festive and delicious,” Alison Holder, Chief Product and Brand Officer at Krispy Kreme, remarked in a statement.

It has been revealed that the latest collection arrives November 28 at participating Krispy Kreme locations nationwide, just two days after the chain wraps up its Thanksgiving doughnut collection. That lineup featured four holiday-inspired flavors: Berry Cobbler, Caramel Pumpkin, Double Chocolate Crumble, and Cinnamon Apple Filled.

As for the new Rudolph treats, you can pick them up individually or grab a dozen in a special collectible-style box featuring the beloved characters.

Recent findings suggest that whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

According to recent reports, turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Recent findings suggest that let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Industry observers note that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too rapidly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

I Learned How Baby Carrots Are Made & Haven't Bought Them Since—Here's Why

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a lover of all veggies, I love every type of carrot out there—except packaged baby carrots.
  • Here’s the truth about baby carrots—and why you might want to think twice about snagging a bag.
  • The bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a lover of all veggies, I love every type of carrot out there—except packaged baby carrots. That’s right: those bright orange cylinders with suspiciously perfect rounded corners that lurk in vending machines, school lunchboxes, and convenience store cold cases across our nation. They might be easy to eat on the go and better for you than a bag of Cheetos, but there’s a lot more going on behind the scenes of this seemingly simple healthy snack.

Here’s the truth about baby carrots—and why you might want to think twice about snagging a bag.

The bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size. Real baby carrots are immature carrots harvested before they reach full size. They’re sold in bunches—unpeeled, often with the tops still attached.

Sources indicate that while a whole carrot has a delicate, nuanced sweetness, the taste of these so-called baby carrots is best described as... factory-fresh. Don’t believe me? Grab a bag of regular carrots and do a side-by-side taste test.

Baby carrots were originally “invented” in the 1980s to make misshapen or broken carrots sellable. This was a smart way to reduce food waste and save money, but it also helped reinforce the unrealistic expectation that produce must look perfect in order to taste good. Today, baby-cut carrots are grown and processed to meet specific standards for size and shape, all to produce those identical little orange cylinders.

Here’s the bottom line: When you buy a bag of baby carrots, you’re buying into a world that’s seemingly as obsessed with unnatural perfection as the modern-day beauty industry.

According to recent reports, energy conservation is top of mind for consumers these days, but making baby carrots look so uniform takes a lot of machinery. After they’re sorted, they chop the carrots into roughly 2-inch pieces and shave them—twice. Then, they go through a rough cutter, which gives them a general shape, before being polished to create those unrealistically perfect rounded edges. That’s a lot of extra work to make something that was completely edible to begin with look a certain way.

To prevent bacterial growth, baby carrots may be rinsed with a diluted chlorine solution before packaging. They’re then rinsed with water, and the chlorine treatment itself is an “acceptable” food-safety practice which doesn’t make baby carrots unsafe to eat. Still, do you really want your “fresh” snack to have undergone chlorine treatments of any kind? For me, that’s a hard no, and I’d rather buy whole carrots and wash and cut them myself.

Because baby carrots have been peeled and cut, they're more prone to drying out and developing something called “carrot blush,” a thin white film caused by dehydration. The film itself is harmless, but it certainly doesn’t make them look appetizing. Worse, they can turn slimy inside the bag, even before you open it. And that’s downright gross.

Sources indicate that prices vary depending on where you shop, but baby-cut carrots can cost more per pound than regular whole carrots. You're essentially paying extra for someone else to handle the peeling, cutting, and polishing. For a task that takes barely any time at home, I'd rather keep the difference in my wallet.

Seriously. Enjoy the taste and texture of whole carrots, potentially save some money, and skip the extra processing by simply buying a bag of whole carrots and cutting them yourself. It’ll take you less time than you spent reading this article.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Industry observers note that whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Sources indicate that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Sources indicate that turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

In a recent development, place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Brave Upcoming Visions Creativity as Rebellion

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 62 min read (12441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PhotoVogue is proud to unveil the shortlist of 100 photographers and video makers selected for Brave Newly introduced Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, our Global Open Call dedicated to the power of creativity to challenge the status quo, question established narratives, and imagine alternative futures.
  • In a recent development, what's Next This shortlist marks the beginning of the next chapter of Brave Newly introduced Visions: Creativity as Rebellion.
  • It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘Farīsāt – Gunpowder’s Daughters’.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PhotoVogue is proud to unveil the shortlist of 100 photographers and video makers selected for Brave Newly introduced Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, our Global Open Call dedicated to the power of creativity to challenge the status quo, question established narratives, and imagine alternative futures. With 95,758 submissions from 9,160 artists across 155 regions, the response to this year's Open Call was extraordinary. But beyond the numbers, what moved us most was the imagination, urgency, and creative courage of the work we received. We live in a world saturated with images. More images are produced and consumed than ever before, yet more images do not necessarily mean more understanding, more imagination, or more freedom. What matters is not simply creating something new, but finding a way to make us see, feel, or question something we might otherwise have overlooked. Perhaps today, one of the most rebellious things an artist can do is refuse to give us another image we already know. Rebellion does not always announce itself loudly. It can be political and confrontational, but it can also be intimate, poetic, playful, uncomfortable, or deeply personal. It can take the form of tenderness, humor, beauty, or an unexpected way of looking at something familiar. What makes it rebellious is the freedom to question what we have been taught to accept and to imagine what might exist beyond it. This year's Open Call brought together an extraordinary range of ideas, emotions, and visual languages. Some works confront urgent social and political realities. Others explore identity, memory, belonging, desire, or the complexities of human experience. What connects the 100 selected artists is not a shared aesthetic or a single definition of rebellion, but a willingness to take risks, experiment, and follow their own vision. Images do more than represent the world. They influence how we understand it, whose stories we recognize, and what we believe is possible. The artists presented here remind us that creativity can do more than reflect reality. It can challenge the assumptions through which we see it and make space for futures we have not yet imagined.

In a recent development, what's Next This shortlist marks the beginning of the next chapter of Brave Newly introduced Visions: Creativity as Rebellion. In the coming weeks, we will announce which artists from the shortlist have been selected to exhibit at the next edition of the PhotoVogue Festival, as well as the three artists who will receive the PhotoVogue Grants. We will also reveal the festival's dates and location. We invite you to return to this page and follow PhotoVogue on Instagram for these announcements. Above all, we want to thank every artist who trusted us with their work. Selecting 100 artists from such an extraordinary response was incredibly difficult. This shortlist represents only a fraction of the talent, imagination, and creative courage we encountered. The future is not something we simply inherit. It is something we have the power to imagine.

Farīsāt - Gunpowder’s Daughters.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘Farīsāt – Gunpowder’s Daughters’. For centuries, tbourida, the Moroccan equestrian tradition reenacting ancient Arab military manoeuvres, was an exclusively male domain. Today, women are mounting their horses, leading their own troupes and rewriting the rules of a centuries-old practice. Known as farisat, these riders are challenging the patriarchal structures that have kept them out of the arena, claiming a place in Morocco’s cultural heritage. Following several all-female sorbas across the country, Pinzi documents a quiet but determined shift in tradition, where simply taking the reins can become an act of resistance.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘Heaven Belongs to You’. What if divinity had never been somewhere above us, but always within us? Okoro reimagines heaven through the presence of contemporary African subjects, casting real individuals as living mythologies whose everyday existence carries the weight of the sacred. Drawing on the power of ancestral narratives, the series challenges the mythologies that have historically dictated who is entitled to embody purity, power and the divine. Here, divinity is neither inherited nor bestowed: it belongs to everyone, and begins with the self.

We Didn't Choose to be Born Here.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Didn’t Choose to Be Born Here’. At its heart are two contrasting responses to Apartheid: while Makepe’s grandfather fled South Africa for Botswana in search of a safer life, his great-uncle became a prominent anti-Apartheid activist and political prisoner. Blending staged portraiture, documentary photography and re-enactments, Makepe brings these histories into the present, collaborating with relatives to reconstruct memories and embody those who came before them. Through this intergenerational portrait, he examines the choices we inherit, the weight of political responsibility and how personal circumstances shape our relationship with collective struggle.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘Grosse’. Taking its title from a word historically associated with shame and stigma, the project turns an insult into a means of questioning the beauty standards imposed on contemporary bodies. Through staged self-portraits, fictional imagery and distorted mirrors, the artist explores the uneasy relationship between self-acceptance and the desire to conform. Drawing on her own experience with weight-loss medication, she confronts the contradictions of a culture that encourages us to love our bodies while relentlessly urging us to change them. A recurring hybrid figure, suspended between reality and imagination, embodies the internalised gaze through which the body becomes both an object of scrutiny and a site of control.

This photograph is part of the project ‘4ever &ver &ver’, an anthology of three video works and one photographic piece exploring how young people navigate a social reality where online and offline lives increasingly overlap. Drawing on digital behaviours, everyday conversations and staged situations, Jip Schalkx examines a generation shaped by visibility, self-performance and the constant possibility of being seen. In a world where even the most mundane moments become potential content, identity and connection are increasingly negotiated through the logic of social platforms. Part observation, part personal inquiry, the four interconnected works form a fragmented yet intimate portrait of the present, where reality and fiction are never quite separate.

We Need To Talk In Whispers: Case Study of Alfred.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘We Need to Talk in Whispers: Case Study of Alfred’. The project began with an unexpected discovery: a weathered notebook found on an overnight train in India, filled with handwritten notes, newspaper clippings and fragments of correspondence documenting lives marked by death and disappearance. Following these scattered traces, Bose travelled to Ebeltoft, Denmark, to investigate the story of Alfred, a man who lived with schizophrenia during the Second World War. Moving between archival research, oral histories, documentary photography and speculation, he reconstructs an inner world through the places, objects and silences left behind. At the intersection of memory and imagination, the work asks what whispers can reveal about the experiences society would rather leave unspoken.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘Untitled’, in which Peristiani turns the domestic interior into a stage for the power dynamics that shape women's lives. A space conventionally associated with intimacy and safety becomes a setting for surveillance, control and quiet acts of rebellion. Through two recurring figures, uncomfortable poses, obstructed mirrors and carefully choreographed gestures, she explores the tension between being watched and attempting to escape the gaze. Here, even the most familiar household objects become instruments of control, while the body itself becomes a means of resistance, reclaiming space through movement and disruption.

Recent findings suggest that this excerpt is part of video project ‘AFK (Away From Keyboard)’. First-person shooter games such as Counter-Strike offer players the chance to embody idealised versions of militarised masculinity, where dominance and aggression are built into the game itself. Drawing on his own teenage experience of struggling with masculinity and sexuality, van Gent revisits this familiar gaming environment through a queer lens. The installation features three looping animations using original 3D game models, whose subtle gestures and unexpected movements disrupt the hypermasculine behaviour expected of their characters. By introducing moments of vulnerability and ambiguity into a world built around military prowess, AFK asks what happens when masculinity refuses to play by the rules. Watch Full Video Here.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the project ‘Una Storia Italiana’. Rivas Bao revisits the story of Imane Fadil, an Italian-Moroccan model and aspiring sports journalist who became a key witness in the trial surrounding Silvio Berlusconi’s infamous ‘Bunga Bunga’ parties. After testifying about the exploitation of young women at his private residence, Fadil died in suspicious circumstances in 2019, aged just 34. Combining archival material, photographs taken inside Fadil’s Milan home and AI-generated imagery, Rivas Bao reconstructs the images that were described in court but never visually documented. Reclaiming the visual language of Berlusconian television and propaganda, the project assembles a counter-narrative from the fragments of a national memory still reluctant to confront its own Me Too moment.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘The Stars That Don’t Look Back’. Drawing on intimate memories shared by three generations of women in Taiwan, Chen weaves together family photographs, historical archives and literature to explore how women's lives are shaped by the forces of history. Against the backdrop of Japanese colonial rule and the White Terror, the project examines how women were represented, remembered and often silenced, from restrictions on personal appearance to the private narratives preserved in family albums. Moving between the political and the deeply personal, Chen traces the quiet resilience passed down through generations, finding in women's shared memories a fragile but enduring sense of belonging and inner peace.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘CLICHES’. Growing up in Morocco means inheriting a wealth of stories, sayings, stereotypes and beliefs that shape how we see ourselves and the world around us. Through staged photography blending documentary references, symbolism, fashion and fiction, Nassereddine Anjar revisits these familiar narratives, transforming them into images that sit between recognition and questioning. Approaching them as a living archive of shared memory, he explores the tensions between tradition and modernity, myth and everyday life, and the contradictions of a generation negotiating its relationship with heritage.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘We Too Have Wings’. Growing up between places, Hajo returns to memories of his grandmother’s house outside Khartoum, where he watched pigeons take flight and find their way home. Having witnessed both the revolution and the war in Sudan before leaving once again, he now reflects on displacement from Doha, where the project was made. Through images of family, places and everyday life, he explores whether home is somewhere we return to, or something we learn to carry and rebuild within ourselves.

Brewed Reflections: The Poetry of Ataya.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘Brewed Reflections: The Poetry of Ataya’. Introduced to Salam by his uncle during childhood, Ataya, a West African tea ritual, becomes a way to reconnect with personal roots and a wider sense of belonging. Beyond the preparation and sharing of tea, these gatherings create space for conversation, debate, laughter and simply being together. In a world increasingly shaped by digital connection and individualism, Salam sees this collective ritual as a quiet form of resistance, celebrating the value of physical presence and the bonds that emerge when people take the time to gather.

If life is a video game, the graphics are great, but the plot is confusing and the tutorial is way too long.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘If life is a video game, the graphics are great, but the plot is confusing and the tutorial is way too long'. Taking Elon Musk as both subject and symbol of our age, Cedric Zellweger examines the contradictions of hyper-consumption, technological utopianism and the fantasies of global elites. Through elaborate still lifes staged with hundreds of objects and photographed on large-format analogue film, he assembles a surreal visual commentary on contemporary politics and late-stage capitalism. Part satire, part dystopian spectacle, the project draws on everything from space exploration to meme culture to ask who gets to shape our collective future, and whether it is one we actually want.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘TRANSFER’. For twenty years, Tan lived in their parents’ apartment while keeping their queer identity invisible. Now, they revisit the space as both a home and a departure lounge, a place to which they remain tied but from which they have long felt the need to escape. Through self-portraiture, the apartment becomes an imagined airport transfer station, suspended between belonging and elsewhere. In Chinese, zhuǎnjī (转机) means both “transfer” and “chance”: a small linguistic coincidence that captures the possibility of departure, transformation and a different beginning.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Sake of Our Resistance’. Through portraits of family, friends and collaborators in Togo and its diaspora, Delali Ayivi explores resistance as an everyday practice rooted in community, creativity and mutual care. Beginning with a familiar story of an orange shared among an entire family, the project traces a belief in collective resources and responsibility across generations. Women’s organisations, village initiatives and the work of hairdressers, designers and sculptors become expressions of a quiet persistence. Accompanied by reflections from ten Togolese voices, the series asks what resistance can look like when protest is not always possible, and how simply sustaining one another can become an act of defiance.

GENESIS, WE WERE TRYING TO BUILD A HOME.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘Genesis, We Were Trying to Build a Home’. Drawing on her experience of growing up in the foster system, Mikhailia Petersen explores displacement as both a physical condition and something carried within the body. Through self-portraiture, performance and ritual, she returns to her relationship with her mother, inherited wounds and the histories of land and belonging in Cape Town. Menstrual blood, flowers, fire and water become materials for mourning and renewal, as Petersen confronts the legacies of colonialism, apartheid and intergenerational trauma. Rather than seeking to erase the past, the work asks how a sense of home might be rebuilt from what remains. Watch Full Video Here.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project Praxis Modulus, by Ayomide Tejuoso aka Plantation. Spanning photography, film, installation and performance, the work constructs a contemporary Black mythology through the visual languages of Ifá, fashion imagery and African American aesthetic philosophies. Blue recurs throughout as a symbol of death, sacredness and liminality, shaping a world populated by self-portraits and portraits of other Black figures. Drawing on the visual practices of Fred Moten and Arthur Jafa, Tejuoso develops an unsettling visual universe where beauty, ritual and decadence converge, confronting the violence of necro-capitalism through acts of image-making and resistance.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Of Animals and Us’. Over the past four years, Irina Werning has visited agricultural fairs and livestock reveals in Argentina and the UK, searching for moments when people and animals seem to mirror one another. Groomed, judged and admired, they become unlikely participants in what the photographer describes as a Darwinian theatre of look-alikes. Behind the humour lies a more uneasy reflection on our relationship with animals: some share our homes and daily lives, while others remain out of sight until they reach our plates. Through images that invite a second look, Werning explores the growing distance between humans, animals and the landscapes they once shared.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the photographic project ‘Muñecas & Muñequerxs’. In its first chapter, set in Guanajuato, Mexico, Silvana Trevale explores the tradition of cartonería, the art of transforming paper and paste into figures used in play, ritual, satire and devotion. Working alongside local artisans, she documents the knowledge passed down through generations while reinterpreting familiar customs through contemporary questions of identity, gender and race. From the ceremonial destruction of Judas figures to the reinvention of a quinceañera ritual through a trans woman, the project reveals how traditions can become spaces of both preservation and resistance, continually reshaped by those who keep them alive.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Loose Fist’. Following a violent homophobic attack in his hometown of Kathmandu, Arhant Shrestha began photographing men as a way to confront the fear and mistrust he had developed. What started as an exercise in exposure gradually became an inquiry into masculinity, intimacy and the possibility of connection. Through portraits and staged encounters with strangers and former classmates, Shrestha revisits the codes of male friendship, aggression and tenderness that shaped his own adolescence. In proposing care as an alternative to militarised masculinity, the project traces a personal journey from isolation towards a sense of community.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of ‘5BFW — 5 Bocas Fashion Week’, a project by Natasha Ribas and Allan Weber that brings fashion into the streets of Rio de Janeiro’s favela of 5B, placing its residents at the centre of the story. Local men with no previous modelling experience become the faces of a campaign that challenges conventional ideas of beauty, style and who gets to occupy fashion imagery. Designer clothes meet gold chains, scapulars and personal belongings, set against the textures of everyday life. Conceived as an unprecedented event for the community, the project uses fashion as a tool for visibility, self-recognition and the reimagining of a place too often seen through the eyes of outsiders.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘What If We Lived Among Gods?’. Dammy Twitch brings African deities into the everyday settings of contemporary Nigeria, imagining a world where the spiritual and the mundane exist side by side. Each image places a different god or goddess within familiar surroundings, challenging the distance that modern life has created from ancestral belief systems. Part visual theology, part cultural reclamation, the series insists that African spiritual traditions have not disappeared, but continue to shape the present. Rather than looking back with nostalgia, Twitch invites viewers to recognise the divine in ordinary life and reconsider what has been inherited, forgotten and kept alive.

This photograph is part of the series 'Hypnagogia'. Drawing on the fleeting state between wakefulness and sleep, Myles Loftin uses fashion photography to build a world where imagination takes the lead. Playful styling and dreamlike imagery explore the shifting boundaries between consciousness and the unconscious, softness and masculinity, fantasy and reality. With a sense of childlike wonder, the series embraces the strange freedom of the hypnagogic state, creating space for dreaming in a world that increasingly leaves little room for it.

good girls go to heaven, bad girls go wandering.

In a recent development, this excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘good girls go to heaven, bad girls go wandering’. Developed in collaboration with poet and artist Ranu Ritamalan through fieldwork across Indonesia, Brandon Lopez’s project follows lives lived outside the expected milestones of family, marriage and belonging.
