Moving between photography, speculative essays, poetry and string figures, the work questions how social structures shape our sense of time, direction and purpose. Its subjects include a monkey navigating Jakarta’s formal economy and a traffic officer observed through the rhythms of a single intersection. Here, wandering becomes a form of refusal: a way to imagine what might emerge beyond the destinations society sets for us.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘New Order’. From the perspective of a young adult raised on pacifist and diplomatic ideals, Louis Roth documents Europe’s shifting relationship with militarisation amid a new arms race. Combining NATO exercises, military parades and official events with quieter scenes of everyday life, the project observes how military and civilian worlds increasingly overlap. Beginning in the Baltic states and expanding across Europe, Roth explores the ambivalence surrounding this transformation, known in Germany as Zeitenwende. His restrained visual language resists military spectacle, using photography to question how a new political reality gradually becomes part of everyday life.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘NORA’. Photographing her sixty-year-old friend, Bettina Pittaluga explores ageing as a process of continual transformation rather than disappearance. Through playful, intimate portrait sessions, the two revisit the many faces Nora has inhabited and those still to come. Against a visual culture increasingly devoted to smoothing wrinkles, erasing grey hair and concealing the passage of time, the project embraces the body's capacity for change, desire and reinvention. Made together as they grow older, the series remains open-ended, allowing identity to shift with every encounter.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘The Garden’. Made between 2020 and 2026, Ville Varumo’s work traces the unsettled feeling of living between a former home and a new city, caught between the desire to escape and the longing to put down roots. Through quiet observations of streets, strangers, nocturnal facades, a recurring white dog and, eventually, the artist’s newborn, seemingly unrelated moments begin to form a personal visual diary. Moving between public and private spaces, the photographs find the extraordinary in the everyday, reflecting on home as something continually built, lost and reimagined.

According to recent reports, this excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘No Man’s Wedding’. Through a twisted, symbolic wonderland, Carolina Dutca and Valentin Sidorenko explore the experience of war using the archetypes and rituals of folk narratives. Their story follows a man going to war as a groom approaches his wedding, descending into an underworld where he attempts to outwit death. Shells, soil and baptismal imagery become ambiguous symbols of passage, faith and mortality. Rather than documenting conflict directly, the artists draw on the language of fairy tales to examine the existential questions that war leaves in its wake.

...The Candle Whispered Them Here.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘...The Candle Whispered Them Here’. Through analogue and tintype photography and photographic sculpture, Delali Cofie imagines an archive for Ghanaian folklore, giving stories a physical place to endure. Five figures from Ghanaian history and mythology, including Anansi, Yaa Asantewaa and Okomfo Anokye, find refuge in everyday household objects, transformed into vessels for collective memory. Blending the intimacy of oral storytelling with the permanence of photographic objects, Cofie reflects on what happens to stories as they fade from memory, and how the rituals of sharing them might keep them alive.

Recent findings suggest that this excerpt is part of the video project ‘Fireworks on the Swamp’. Begun in 2013 and completed in 2020, Sergei Prokofiev’s work emerged from a period of political disillusionment and growing social tension in Russia. Conceived as an attempt to make art outside the expectations of the market and institutional system, the project uses pyrotechnics in a desolate, swamp-like landscape to evoke an atmosphere of hostility and uncertainty. Developed over seven years, it reflects on the limits of artistic interpretation and the possibility of experiencing reality directly, before it settles into a coherent narrative. Watch Full Video Here.

According to recent reports, this excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘The Boat’. Over two years, Stein Henningsen pushed an old traditional wooden boat through winter landscapes, rowed it across open water and drift ice, and eventually set it alight in front of a glacier. Bringing fire and ice into direct confrontation, the performance turns the boat into a striking image of our relationship with the natural world. Part of Henningsen’s ongoing exploration of elemental forces, the work confronts the paralysis that often accompanies awareness of the environmental crisis, inviting viewers to experience the fragile balance between human life and the forces of nature. Watch Full Video Here.

This photograph is part of Elizabeth Haust’s "All About Loneliness", an evolving collection of images connected by an interest in magic, ritual, solitude and the body. Moving between self-observation and fiction, Haust treats photography as a way to give shape to experiences that resist straightforward expression. Ordinary spaces become stages for private ceremonies, while gestures and objects take on symbolic meaning. Together, the images form an intimate emotional archive, exploring vulnerability, desire, isolation and the invisible systems of belief we build to make sense of being alive.

Industry observers note that this excerpt is part of the film ‘STARE’. Created by Bijoy Shetty in collaboration with designer Bhavya Ramesh for Bhavya Ramesh Jewellery and NorBlack NorWhite, the work explores the female form beyond the limits of expectation. Moving between softness and rage, vulnerability and strength, the film embraces femininity in its extremes, drawing on the mystical as a space for release and self-acceptance. Watch Full Video Here.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘The Holy Mountains’. Bringing together the mountains of Mexico’s Chiapas highlands and the Swiss Alps, Diego Moreno creates a fictional landscape where two seemingly distant cultural worlds become mirrors of one another. Through photography, collage and graphic intervention, he draws on ancestral myths, folk tales and religious traditions to explore the ways identity is shaped by territory, colonisation and cultural mixing. The result is a personal mythology in which folklore becomes a way to revisit inherited histories and imagine new ones.

This photograph is part of the ongoing project ‘Everything I Want to Tell You’. Through a weekly exchange of images, videos and shared fantasies, Sadie Cook and Jo Pawlowska trace the ways class, illness, migration, gender and sexuality leave their marks on the body and everyday life. Moving between personal archives and staged scenes, their collaboration builds an ever-expanding visual world where memory and desire blur. Presented through large-scale installations of thousands of images, the work captures identity as something continually unsettled, taken apart and reassembled.

A bit more yellow, a bit more sour...

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘A bit more yellow, a bit more sour...’. Through portraits of friends and family, Eszter Sárkány explores the complicated relationship younger generations have with Hungarian traditions, caught between the desire to reconnect with their cultural roots and the need to distance themselves from their political appropriation. Rather than turning away from the past, she looks for ways to reinterpret it, finding in familiar rituals and symbols room for personal expression, autonomy and new forms of belonging. As Hungary enters a period of political transition, the series shifts from anger towards a more open-ended reflection on what might come next.

Please pierce your bones into mine.

This photograph is part of the prokect "Please pierce your bones into mine", dedicated to the artist’s great-aunt, Jacoba Manders. Despite a 71-year age difference, the two shared a bond that felt more like friendship than family, becoming a way for the artist to reflect on ageing, intimacy and the experience of saying goodbye. Through images that hold both Jacoba’s history and the artist’s imagined future, the work considers what passes between generations beyond material inheritance. What remains is an emotional legacy of tenderness, resilience and truth, quietly shaping the lives of those who carry it forward.

This excerpt is part of the video installation ‘Afterparty’. In a vast desert landscape, fifty figures repeat familiar routines: gambling, scrolling, digging holes, burning books, practising yoga. Gabriel Barcia-Colombo imagines a world after collapse in which the spectacle may be over, but everyday life carries on as if nothing has happened. Structured around three pillars of contemporary life, knowledge, connection and leisure, the triptych examines our growing dependence on technology and the systems that shape what we know and believe. In its final moments, the figures turn towards the viewer, extending an invitation to join the party, or recognise we never really left. Watch Full Video Here.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Touch’. Drawing on Alexis Kleshik’s own experience of sex work and queer life, the series explores the relationships that take shape between friends, lovers, clients, coworkers and chosen family. Working collaboratively with those they photograph, Kleshik moves between spontaneous encounters and staged scenes, using humour, styling and performance to create images grounded in agency and shared imagination. Beyond conventional definitions of intimacy, ‘Touch’ celebrates the forms of tenderness, play and belonging that emerge when people are free to define their own connections.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the project ‘The Journey Home’. Working with young people connected to four local NGOs in South Africa, Laura Pannack explores the daily journey to and from school as a space of friendship, independence and self-discovery. Through workshops, cameras change hands and participants become active image-makers, documenting their own experiences alongside the photographer. Combining analogue photography, drawings, collage and cyanotypes, the project builds a collective portrait of a generation navigating volatile environments, told through the humour, spontaneity and shifting perspectives of those who live it.

Recent findings suggest that this excerpt is part of the video project ‘KAPULUAN’. Rooted in the ancestral knowledge and ecological traditions of the Philippine archipelago, Gab Mejia brings together the voices of 700 Indigenous and frontline community members across 18 regions. Co-created with Indigenous women, queer youth leaders and local artists, the four-part film series weaves oral histories, poetry and traditional dance into a collective vision of Filipino identity. Against the backdrop of climate collapse and cultural displacement, ‘KAPULUAN’ becomes an act of remembrance and resistance, looking to ancestral wisdom for upcoming ways of imagining the future. Watch Full Video Here.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Nebulous’. Born in Upcoming York to a family from Istanbul, Devin Oktar Yalkin has long experienced belonging as something split between places, shaped by migration, memory and distance. Bringing together black-and-white photographs made across different years and locations, the series traces the emotional imprint of a home that can no longer be returned to as it once was. Water, recurring throughout the images, becomes a passage between departure and return, familiarity and estrangement. Rather than documenting a place, Yalkin follows the traces it leaves behind, wherever he goes.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series "Ghosts Follow Us", exploring the spirits and changing landscapes of Isaan, northeastern Thailand. Through analogue photography, the artist documents a culture in which ghosts inhabit banyan trees, rice fields and everyday rituals, shaping the relationship between people and the natural world. Yet another kind of haunting runs through the images: an uncertain future, as shifting weather patterns unsettle generations of agricultural knowledge. Focusing particularly on the children who will inherit this changing landscape, the series captures a place suspended between ancestral beliefs, ecological loss and the passage of time.

The Architecture of Guāi (乖與不乖之間).

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Architecture of Guāi (乖與不乖之間)'. Returning to his former primary school in Taiwan, Adam Lin revisits the culture of discipline and obedience that shaped his childhood. At the centre is guāi, a Mandarin word used to praise children for being well-behaved and compliant. Through workshops with current students, Lin turns the classroom into a space for playful disruption, where everyday objects, gestures and postures become tools to challenge institutional rules. What emerges is a collaborative portrait of the tension between conformity and the freedom to imagine otherwise.

POR FAVOR, NO TE VAYAS / PLEASE, DONT LEAVE.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Por Favor, No Te Vayas / Please, Don’t Leave’. After years in New York, Andrés Rios returned to Bogotá to photograph the city he grew up in and the people who make it home. Through portraits of friends, familiar streets and everyday encounters, he captures a place marked by uncertainty and contradiction, yet sustained by creativity, warmth and a sense of community. At its heart is a tension between the impulse to leave and the desire to stay, finding hope in the small, collective acts of building a life together.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Down There’. Across Mississippi, Sophia Cutino documents the networks of lesbian communities creating spaces for love, care and self-determination amid a climate of religious conservatism and anti-LGBTQ+ legislation. Through intimate 35mm portraits and handwritten notes, the project moves between private homes and shared spaces, allowing women to shape how their lives are seen and remembered. Rather than centring hardship, Cutino focuses on the everyday acts of connection, creativity and belonging through which these communities make a life on their own terms.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Newly introduced Paris’. Begun when he was just seventeen, Adali Schell’s project grew out of a period of family upheaval and grief, following his move from Southern California to his mother’s hometown in rural Ohio. Turning his camera towards friends, relatives and neighbours, he builds an intimate portrait of a community through its living rooms, bedrooms and backyards. What begins as a personal record gradually opens onto a wider picture of contemporary America, where economic hardship, loss and social neglect are woven into the fabric of everyday life.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘One Day I am gonna be a man’. Jonas Glanz examines looksmaxxing, an online culture of male self-optimization in which attractiveness is measured, ranked and endlessly corrected. Drawing on its visual language, from rating scales and before-and-after images to grooming routines and idealized masculine figures, he stages the male body as both an object of desire and a project under constant construction. Moving between fashion photography, still life and video, the work exposes the contradictions of a pursuit in which self-improvement becomes discipline, performance and an ideal that can never quite be reached. The photograph, 'False Adam' highlights a young man among apple trees, crowned with golden laurel, an artificial snake wound around his arm. In looksmaxxing, "True Adam" names the highest rank of male beauty, an ideal no one reaches. The biblical Adam is the first to feel shame about his body.

This photograph is part of the series ‘I Hope Your Family Is Safe’. After nine years abroad, Anya Tsaruk returned to Ukraine to document the lives of her loved ones during the war. Rather than focusing on destruction, she turns her attention to the quiet moments of everyday life: gestures of care, familiar places and the closeness of family and friends. With tenderness and restraint, the series reveals how ordinary experiences take on upcoming meaning under the constant threat of war, offering a portrait of Ukraine grounded in human connection rather than distant spectacle.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Rotting from Within’. Beginning at seventeen, when he reconnected with his estranged father, Abdulhamid Kircher turned to photography to make sense of his family history and his own Turkish heritage. Combining portraits, candid observations, archival material and personal writings, he traces the generational trauma passed down through the men in his family, confronting the myths of masculinity, violence and inherited identity. Part autobiography, part visual investigation, the work explores how photography can help us approach the people closest to us, even when their histories remain partly unknowable.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Mannequins’. Using taxidermy as an unexpected departure point, the artist examines sculptural form within narrative imagery to reflect on aging, inherited femininity, and the labor behind entertainment. Moving between taxidermied figures and intimate portraits of herself and her mother, the work draws a piercing parallel between preserved animal specimens and the expectations placed on young women in Hollywood: rendered pristine, suspended in time, and meticulously packaged for consumption. Part conceptual study, part personal inquiry, the series interrogates the artifice of beauty and the cost of eternal preservation.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘The Moon in Your Throat’. Asking what happens to the grief swallowed in pursuit of success, the work depicts Koreans living across the United States seated inside darkened homes, illuminated only by the faint glow of refrigerators, screens, and digital clocks. Through long-exposure portraits, contemplative still lifes, and family-photo collages, the artist explores how displacement, collective history, and unresolved emotion physically inhabit the body. Guided by the Korean concept of Han and Jung’s archetype of the shadow, the series creates a quiet space for collective mourning, asking what transformative healing might emerge when buried sorrows are finally permitted to surface.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Room 房间’. Drawn from the artist’s life lived between Chengdu and Latest York, the work gathers tender glimpses of friends, lovers, and intimate, familiar interiors. Originally published as their debut photobook in 2025, the series functions as an architecture constructed entirely through imagery and deliberate pairings, tracing how the concept of home gradually evolved from a fixed physical location into a portable emotional state. Part visual diary, part spatial meditation, the photographs reflect on transience, connection, and the quiet spaces we assemble within ourselves to belong.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Effigy of Man’. A decade after his passing, the artist’s grandfather endures in family photographs as a revered, often feared patriarch—a strict, orthodox figure whose temperament was indelibly forged by his displacement from Multan to Haryana during the 1947 Partition of British India. Through studio portraiture and physical collage, the artist directly intervenes in these inherited portraits to challenge dominant codes of masculinity embedded in family archives. Part reckoning, part tender excavation, the work unpicks the myth of the unyielding patriarch, suggesting that one must dismantle the monument of a man in order to truly see him.

MY HEAD IS A DESERT FULL OF TULIPS.

This photograph is part of the series ‘MY HEAD IS A DESERT FULL OF TULIPS’. Conceived as an ongoing photographic universe suspended between reality and fiction, the work captures subjects suspended in media res, leaving their relationships, histories, and interior motives deliberately unresolved. Through recurring gestures, shared hairstyles, synchronized clothing, and uncanny everyday scenarios, disparate people and landscapes begin to rhyme and echo across frames, building a fractured, collective realm. Part cinematic daydream, part surrealist taxonomy, the series distills the tension between isolation and kinship, showing how easily the familiar can tilt into the strange, the intimate, and the absurd.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Ohnmacht’. Exploring the visceral experience of losing control over one’s body—a state of profound helplessness—the work captures women collapsing inward, where the tactile softness of their clothing clashes against stark, unforgiving environments to lay bare the weight of feminine expectations. Drawing from archival imagery of Victorian fainting spells and histories of mass hysteria, the artist uses shifting warm and cold light to expose the contradictory faces of disempowerment: fragile beauty, desperate cries for help, and latent resistance. Part psychological study, part quiet protest against patriarchal structures, the series gives tangible, enduring form to a silent exhaustion known intimately by women across generations.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Puerpera’. Born from the artist’s own birth trauma and the amnesia that enveloped the hours immediately following labor, the work offers a visceral exploration of a profound, near-universal threshold in womanhood: the disorienting stillness that arrives right after giving birth. Through intimate imagery, recorded conversations, and contemplative reflection, the series attempts to reconstruct an emotional landscape so intense, fleeting, and overwhelming that memory itself often fractures. Part personal catharsis, part raw maternal record, the project gives voice to the unspoken shock and tender vulnerability of early postpartum, reclaiming a physical reality too often eclipsed by silence.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘Neti È Kon’. Translating into "The Night is Coming," the work documents nocturnal portraits and nocturnal scenes across Suriname, capturing the enigmatic spirit of the evening through the cultural cadence of its local dialect. Imbued with a quiet intimacy where darkness evokes memory and longing, the photographs examine the subtle sensory elements that trigger a sense of belonging, redefining home not as a fixed geographical border, but as an emotional construct carried within. Part cultural ode, part lyrical meditation on displacement and longing, the series reveals how the twilight hours can bridge distance and resurrect familiar worlds.

Sources indicate that this video is part of the series ‘Hands, trees, heads, scars’. Conceived as a tender meditation on care, active listening, and hope, the work examines the fragile geography of skin and scars among amputated Ukrainian soldiers undergoing rehabilitative massage therapy in Lviv. Continuing their long-term research into relational dynamics within healthcare, Alberto Gottardo and Francesca Sironi quietly observe the gestures of solace exchanged between international practitioners and recovering servicemen like Sergei and his peers. Part clinical witness, part intimate humanitarian tribute, the series captures the quiet dignity of recovery, demonstrating how touch can transform sites of violent trauma into spaces of profound resilience and connection. Watch Full Video Here.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Reconfigurations’. Conceived as an unbound portfolio of black-and-white figure studies, the work deliberately unsettles classical conventions of nude photography. Employing a split-field diopter, the camera folds the human form back onto itself, dissolving the boundaries between nearness and distance, the sensuous and the grotesque. Across eighteen loose, unsequenced prints, the project invites the viewer to touch, reorder, and physically recompose the imagery, transforming passive spectatorship into tactile engagement and leaving both the anatomical body and the act of looking open to endless reconfiguration.

This photograph is part of the series ‘D,D&D’. Framing the examination of one’s own life as an intentional act of role-play, the project stages an alliterative rite of passage where subconscious dreams and primal drives are confronted to forge inner strength. Moving through the shadow worlds of darkrooms and the grit of dirt, the artist harnesses photography to declare vulnerability while demanding personal power—meeting internal demons, owning forbidden desires, confronting and reshaping paternal lineage, and learning to dance with fear rather than submit to it. The series chronicles years of dedicated discipline and ritual transformation, insisting that one can actively draw destiny rather than remain doomed to it.

This photograph is part of the series ‘I owe you’. Approaching physical and emotional pain not as an isolating affliction but as a shared human threshold, the project considers discomfort as an unexpected site for connection, cooperation, and mutual care. Combining still photography and moving image, the artist studies how individuals navigate enduring suffering through subtle physical gestures, repetitive daily routines, intimate healing rituals, and collective support practices. Rather than fixating on the sensational depiction of hurt, the work investigates the quiet architectures of trust and vulnerability that emerge when bodies rely on one another through dependence, tenderness, and shared endurance.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Joyless Sex’. Chronicling the quiet desolation of intimacy unmoored from desire, the work lays bare the unvarnished realities of clandestine side hustles, the claustrophobia of lingering in rooms with lovers already outgrown, and the fragile currency of relationships alternately discarded and desperately preserved. Photographed across Paris and Fresh York from 2018 to the present day, the series captures the raw friction between loneliness and physical proximity in modern metropolises. Part unflinching diary, part contemporary social record, the images excavate the silent compromises, hidden transactions, and enduring vulnerabilities that shape life behind closed apartment doors.

Crossing the River by Feeling the Stones.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Crossing the River by Feeling the Stones’. Rooted in a concealed bodily experience from childhood, the project charts an intimate investigation into personal desire, latent fantasy, and emerging sexuality. Moving through a tender, playful, and deliberately clumsy visual navigation, the artist traces the fluid transformations of desire as it encounters migration, displacement, and restless curiosity. The project completely reimagines the female form, liberating the body from the confines of conventional gazes and reclaiming it as a sovereign territory of exploration and self-possession.

That Moment When You Can See The Crack In The World.

This photograph is part of the series ‘That Moment When You Can See the Crack in the World’. Using the human body as mutable raw material, the work navigates the terrain of metamorphosis, queerness, and the porous boundary separating conventional beauty from monstrosity. Within this altered universe, reality becomes elastic and physical forms are liberated from prescriptive aesthetics, recasting the deemed "abnormal" not as an aberration, but as a fertile site for radical reimagining. The series celebrates physical disruption as a portal, exposing the fissures in our rigid societal architecture to glimpse alternative ways of being.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘Near’. Bringing people, bodies, and everyday objects into unexpected physical configurations, the work allows familiar forms to dismantle their everyday functions and take on radical latest possibilities. By deliberately loosening the rigid grip of established social identities, inherited norms, and conventional values, the artist constructs an open, liminal space of encounter. The series invites the individual to step beyond prescribed ways of being, creating a rare clearing where one might encounter the self—and the other—entirely anew.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘Self-Portraits of No One’. Begun in 2013 prior to the artist’s gender transition, this ongoing photographic archive utilizes their own body as both subject and canvas across domestic interiors, untamed landscapes, and staged performances to interrogate identity, visibility, and physical metamorphosis. Resisting the tidy impulse of a linear transition narrative, the work approaches self-portraiture as a radical assertion of agency—reclaiming complete visual authorship over how the evolving body is documented, perceived, and remembered. The series reflects on the fluidity of becoming, demonstrating that the self is an open, ever-shifting horizon rather than a fixed destination.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘Dublin Girls’. Exploring contemporary Irish girlhood through portraits captured across the artist’s hometown, the project is intimately rooted in her lived experience as an older sister and young Irish woman navigating sisterhood, identity, and the tender, quieter thresholds of coming of age. Moving beyond reductive cultural stereotypes and performative notions of femininity, the work captures its subjects in unvarnished authenticity, preserving an essential archive of what it feels like to discover and inhabit oneself in modern Dublin. The series celebrates the quiet resilience, vulnerability, and kinship forged on familiar streets.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Muted Ember’. The project observes younger generations navigating life in contemporary China as economic uncertainty fractures the long-held promise of steady upward mobility. Through quiet portraits and observational scenes, the work captures the quiet anxieties, disillusionment, and resilience of youth confronting a rapidly shifting social reality. Part generational portrait, part contemporary document, the series examines the tension between inherited aspirations and an uncertain future.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘Sacrilegio’. Using constructed photography, the project reinterprets standard biblical imagery through the lens of modern Mexico and its northern border. By blending sacred iconography with popular culture, the work explores how religious symbols mutate when confronted with realities of violence, gender, and territorial power. Rather than challenging faith, it captures the living, breathing contradictions of contemporary devotion.

Anna Göldi: Memoria di una Strega, Rituale di Restituzione.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Anna Göldi: Memoria di una Strega, Rituale di Restituzione’. The project stems from the historical tragedy of Anna Göldi, navigating the distance between archival records and the enduring resonance of her myth. Moving between reality and imagination, the imagery opens a symbolic space of restitution where her presence and memory can be reclaimed and told anew.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘Fade into you.’. Combining original photography with subtitle stills drawn from popular media, the work uses cropping, sequencing, and visual treatment to detach familiar imagery from its initial context. Reconstructed into an altered narrative, the series examines how meaning degrades, shifts, and transforms as it circulates through systems of cultural reproduction.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Set in Stone’. The work captures the tender, fleeting connections found in daily life, grounding delicate emotions into permanence by printing the imagery directly onto stone. By anchoring transient intimacy to an unyielding surface, the series suggests that even the softest feelings leave enduring traces, holding a weight and memory that outlast time itself.

This video is part of the series ‘tranSformarse’. Moving from the safe enclosure of early beginnings to the inevitable compulsion to shed one’s skin, the work serves as an ode to blooming out of step, in one's own authentic hues. By leaving behind inherited expectations to embrace the painful, miraculous nature of metamorphosis, the series stands as a vital reminder that to truly inhabit the world is, at its bravest, a lifelong act of self-transformation. Watch Full Video Here.

EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me).

This photograph is part of the series ‘EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me)’. Created by Alcira Angelo, the project is an intimate photographic odyssey that explores self-discovery through the emotional and psychological terrain of duelo—a concept evoking both inner struggle and the reckoning that follows loss. The work unfolds as a visual dialogue with the self and others, constructing a quiet yet insistent collective portrait of grief and resilience.

This photograph is part of the series ‘My friend, Whisky’. The project chronicles the eight-year creative bond between photographer Fee-Gloria Grönemeyer and her muse and collaborator, Whisky Boonjongrux. Having developed multiple photographic dialogues together that consistently push both toward new creative horizons, the series stands as an intimate reflection on artistic trust, mutual growth, and the quiet courage required to be wholly oneself.

This photograph is part of the series ‘UNCOOL’. A study in visibility, embodiment, and representation, the project brings together twenty-seven portraits of individuals with disabilities and visible physical differences. Informed by the artist’s lived experience as a wheelchair user, the work examines how bodies are perceived, categorized, and normalized through imagery, critically questioning which bodies are granted visibility, under what conditions, and through which prevailing visual conventions.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Matriphagie’. The project investigates how societal structures transmit and internalize prescribed norms of femininity from an early age. Structured around interviews and encounters with young girls aged four to eleven, the work uses their testimonies—balancing between learned clichés and instinctive transgressions—to ground a visual inquiry into the ambivalences, tensions, and shifting definitions of the feminine.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Look at me like you love me’. Informed by the artist’s identity as a queer, nonbinary individual, the work explores the complexities of personhood, desire, intimacy, and family. Motivated by an existential search for self-understanding and human connection, the project centers on the radical necessity of living authentically and the mutual power of seeing and being seen, using intimate storytelling to invite viewers into deep reflection on their own identities and relationships.

It has been revealed that this photograph is part of the series ‘t-fags’. Bringing together photographs and interviews with trans men, transmasculine, and non-binary people who identify with the reclaimed term ‘fag’, the project explores masculinities that openly embrace femininity and gender expansiveness. By challenging heteronormative expectations around gender transition, the work documents a community asserting radical self-definition. Created between 2022 and 2025, the series was self-published as a limited-edition artist book in 2026, serving as a vital archive of contemporary queer identity.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘People’. Built on friendship, attraction, and creative collaboration, this ongoing portrait project actively reclaims who is pictured as desirable and who holds the authority behind the lens. Centering disabled subjects through the perspective of a gay, disabled photographer, the work employs nudity, fashion, and playful experimentation to capture beauty infused with sexual confidence, humor, and unfiltered desire.

I Love My Friends But They’re Killing Me.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘I Love My Friends But They Are Killing Me’. The project examines contemporary beauty standards and their psychological toll through portraits of young Indian women navigating micro-celebrity—influencers, reality television figures, and aspiring actors pictured inside their private bedrooms and homes. Shot primarily on 35mm film with harsh direct flash and framed by episodic, reality-TV-style text, the work strikes a deliberate tension between cultural critique, intimate vulnerability, and biting absurdity.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Cut from the Street’. The project examines hair as a medium of self-expression, identity, and resistance among young men across north and central Chennai. Through portraits and interviews, the work interrogates how caste, class, skin tone, and urban geography dictate who is granted social legitimacy and visibility. Highlighting how identical aesthetics celebrated as fashion on privileged bodies are condemned as “indecent” or suspicious on others, the series reveals everyday styling as an act of defiance—a vital claim to presence and the right to be seen.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘TOPS’. Extending the world of the companion short film, the work gathers intimate moments captured before, during, and after production to trace the profound physical and emotional journey of top surgery. Through quiet, behind-the-scenes glimpses, the collection documents the urgency of gender-affirming care, the essential networks of community support that sustain it, and the deep vulnerability that shapes the path toward embodied self-realization.

The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back.

This photograph is part of the series 'The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back', a project that explores the Gullah Geechee corridor as a landscape of memory, survival, and spiritual continuity. Drawing on a Gullah proverb and the Bakongo cosmogram, the project examines water as both rupture and return—marking histories of the Middle Passage while sustaining cultural resilience. Through photographs of the Low Country, the work considers how Geechee communities navigate displacement, climate change, and enduring ancestral presence.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Who’s Afraid of the Bad Wolf?’. Documenting the bedroom as the foundational universe of childhood, the work explores a space where solitude, play, and resilience are first tested, and where fantasy and reality seamlessly coexist. Centered on the intimate bedtime rituals invented by children to cultivate safety and ward off fear, the ongoing archive right now traces the private domestic worlds of eleven children across Piedmont, Italy.

Recent findings suggest that this photograph is part of the series ‘An Anatomy of Fear’. Reflecting on fear as a collective condition shaped by uncertainty, instability and the accelerating pace of contemporary life, Alvaro Deprit explores the fragile territory between identity and transformation. Through images of unfinished clay and plaster sculptures, alongside the students who inhabit the art school where the work was made, he draws a parallel between bodies and forms in the process of becoming. Adolescence emerges as a particularly charged moment of this transition, when identity remains fluid and the boundaries between vulnerability and possibility are still being negotiated.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘Thoughts, Feelings, Behaviour’. Begun in 2024, the project employs staged photography to interrogate narcissistic self-image, emotional isolation, and the alienating demands of the capitalist attention economy. Exploring the fraught boundary between self-sufficiency and raw vulnerability, the work navigates currents of desire, aggression, and melancholy. Through an experimental synthesis of body paint, collage, and sculptural props, the imagery blurs the lines between lens-based practice, painting, and tactile material experience.

Industry observers note that this photograph is part of the series ‘Ọ Hụrụ M’—translating to “She Saw Me” in the artist’s native tongue, Igbo. Conceived as an intimate dialogue across her past, present, and future selves, this self-portrait project treats the camera lens as both a transformative portal and an unbound playground. Navigating life as a young Nigerian woman raised in the United States, the artist claims absolute authorship over her representation. Standing firmly as both creator and subject, she transforms self-imaging into a sovereign act of agency, radical ownership, and resistance against cultural erasure.

Rose Sarajevo: Girls from the East.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the series ‘Rose Sarajevo: Girls from the East’. Weaving together portraits of young women, local architecture, and surrounding nature, the project traces the enduring scars of conflict across an urban landscape under quiet reconstruction—most visibly marked by the “Sarajevo Roses,” mortar damage filled with red resin to memorialize fallen lives. Guided by fragmented memories, the artist undertakes an intimate quest for the origins of her own identity, using photography as an act of personal and historical reconciliation, an attempt to mend and bridge the fractures of time.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Home Story’. Combining documentary and staged photography, the project unearths fragmented, visceral narratives within a space fundamentally promised as a sanctuary: the domestic home. Acknowledging the difficulty of articulating trauma into daily reality, the work interrogates how patriarchal structures isolate survivors of domestic violence into silenced, individualized tragedies. By confronting the quiet complicity of institutional secrecy, the imagery functions as an act of disclosure—insisting that giving voice to these hidden experiences dismantles the systemic machinery that thrives on their suppression.

Sources indicate that this photograph is part of the series ‘Scarlet Spirit’. Grounded in the enduring legacy of the 1947 Partition of India, the project traces the artist’s familial migration through ancestral memory and oral histories gathered across Kolkata’s refugee colonies. Synthesizing contemporary portraits, archival material, and surreal visual metaphors, the work constructs a layered archive of displacement that interrogates severed roots, cultural erasure, and collective resilience. Created in resonance with the milestone commemorations of Partition, the series links generational trauma and the arduous labor of rebuilding to the broader, ongoing realities of global displacement today.

The Drying Leaves: A Domestic Cartography Initiative.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Drying Leaves : A Domestic Cartography Initiative’. Set beneath the ancestral neem tree of Suktara, the work adopts the seasonal descent of winter leaves as a poignant metaphor for the passage of time and human mortality. Through a three-dimensional visual approach that weaves together photography, family archives, and spoken histories, the initiative maps intimate domestic geographies to resist alienation and stave off the "third death"—the quiet disappearance that occurs when a person’s name is spoken for the very last time.

Everything I Am or Have Since Become.

In a recent development, this video is part of the series ‘Everything I Am or Have Since Become’. Centering on the elemental nature of water as a metaphor for queer safety—at once life-giving sanctuary and volatile peril—the project weaves together collective oral histories, writings, and movement developed collaboratively with an all-queer cast and crew. Created by diasporic artists navigating New York City in resistance to systemic precarity, the work follows three figures across aquatic terrains in ritualistic choreography. Through sustained cycles of grief, repetition, and bodily rebirth, the series meditates on the search for refuge in hostile environments, embodying the fluid, precarious nature of both sanctuary and identity. Watch Full Video Here.

In a recent development, this photograph is part of the project ‘Driving License’. Exploring an online subculture where people buy and sell photographs of other people’s faces to use as their own, Lean Lui examines the shifting boundaries between identity, ownership and authenticity in the digital age. Through a three-month investigation in which she actively participated in these transactions, Lui explores how a face can become a commodity, a disguise or a fresh identity altogether. The work questions what it means to be seen, and whether an image can stand in for a person who does not exist.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Mixed / Unmistakably You’. Created by Norwegian-Indian artist Dev Dhunsi, the project takes the artist’s own mixed heritage as an inquiry into the nuances of cultural and personal identity. In a society where language lacks a direct term for mixedness, the work pairs photography and text to articulate experiences that have long remained unnamed. Interrogating how belonging, visibility, and intimacy are mediated by race, gender, and desire, the series constructs a luminous visual vocabulary for self-definition beyond existing cultural lexicons.

According to recent reports, this photograph is part of the series ‘Constructed Portrait’. In an era marked by frictionless image oversaturation, the project investigates the blurred boundaries between the tangible and the synthetic. Confronting the extractive reality of digital photography—where personal images are systematically harvested as training data for artificial intelligence—the artist restricts the source material strictly to their own intimate photo archive. By algorithmically synthesizing and deconstructing these personal traces into a self-portrait, the work deploys technology against itself, functioning simultaneously as an ethical data citation, a formal technical critique, and an enduring act of self-reflection.

In a recent development, this video is part of the series ‘Nox’. Drawing from Rio Nakada’s lived experiences of complex PTSD, dissociation, and Alice in Wonderland Syndrome, the work translates internal psychological instability into an embodied sensory environment. Through fractured memories, shifting architectures, mirrored reflections, and visceral bodily distortions, the imagery renders an otherwise invisible, disorienting mental landscape spatial and tangible. Selected for the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, the project functions as an intimate bridge between isolation and communion, inviting the viewer into a briefly shared architecture of altered perception. Watch Full Video Here.

We Knew the World in Fragments of Color.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Knew the World in Fragments of Color’. Reflecting on the personal journey of migration from Venezuela to the United States, the project explores the dislocating experience of diaspora, cultural belonging, and the fractured nature of memory. Through meticulous staged compositions and handcrafted wearable constructions, the work harnesses heightened chromatic symbolism to reconstruct a displaced home, transforming personal nostalgia into a vivid, allegorical visual language.

Meet the international jury of Brave Fresh Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, bringing together artists, photographers, editors, curators, and creative voices from different disciplines and backgrounds. Together with the Vogue and Condé Nast Committee, comprising more than 100 editorial and creative professionals from across our global brands, these jurors have brought their individual perspectives and sensibilities to the selection process. Their participation reflects something fundamental to PhotoVogue's philosophy: there is no single authority on what makes an image meaningful, no universal definition of beauty, and no one way of seeing the world. It is through the encounter of different perspectives that new possibilities emerge.

Photographer, Filmmaker & Curator.

Recent findings suggest that born in Addis Ababa in 1974, Aïda graduated from Howard University with a degree in Communications, majoring in Film. Her photography is in major collections including MoMA, the Smithsonian, and the RISD Museum. She’s received numerous awards, including the EU Prize in Bamako, the CRAF Award, and the Royal Photographic Society Award. Aïda co-curated the Nobel Peace Prize exhibition in 2019 and was a commissioned artist in 2020. A Canon ambassador and founder of Addis Foto Fest and Africa Foto Fair, she also leads Africa Print House and advocates for health, the environment, and photography across Africa.

According to recent reports, alex Consani is a model and actress who was named 2024 Model of the Year at the Fashion Awards in London, becoming the first transgender woman to receive the award. A face of Gucci and YSL Beauty, she has graced the digital cover of American Vogue and made history as one of the first transgender women to walk the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Her acting credits include American Horror Story: 13 and A24’s upcoming film Peaked.

Curator, Founder & Artistic Director, Culture Art Society (CAS).

Awa Konaté is an independent curator, cultural strategist, and founder of Culture Art Society (CAS), a platform dedicated to research, exhibitions, and critical discourse on African and diasporic visual arts. Her practice draws on archival research, Black feminist pedagogies, and memory work, with a focus on interdisciplinary and lens-based practices by artists of African descent. She has collaborated with institutions including Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, Serpentine Galleries, Raven Row, and the Barbican, and served on juries for Rencontres de Bamako and BlackStar Film Festival. Her writing has appeared in Third Text, Foam Magazine, and Phaidon, among other publications.

Director, Foto Colectania (Barcelona).

In a recent development, elisa Medde is an Art Historian specializing in Photography and Visual Culture, focusing on image, communication, and power structures. She has chaired juries for awards like the Luma Rencontres Book Award and MAST Foundation Grant. Elisa collaborates with European universities including ECAL, HSLU, and UWE Bristol. She has curated photobooks and exhibitions, with writings in FlashArt, Time Magazine, Vogue Italia, and more. Editor-in-Chief of Foam Magazine (2012–2023), she won two Lucie Awards and received the 2023 Royal Photographic Society Award for outstanding achievement in Photography Publishing.

Global Head of Photography, The Guardian.

Fiona has over 20 years of picture editing experience across newspapers and is a curator, speaker on photojournalism, and mentor in the photography community. She was picture editor of The Guardian for ten years before becoming Head of Photography for Guardian News and Media Group. Fiona covered major historic events like 9/11, global conflicts, natural disasters, and refugee crises. She has judged awards including the Sony World Photography Awards, Taylor Wessing Portrait Prize, and chaired the 2024 World Press Photo Awards jury. Fiona also serves on the board of Stills Gallery, Edinburgh.

Florence Bourgeois has been Director of Paris Photo since 2015. With a background spanning fashion, luxury, and the art world, she previously held positions at Givenchy Parfums, Artcurial, and the Pavillon des Arts et du Design (PAD) in Paris and London. At Paris Photo, she has introduced initiatives including PRISMES, Emergence, and Elles x Paris Photo, developed in partnership with the French Ministry of Culture and Kering’s Women In Motion to increase the visibility and recognition of women artists. She has also overseen the fair’s international expansion in Los Angeles and New York and championed the acquisition of works by women artists through institutional partnerships. Actively involved in the photography ecosystem, she serves on numerous juries and commissions, supporting emerging talent and contemporary photography. In 2023, she was awarded the title of Officière des Arts et des Lettres by the French Minister of Culture.

Performance Artist & Choreographer.

Recent findings suggest that florentina Holzinger is an Austrian performance artist and choreographer whose work spans dance, theatre, and opera, exploring the limits of the body through extreme physicality and theatrical experimentation. Her practice challenges the boundaries between high culture and counterculture, spectacle and subversion, often incorporating body modification and a wide range of body-based disciplines. Her productions have received the Nestroy Award for TANZ (2020) and the Faust Award for Ophelia’s Got Talent (2023), and have been selected four times for Theatertreffen Berlin. Since 2021, she has been an associate artist at Volksbühne am Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz in Berlin. In 2026, she represents Austria at the 61st Venice Biennale.

Freelance Writer, Host, Brand Consultant, The Messy Truth Podcast.

In a recent development, gem Fletcher is a writer, consultant and podcaster. Her work has been published in Foam, Aperture, Dazed, Creative Review, 1000 Words and The British Journal of Photography. She also hosts The Messy Truth podcast, a series of candid conversations that unpack the future of visual culture and what it means to be a photographer today.

Artist, Stylist & Creative Director.

In a recent development, ib Kamara is a Sierra Leone-born artist, stylist, and creative director known for his daring, interdisciplinary approach to fashion image-making. Raised in Gambia and educated at Central Saint Martins in London, he served as Editor-in-Chief of Dazed from 2021 to 2025 and Creative Director of Off-White from 2024 to 2026. His work spans editorial and commercial collaborations with artists including Beyoncé, Rihanna, Madonna, and Rosalía, and brands such as Chanel, Louis Vuitton, and Gucci. A contributor to international editions of Vogue, AnOther, and i-D, his work has been exhibited at Somerset House, Red Hook Labs, and the Victoria & Albert Museum. In 2021, he received the British Fashion Council’s Isabella Blow Award for Fashion Creator.

Stylist, Creative Consultant & Fashion Editor.

Imruh Asha is a Paris-based stylist, creative consultant, and Fashion Director of Dazed, where he has been part of the team since 2021. Drawing on his Dutch-Caribbean roots and contemporary art, he brings a concept-driven and interdisciplinary approach to fashion image-making. Since his appointment as Fashion Director in 2022, he has pushed the boundaries of fashion imagery through ambitious collaborations, including projects that have broken three official Guinness World Records. In 2021, he presented Future Shock, his first sculpture exhibition, in collaboration with the Ere Foundation at Dover Street Market’s 3537 space.

Global Creative Director, Vanity Fair.

Sources indicate that jennifer Pastore is an award-winning visual storyteller with more than two decades of experience shaping the imagery of leading magazines and cultural institutions. She is currently the Global Creative Director of Vanity Fair Magazine and previously held roles as the Visuals Director of Sotheby’s Magazine and the Executive Photography Director of WSJ. Magazine, where she commissioned photography, film, and illustration. Earlier in her career, she held roles at Harper’s Bazaar, Teen Vogue, and T: The Newly introduced York Times Style Magazine. In 2022, she was awarded the Rome Prize in Design by the American Academy in Rome.

Recent findings suggest that photo Director, Artist & Curator. Former Director of Photography, The New York Times Magazine.

Kathy Ryan was the longtime Director of Photography at The New York Times Magazine, where, over 39 years, she pioneered the integration of fine art photography and photojournalism, collaborating with leading photographers and championing new talent. She edited The New York Times Magazine Photographs (Aperture, 2011), which inspired an international touring exhibition, and is the author of Office Romance (Aperture, 2014), a collection of photographs made entirely on her iPhone. Since leaving the Times, she has focused on her own photographic practice, curating exhibitions, teaching at Yale, and speaking internationally. Her numerous accolades include the Royal Photographic Society Award for Outstanding Service to Photography (2012), the International Center of Photography's Spotlight Award (2024), and the Dr. Erich Salomon Prize (2025).

Visual Journalist, Researcher & Curator.

Recent findings suggest that kira Pollack is a creative director and photo editor pioneering visual storytelling through photography, technology, and digital media. A 2025 Walter Shorenstein Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School, she explores AI’s role in preserving visual history. Formerly Creative Director at Vanity Fair and Director of Photography at TIME, she led iconic projects including The 100 Most Influential Photographs and TIME’s first documentary film unit. Pollack’s work earned Emmy, Lucie, Webby, and National Magazine Awards. She has served as a juror for World Press Photo and Tribeca Film Festival and is based in New York City.

Founder & Creative Director, Be Good Studios.

According to recent reports, lina Kutsovskaya is a creative director whose work bridges fashion, art, and advertising. She has led influential campaigns including #MyCalvins at Calvin Klein and creative collaborations with Virgil Abloh at Louis Vuitton. After beginning her career at Vogue, she held creative leadership roles at Nylon, Teen Vogue, Barneys New York, and Calvin Klein, before founding Be Good Studios, a creative agency working across campaigns, brand identity, publishing, and exhibition-making. From 2024 to 2026, she served as Art Director of Another Man, and in 2025 was appointed Contributing Creative Director of Vogue Japan. She is also the founder of Little Massive Man, a gallery and publishing project based in Los Angeles.

Melissa Harris is Editor-at-Large at Aperture Foundation, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of Aperture magazine from 2002 to 2012, earning the publication a National Magazine Award for General Excellence. During her more than twenty years at Aperture, she edited over forty photography books and curated exhibitions internationally. Her curatorial projects include Mary Ellen Mark: Encounters (2023–2024), A Kind of Language at Fondazione Prada (2025), and a retrospective of Graciela Iturbide’s work at C/O Berlin (2026). She has taught at Yale, Columbia Journalism School, and Latest York University, where she has been part of the Tisch School of the Arts for twenty years. She is also Creative Director of Magnum Foundation’s ongoing US Dispatches / Time Capsule project.

Writer, Art Curator & Professor, Newly introduced York University.

Industry observers note that nicole R. Fleetwood is a writer, curator, and professor at Upcoming York University, as well as a MacArthur Fellow and elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. She is the author of Marking Time: Art in the Age of Mass Incarceration, which received the 2020 National Book Critics Circle Award, as well as On Racial Icons and Troubling Vision. Her curatorial projects have been presented at institutions including MoMA PS1, Aperture Foundation, the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, and the Brown Arts Institute. Her work has received support from leading cultural and research institutions, including the Mellon Foundation, Ford Foundation, and New York Public Library’s Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers.

US Head of Photography, The Guardian.

Recent findings suggest that noelle Théard is a photographer, educator, and the US Head of Photography at The Guardian. Previously, she was Senior Photo Editor at The Upcoming Yorker, where she also produced Photo Booth, the magazine’s photography column. Her work focuses on social justice, community engagement, and the intersection of education and visual storytelling. She co-founded FotoKonbit, a nonprofit empowering Haitians to tell their own stories through photography, and has held roles at Magnum Foundation, Parsons, and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Miami. She has also taught African Diaspora and Art History at Florida International University.

Member of the Board of Directors, Friends of Palais de Tokyo.

Olivia Anani is a Paris-based curator, writer, and art market expert with a background in Asian Studies and Contemporary Art. She has worked at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips, contributing to the sale of major masters and the reevaluation of African artists. Olivia serves on the Board of Friends of Palais de Tokyo and leads its Young Patrons initiative. She supports institutions like the Louvre and is involved in developing a new cultural institution in Benin. Anani has contributed to major monographs and was named among France’s 100 Most Influential Women in Culture in 2021.

Co-founder & Editor-in-Chief, Atmos.

Willow Defebaugh is the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Atmos, an award-winning climate and culture magazine that seeks to re-enchant people with our shared humanity and the Earth. She is the author of The Overview, a deep ecology newsletter and book, and host of The Nature Of, a podcast from Atmos. She is a lifelong student of nature and graduated with a degree in creative writing from the University of Michigan. Her work has been featured in Vogue, Harper's Bazaar, Teen Vogue, V Magazine, Interview, i-D, BBC, The Guardian, Them, Latest York Magazine, and more. She lives in Brooklyn on unceded Lenape territory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that celebrities have taken over the liquor store, with everyone from rappers to actors to athletes launching their own bottles. And the section with the most star power is definitely the wine aisle.

Sources indicate that whether they own their own vineyards or simply slap their names on a label, celebrities sell wines from almost every corner of the world. To see whether any of them are worth the A-list endorsements, we tasted a selection of their most popular red wines. Here are the ones that won over Delish editors.

Cameron Diaz's wine brand, Avaline, specializes in bottles made with organically farmed grapes and minimal additives. Avaline's red blend is made in France with Rhône varietals like Grenache and Syrah.

According to recent reports, our editors appreciated its light- to medium-bodied flavor and bone-dry finish. Notes of red fruit and light spice add just enough depth to keep each sip interesting. And at $24 per bottle, this is a solid table wine that tastes much more expensive than it is.

Reality TV legend Lisa Vanderpump is no stranger to the food and beverage business. In addition to operating six restaurants, she’s also the mind behind her eponymous wine brand. And LVP’s Sonoma County Cabernet Sauvignon is as elegant and sophisticated as she is.

While other Cabernets can be bold and intense, this wine's beauty lies in its subtlety. One editor described it as a “summer Cab” because of its soft, delicate fruit profile. The flavor is complex without feeling too rich or heavy, making it an ideal red for dinner. And at $26 a bottle, it’s a good deal, too.

Sources indicate that famed film director Francis Ford Coppola isn’t just known for his Oscar-winning movies—he’s also a prolific winemaker. He sold his namesake winery to Delicato Family Wines in 2021, but the lineup is still just as strong as it was under his leadership.

Recent findings suggest that we enjoyed all of Coppola’s reds, but the Archimedes Cabernet Sauvignon was a clear standout. Made with California-grown grapes and aged for 20 months in French and American oak barrels, this wine delivers what our editors described as the quintessential Cab, with a full-bodied, smooth flavor and notes of dark fruit and tobacco.

Industry observers note that depending on the vintage and retailer, prices can start around $70 and climb past $100. But if you want to impress both the film buffs and wine snobs in your life, it’s worth the splurge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Recent findings suggest that whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

According to recent reports, turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

It has been revealed that arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

More difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

Newly introduced in this patch: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

Recent findings suggest that food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

There are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

According to recent reports, the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Good Grips 3-Piece Silicone Utensil Set.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

What we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No.

Sources indicate that what we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

In a recent development, once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

According to recent reports, if crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

In a recent development, if steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Industry observers note that whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

In a recent development, A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

The same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

According to recent reports, with five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That said, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

In a recent development, high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

It has been revealed that not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.
