In a recent development, for those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Industry observers note that whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

In a recent development, transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Sources indicate that drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honestly, we can’t think of anything better than a galette. They've got all the delicious elements of pie—flaky, buttery crust and tender baked fruit—but none of the fussy technique. With galettes, you don’t have to worry about any crimping, latticework, or blind baking. Sometimes, it's okay to take the easy road. This classic apple galette is one of our favorite examples. Warm, comforting, and bursting with sweet, spiced flavor, it’s everything you love about apple pie with a fraction of the effort.

What People Are Saying:“I've already made this twice. Really really nice recipe. So fast and simple, not too sweet and not at all goopy. This will be my go-to filling for apple galettes from now on.” - PurpleRing.

Recent findings suggest that first, combine the apples, brown sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon, and salt in a large bowl. Then, preheat the oven to 400° and prepare a baking sheet by lining it with parchment paper. Coat a clean surface with a dusting of flour, then roll the chilled pie dough into a 12” circle that is about ⅛” thick. Transfer the dough to the baking sheet.

It has been revealed that arrange the apple slices on top of the dough in alternating rows, leaving about a 1 ½” border around the edge. Then, fold the dough edge nearest to you toward the center and rotate the baking sheet, repeating this step until all 4 edges of the dough are folded in toward the fruit.

According to recent reports, brush the egg wash over the crust and sprinkle demerara sugar over the top. Then place the galette into the oven to bake for 40 to 45 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the fruit is fragrant and tender. Remove the galette from the oven and transfer it to a cooling rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Industry observers note that A galette is essentially an open-faced pie. Thinly sliced apples are tossed in cinnamon and sugar and layered on top of a single sheet of pie crust. The crust is folded over the apples in a rough circle and baked until the crust is flaky. Apple pie has a top and bottom crust and is usually formed in a pie dish. The extra crust and overall shape are the only real differences, and for the apple obsessed, galettes provide the perfect ratio of crust to filling.

Anything you'd serve with an apple pie would work here as well. That means your favorite ice cream, frozen yogurt, caramel sauce, or candied nuts would be great galette sidekicks.

Any leftover galette can be stored for up to 4 days in the refrigerator.

When the Polish jewelry designer Natalia Kopiszka was planning her August 2026 wedding to actor Aleksander “Olek” Kaleta, she found herself at a bridal fashion crossroads, stuck between two stylistic pillars of her own brand: vintage and modern.

It has been revealed that first, the Warsaw-based designer of Kopi traveled to Paris to shop for a vintage wedding dress, but returned home empty-handed. “I didn’t find anything that I liked, so I thought: I will design my own wedding dress,” Natalia indicates.

For the body of her ceremony dress, she ordered fabric—silk taffeta—from Etsy. “I was on a mission to find the absolute dream silk fabric,” she indicates. “I started by checking out local fabric shops and silk wholesalers, but I just couldn't find the right silk taffeta with that delicate, subtle sheen anywhere.” She searched online and stumbled upon a listing from a New York-based seller, which she ordered on the spot. Luckily, “it turned out to be even more breathtaking in person than in the photos,” she says.

Then, on a weekend trip to Amsterdam with a friend, she wandered into a vintage store where she found antique lace, which she used for the bodice detailing. “The lace is truly unique because it dates back to the early 20th century, and I only had a tiny piece of it—which happened to be just enough to trim the bodice,” Natalia notes. “It was such a special way to check off the ‘something old’ tradition.” She sketched the dress, then shared her designs with a dressmaker who sewed it, making her vintage-modern dream a reality.

According to recent reports, natalia and Olek first met in February 2021 at a house party in Warsaw. “For me, it was love at first sight,” Natalia recalls. “A friend of mine who lived in the apartment below me threw a get-together, and her roommate happened to be friends with Olek. As soon as he walked in, we instantly locked eyes. I’m pretty sure he was the one who came over and started the conversation first,” she adds. “It also turned out that Olek lived directly across the street from my apartment, so we used to wave at each other from our windows. Ever since that night, we started seeing each other almost every single day.”.

Recent findings suggest that after a year, they moved in together in Warsaw. In 2024, Olek proposed to Natalia during a trip to Italy, in the coastal town of Polignano a Mare. “It was a warm, romantic evening with a huge moon, and surprisingly, I didn't see it coming at all,” Natalia says. “It turned out to be such a sweet, funny moment because neither of us could stop laughing.”.

Recent findings suggest that on August 8, 2026, the couple held their wedding at Pałac Pstrokonie, a historic 19th-century palace in a small village outside of Warsaw. They worked with the wedding planner Kasia Fastyn, who brought Natalia’s vision—a romantic, whimsical wonderland of sorts—to life, pairing them with the event studio MyBigDay, who designed the florals and draped their dancing tent in pink fabric.

As a jewelry and accessories designer, Natalia zeroed in on all the details of her wedding looks from the beginning. She knew she didn’t want a traditional floral bouquet, for example, so she opted for a small silk bag in the shape of a bouquet from the Fresh York-based designer Camille Albertine, after finding her work on Instagram. Albertine custom-made Natalia’s bouquet purse in the same fabric as her dress. “Everyone was so surprised that I didn’t have a typical bouquet,” Natalia notes. “It’s versatile enough that I can wear it with everyday outfits. It’s going to stay with me for a long time, and I’ll even be able to pass it down through generations.”.

For her reception look, the bride changed into a dress by the Polish designer Magda Butrym, pairing it with an unexpected accessory: a crochet veil cap that her sister made. “It was a really simple dress, also silk, but I put something really crazy on my head,” Natalia says.

Natalia incorporated her own jewelry into the crochet cap-like veil, which was bedazzled with charms and pendants. “They are specially made charms with little lobster clasps so you can clip them onto the crochet work however you like. They’re gold-plated and feature Swarovski crystals,” Natalia says. (Charms are a signature of Natalia’s brand, she explains, so it was only fitting to work them into her bridal looks.) Her love of historical pieces, particularly from the Victorian era, inspired the final design, which included blue stones for her “something blue.” A look inspired by it is now for sale as part of Kopi’s “I Do” bridal line.

It has been revealed that the bride also made Olek a pocket square with the same vintage lace as her dress, so they were matching (and so he had “something old” as well). They completed their looks with wedding bands that Natalia designed. “Mine has a retro feel, crafted in gold and set with 12 small diamonds,” she states of the rings. “Olek went for a classic look—a simple, wide gold band with my nickname engraved on the inside.” Reflecting on the wedding months later, Natalia says: “Everything was perfect.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table. If you’re looking to take the classic from good to million-dollar-price-tag-worthy, then this is the recipe for you. My million-dollar mac & cheese is what happens when you decide to take basic mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy, crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food will take center stage on any table it hits.

Recent findings suggest that the cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese. For this million-dollar mac, I chose Pecorino Romano as my accent, but went slightly rogue with the other two and paired fontina and French raclette, which both melt well and have quite a bit of funk. French raclette is particularly great for a mac & cheese sauce since it becomes almost fondue-like when melted, giving you cheese pulls beyond your wildest dreams.

According to recent reports, the combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac. That remarked, if you absolutely can’t find them, you could try combining comté and Camembert or Gruyère and brie with the Pecorino to give you a similar result.

The crispy topping:With a dish as rich and creamy as this mac & cheese, a crispy, crunchy topping is key. Pre-toasting the panko in butter on the stove ensures a truly golden-brown, delicious topping, without the nail-biting broiler-watching session. Using a higher butter-fat European-style butter here (as well as in the sauce) brings additional richness, ensuring this million-dollar mac is as decadent as it should be. In testing, I found that the breadcrumbs on top of the mac didn’t brown much more when they were on top of the mac in the oven, but if you’re concerned about them getting too dark, you can always lightly tent the pan with foil.

The gold leaf topping is a fun way to cue the whole “million-dollar” thing, but it’s totally not necessary. Use it if you want, but don’t feel obligated!

In a recent development, storage:Any leftover mac & cheese can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave, covered, in 30-second bursts until warmed through or, if you have enough, in the oven in a covered ceramic dish.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

In a recent development, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Recent findings suggest that stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

It has been revealed that bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Brigadeiros are like a cross between fudge and Tootsie Rolls in truffle form. They're easy to make at home, and even easier to pop in your mouth.

As a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form. Brigadeiros have the familiar flavor and fudgy center of a really good chocolate truffle, but they’re even easier to make because they don’t require melting any chocolate. Everything happens in one small saucepan, and the only difficult part is waiting for the mixture to chill.

Brigadeiros start with a can of sweetened condensed milk, plus cocoa powder and butter. The butter is key to carrying the flavor of the cocoa powder and giving the bite-sized treats their signature soft bite. They end up as glossy little chocolate balls covered in sprinkles that taste halfway between a chocolate truffle and a piece of fudge: dense and chewy with a deep cocoa flavor and a center so creamy it nearly melts on contact.

Recent findings suggest that brigadeiros are Brazilian confections made by cooking a mixture of sweetened condensed milk, cocoa and butter until it’s thick. Once cooled, the mixture is rolled into bite-size balls. A Brazilian birthday party isn’t complete without a tray of brigadeiros, but they also show up at weddings, baby showers and holiday gatherings. Some cooks skip the rolling altogether and eat the soft mixture with a spoon, a style called brigadeiro de colher.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a small saucepan, combine the sweetened condensed milk, cocoa powder and butter. Cook, stirring constantly, on medium-low heat until the mixture is thickened, 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer the mixture to a medium bowl. Refrigerate it, covered, for two hours or until it’s firm enough to be rolled.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Shape the chilled mixture into 1-inch balls. Roll the balls in chocolate sprinkles.

According to recent reports, editor’s Tip: Rub a little butter on your palms before rolling, and grease them again every few balls. This will keep the mixture from sticking and give each truffle a smooth surface.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Industry observers note that keep brigadeiros in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Store them in paper candy cups or in a single layer separated by parchment so they don’t stick together. Cold brigadeiros get firm, so let them sit out for about 15 minutes before serving to bring back their soft, fudgy centers.

Brigadeiros last up to one week in an airtight container in the refrigerator. They taste best within the first few days while the sprinkles are still crisp.

Yes, you can make brigadeiros ahead of time. Cook the chocolate mixture up to two days in advance and keep it covered in the refrigerator, then roll and coat the truffles the day you blueprint to serve them. If the mixture is too stiff to scoop, let it stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes.

Yes, brigadeiros freeze well. Arrange the rolled truffles on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them until they’re firm, about one hour, then transfer them to an airtight container and freeze them for up to three months. Thaw them overnight in the refrigerator.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Recent findings suggest that when the brigadeiro mixture stays soft and sticky even after chilling, it almost always means that it needs more time on the stove. Scrape it back into the saucepan and cook it over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for a few more minutes until it thickens and pulls away from the bottom of the pan in one mass. Watch the mixture closely because overcooking will turn it stiff and grainy.

It has been revealed that no, brigadeiros won’t work with regular milk. Brigadeiros depend on the concentrated sugar and milk solids in sweetened condensed milk to cook down into a thick fudge that can be rolled. If you’re out of it, you can make your own sweetened condensed milk by simmering whole milk and sugar until the mixture reduces by about half.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable.
  • The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • In a recent development, it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

In a recent development, it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

It has been revealed that while this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

But getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

According to recent reports, this is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an notable role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

Industry observers note that I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Industry observers note that smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

Want to treat yourself to five-star brunch without making a ton of dishes—or taking off your pj’s? Hack the classic croque madame by making it in the air fryer. Here, crispy toast is topped with an egg and smothered with ham, cheese, and béchamel for a simpler version of the classic French dish that will transform the comfort of your sofa into a fancy brunch spot in five seconds flat.

How is this a croque madame?A classic croque madame is a toasted ham and cheese sandwich that’s topped with a layer of béchamel, broiled until bubbly, and then topped with a fried egg. This air fryer version takes all those components—toasty bread, fried egg, béchamel, ham, and cheese—and reconfigures them into a form that cooks much easier in the air fryer. You might say it almost looks like a classic egg-in-the-hole, but don’t worry! If you close your eyes, you’ll still taste croque madame.

According to recent reports, the microwave béchamel:There’s nothing wrong with making béchamel in a pot on the stove, but making it in the microwave means fewer heavy dishes to clean—and it’s also a great hack to know if you’re somewhere with limited (or no!) stove space. Rather than standing over a pot, whisking constantly, you’ll simply whisk the flour into the melted butter, microwave until it’s bubbling, then whisk in the milk and microwave again. Once it’s thickened, you can fold in the cheese. Though I don’t recommend microwaving after the cheese goes in—that’s a sure way to break your sauce—if it absolutely needs it, you can microwave it for very short bursts just till it melts together.

Industry observers note that delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

Make-ahead & storage:Once cooked, the air fryer croque madame should be eaten immediately. That said, the béchamel can be made 2 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator. I recommend gently reheating it before using. I typically do this in the microwave in 15-second increments, stirring in between—this prevents the sauce from breaking.

Sources indicate that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

It has been revealed that add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

In a recent development, add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Sources indicate that let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

According to recent reports, this is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

Whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

Kim and Khloé Kardashian’s Beauty Trip Didn’t Quite Go to Strategy—Here’s What to Know Before Booking Yours

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • On Wednesday’s episode of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, Koko and her close friend La La Anthony reminisced about their August 2025 trip to South Korea, where they enthusiastically availed themselves of the country’s advanced cosmetic treatments—with some less-than-desirable results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between the salmon sperm facials, the skin boosters, and the next generation of lasers, there’s plenty to pique the interest of the beauty obsessive in South Korea. So much so that vacations are increasingly being organized around visits to the dermatologist’s office. But how much is too much when it comes to our beauty itineraries? Just ask Khloé and Kim Kardashian.

On Wednesday’s episode of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, Koko and her close friend La La Anthony reminisced about their August 2025 trip to South Korea, where they enthusiastically availed themselves of the country’s advanced cosmetic treatments—with some less-than-desirable results.

“Kim and I came back deformed, you came back beautiful and the plane ride just made it so much worse,” Kardashian told Anthony, recalling how their post-treatment appearances had kept them holed up in their hotel room.

The Kardashians are, of course, well-versed in the world of aesthetics. Over the years, the sisters have been particularly candid about their experiments with everything from the vampire facial to regenerative skin treatments. But even for those with the world’s most sought-after dermatologists on speed dial, things don’t always go to strategy.

Recent findings suggest that while it’s unclear precisely which procedures the sisters underwent—photos shared on Kim’s Instagram at the time indicated her receiving facial treatments and an IV infusion—their experience raises some pertinent questions. How much research should we be doing before traveling abroad for cosmetic treatments? How many procedures can we feasibly—and safely—fit into a vacation? And how do we know when something has actually gone wrong?

The lure of a beauty vacation is understandable. South Korea, in particular, is at the forefront of aesthetic innovation, with technologies and treatments that aren’t yet widely available in the United States. And as our collective beauty literacy has expanded, so too has our appetite for more technologically sophisticated treatments. A facial no longer necessarily means an hour of extractions and massage. But there is a distinction to be made between a beauty treatment and a medical procedure. Just because something is marketed as minimally invasive, or requires no incisions, doesn’t mean it is without risk. Nor does its ubiquity on TikTok necessarily speak to its suitability for your own skin.

According to recent reports, “Traveling for treatment isn't the same as having unsafe treatment,” claims consultant dermatologist Dr. Sidra Khan. “What travel adds is complexity: a different regulatory system, possibly a language barrier, often a compressed consultation, and being thousands of miles from your practitioner during recovery.”.

It has been revealed that “A beautiful clinic, an impressive Instagram following and a gallery of celebrity clients don’t really tell you much about the practitioner’s medical credentials or what results you might expect,” adds cosmetic surgeon and aesthetics specialist Dr. Paul Banwell. Independently verify your practitioner’s qualifications and registration with the relevant medical regulator, and establish whether the clinic is equipped to manage complications. Khan recommends arranging a virtual consultation with the treating doctor before booking anything, and asking about their experience with your particular skin tone, the products and devices they intend to use, and why. “A holiday itinerary shouldn't replace informed consent.”.

It has been revealed that for London-based aesthetics and NHS doctor Dr. Alicia Gonzalez-Fernandez, the marketing of medical procedures as vacation packages is itself a red flag. “On a handful of occasions, I have encountered patients that have come into A&E straight from the airport,” she says of her experiences working in emergency medicine. She cautions against practitioners who pressure patients into additional procedures or fail to adequately discuss complications and aftercare. “We are not in the business of making people self-conscious about things that are not a problem for them.”.

In a recent development, then there’s the phenomenon of “treatment stacking.” While certain procedures can complement one another, squeezing several into a short period of time can increase the likelihood of complications. “Many of these treatments work by creating a controlled injury that the skin then repairs, and doing several close together doesn't give it time to recover,” explains aesthetics doctor Dr. Priya Verma. “That raises the risk of prolonged inflammation, infection and pigmentation changes, particularly in darker skin tones.”.

Multiple procedures can also make it harder to establish which treatment is responsible for an adverse reaction, notes aesthetics doctor Dr. Ahmed El Muntasar. “Ultimately, I’d much rather a patient’s treatment schedule was dictated by how their skin is recovering than by the date of their flight home.”.

Recent findings suggest that consider, too, how conducive the rest of your vacation itinerary is to your skin’s recovery. As Verma notes, the low humidity in airplane cabins can exacerbate dryness and sensitivity in already compromised skin, while sun exposure can increase the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. There is no universal rule about how soon you can fly after a non-surgical cosmetic procedure, says Khan, but you should allow ample time for recovery and an in-person review before your departure. (With surgical procedures, flying also carries an increased risk of blood clots, making a conversation with your surgeon about your travel prepares particularly vital.).

There's also the question of downtime. An unfortunate-looking reflection in the hotel bathroom mirror doesn’t necessarily mean a treatment has been “botched.” Verma makes an vital distinction: “Downtime is the expected redness, swelling or flaking that settles over a few days. Dissatisfaction is when the skin has healed but you're not happy with the result. A complication is a medical problem that needs treating.”.

Knowing what to expect—and for how long—is something to establish with your practitioner well before the treatment itself. The trajectory of your recovery is key: Increasing pain, spreading redness, heat, discharge, or fever warrant prompt medical attention.

Industry observers note that there are, however, symptoms that warrant immediate medical attention. Following dermal filler injections, for example, the FDA advises seeking immediate medical care for unusual pain, changes to your vision, white, gray, or blue discoloration around the injection site, or signs of a stroke. These may indicate that the blood supply has been compromised.

“If there are red-flag symptoms, don't just get on a plane because you'd rather deal with it at home,” stresses Khan. “Some complications are time-critical, so get seen locally.”.

Industry observers note that in non-emergency situations, contact your original practitioner for an in-person review and document your recovery with photographs taken in consistent lighting. El Muntasar recommends obtaining your full treatment records, including the names, quantities, and batch numbers of any injectables, or the device and settings used for laser treatments. Seek an independent medical opinion from someone experienced in managing complications if you remain concerned.

Recent findings suggest that as distressing as it can be to feel unhappy with your appearance, resist the temptation to immediately book another aesthetic procedure. “Swelling can make certain areas appear overfilled or disproportionate, and adding more filler to try to balance things out can leave a patient with an entirely different problem once that swelling subsides,” explains Banwell.

Industry observers note that “More treatment isn’t always the antidote to treatment,” indicates Khan. Anti-wrinkle injections can take around two weeks to reach their full effect, filler can take several weeks to settle, and collagen remodeling following laser treatments or microneedling continues for months. The same caution applies to overzealous at-home skincare. “Your freshly lasered face is not the moment to try the acids and retinoids you picked up at duty-free.”.

And while you might have meticulously mapped out your Seoul shopping itinerary, restaurant reservations, and dermatology appointments, have you given quite as much thought to what happens when you get home? Establishing a plan for follow-up care, obtaining a record of your procedures, and checking whether your insurance covers complications should all factor into the planning process. El Muntasar recommends getting your aftercare plan in writing, including details of who you can contact outside of clinic hours and who is responsible for any additional medical expenses should you need to extend your stay.

By all means, indulge your K-beauty curiosity. Just make sure you’re approaching your dermatological appointments with a little more discernment than your haul at Olive Young.

Wednesday isn’t typically a massive night for restaurants and bars—but the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is different. Most people have the next day off, and college students or young professionals are typically back in their hometowns for the holiday. What better way to kick off the long weekend than to get off your parents’ couch and hit up the local watering hole?

According to recent reports, that’s how Thanksgiving Eve came to be known as “Blackout Wednesday” or “Drinksgiving,” one of the busiest drinking nights of the year. A 2023 study found that in 2022, liquor sales grew by 156% and beer sales increased by 85% on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Cocktail orders surged by 69%.

DoorDash has even named the day one of the busiest for alcohol deliveries. Among 10 more traditional holidays like New Year’s Eve and July 4th, Blackout Wednesday ranks right in the middle. “As families and friends return home for the winter holidays, the day before Thanksgiving has become the fifth most popular day for alcohol delivery,” DoorDash’s website reads.

Going out in your hometown is prime time for idly snooping on people from high school, witnessing some truly unlikely pairings (Tyler and Kayla?!). It’s social and nostalgic, but it’s also a day when one drink can easily turn into one too many.

According to recent reports, it’s not all fun and drinking games, however. This unofficial holiday marks the start of so-called “DUI Season,” with checkpoints ramping up before Turkey Day. Your risk of coming into contact with a drunk driver also becomes 55% higher than on average days.

Recent findings suggest that short-term risks of heavy drinking and blacking out include vomiting, seizures, depression, and accidental injuries, as well as next-day anxiety and depression. Long-term, recurring binges are linked to liver damage, high blood pressure, and mental health issues. Alcohol-induced blackouts can also occur more rapidly after just a few drinks, especially if you are taking certain medications, drink on an empty stomach, or have a low body weight.

It has been revealed that it’s totally valid to blow off some steam (or get out of chopping celery), just plan it smart. With actually-delicious mocktails, non-alcoholic beers, and ride-shares, there’s very little reason to put yourself—or others—in danger, especially during the holidays.

Hosts and guests alike can benefit from making a strategy for keeping everyone safe until well after New Year’s Day by providing plenty of non-alcoholic options at gatherings, opting in on a “Dampsgiving,” checking in with loved ones (and designated drivers) before they hit the road, and always making sure there’s a spot on the couch for anyone who helped themselves to a few too many eggnog espresso martinis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.

It’s the morning after Thanksgiving. The good dishes are still drying, the fridge is a Tetris board of foil-wrapped leftovers and you’re standing over the kitchen sink eating cold stuffing with your bare hands. No plate, no judgment.

As it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience. It’s called Sinkie Day, and it’s been around since long before TikTok made girl dinner a thing.

For that, we have Norm Hankoff to thank. An advertising consultant from California, he had his lightbulb moment in 1991 “while wolfing down some tuna salad over his sink, using extra-strength potato chips as utensils,” according to a 1997 Associated Press report.

In a recent development, convinced he couldn’t be the only one, Hankoff founded the International Association of People Who Dine Over the Kitchen Sink and declared the day after Thanksgiving Sinkie Day. By 1997, more than 1,000 people had joined, and each one received a membership certificate stamped with a double sink and the group’s motto: “Everybody does it. Sinkies proudly admit it.”.

Naturally, there was a cookbook—or rather, a don’t-cook book. Published by a manufacturer cheekily called Digester’s Reader, The Official Sinkies Don’t Cook Book included such culinary masterpieces as “cakeless frosting” and “meat loaf in your fist.” Other recipes called for little more than a handful of mashed potatoes or a piece of chocolate cake dunked in a glass of milk.

Industry observers note that hankoff even set his sights on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. When Hillary Clinton was looking for a chef in 1994, he sent her a copy of his book and suggested the first family give sink-side snacking a try. No word on whether they took his advice, but the White House did send him a thank-you letter.

Industry observers note that the beauty of Sinkie Day, which falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, is that it’s perhaps the only food holiday that actively encourages you to do less. A fridge full of Thanksgiving extras is all it takes, though a few upgrades never hurt:.

Of course, a holiday devoted to leftovers is also a good excuse to brush up on food safety. As long as everything hit the fridge within two hours of cooking, you’ve got three to four days to work your way through it.

It has been revealed that are you a proud Sinkie? Let us know in the comments below!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

Industry observers note that the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

According to recent reports, "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Sources indicate that NASA's Voyager 2 probe introduced before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Sources indicate that voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

The close-up view revealed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

Recent findings suggest that while passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely latest avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker remarked. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

Recent findings suggest that by viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any significant craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker remarked.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

Sources indicate that some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker mentioned, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

According to recent reports, the mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

In a recent development, by 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

Recent findings suggest that in a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

Sources indicate that "We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

Recent findings suggest that we rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

It has been revealed that reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that I have a particular weakness for antique dishes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

Industry observers note that I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Sources indicate that then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

Ellie Martin Cliffe For Taste Of Home.

According to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

Moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He claims that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

In a recent development, for gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

This is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

According to recent reports, and if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

#134783. White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps.
  • Somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice.
  • The color comes down to a protein called myoglobin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps. There's Team White Meat, politely asking for "just a slice of breast, please." Then there's Team Dark Meat, already eyeing the drumstick like it's the last Pop-Tart in the box. It's basically Team Edward vs. Team Jacob, but with gravy.

Somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice. As a dietitian, I get asked about this a lot, especially the week of Thanksgiving. The short answer is that dark meat isn't the villain it's made out to be. The long answer is way more interesting, so grab a fork. Cranberry sauce optional.

The color comes down to a protein called myoglobin. Myoglobin stores oxygen inside muscle cells, and muscles that work steadily over long periods need more of it. On a turkey, that means the legs and thighs, which the bird uses to stand and walk around all day.

In a recent development, domestic turkeys use their breast muscles far less, so they carry less myoglobin and stay pale. Myoglobin contains heme iron, which matters for nutrition. More on that in a minute.

So when you choose dark meat, you're eating hardworking muscle. That changes its nutritional profile in a few notable ways.

Both cuts are excellent sources of protein. A 3-ounce serving of roasted, skinless turkey provides roughly 24 to 25 grams of protein, whether it's white or dark meat. White meat edges ahead by a gram or two, but in practical terms, both will do the job.

If protein is a priority, either cut gets you there. No need to stage a dramatic family intervention over the drumsticks.

Skinless dark meat does have more fat than skinless white meat, typically a few extra grams per 3-ounce serving. Some of that is saturated fat.

Recent findings suggest that context matters, though. The difference amounts to a few grams on a single plate, not a massive gap. Keeping the skin on also adds more fat to either cut. A slice of breast with crispy skin can end up in a similar ballpark to skinless thigh meat.

Saturated fat and heart health remain an active area of research. A Cochrane systematic review found that reducing dietary saturated fat was linked to a modest reduction in cardiovascular events over time. That finding reflects overall eating patterns across months and years, though, not what you eat at one holiday meal. A few extra grams of fat from turkey thighs won't make or break anyone's health.

Fat also brings flavor and moisture, which is why dark meat rarely turns into the dry, sawdust situation that can happen to an overcooked breast.

Remember myoglobin? Thanks in part to its heme iron, dark meat generally contains more iron than white meat. Heme iron, the type found in animal foods, is generally absorbed more efficiently than the non-heme iron found in plants.

In a recent development, that's meaningful, because iron deficiency is the most common cause of anemia worldwide. It's especially common among people who menstruate, pregnant people, and young children. Turkey thighs won't fix a deficiency on their own, but they can absolutely contribute to your overall iron intake.

Recent findings suggest that dark meat also delivers noticeably more zinc than white meat. Zinc plays a key role in immune function, wound healing, and taste perception. Not bad for the part of the bird some people skip.

This is where things get fun, because each cut has its own nutritional strengths.

These B vitamins help your body turn food into usable energy. Vitamin B12 also supports nerve function and red blood cell production, and B12 deficiency is more common in older adults and people who eat few animal foods.

Neither cut offers a complete B vitamin package on its own. Together, though? They make a pretty great team.

Industry observers note that not really. It's just different. White meat offers slightly more protein and less fat, plus more niacin and B6. Dark meat has more iron, zinc, and riboflavin, plus richer flavor and a juicier texture. Both provide vitamin B12.

Industry observers note that neither one deserves a "good" or "bad" label. Health is shaped by your eating patterns over time, not by which slice you pick from the platter on one Thursday in November.

It has been revealed that if you have a specific health condition, a registered dietitian can help you figure out what works best for you. For most people, though, the best turkey is the one you actually enjoy eating.

Pick the cut you love. Better yet, take a little of both. Dark meat isn't a nutritional compromise, and white meat isn't a punishment. They're two parts of the same bird, each with its own strengths.

According to recent reports, so go ahead and claim that drumstick. Or the breast. Or both. Your plate, your call. Just save some gravy for the rest of us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “There is and will always be only one Veruschka,” Richard Avedon wrote in the May 1972 issue of Vogue in an impassioned tribute to his muse. More than half a century later, his words still ring true. Since news broke of the German supermodel’s death at the age of 87, generations of fashion’s image-makers, designers, and models have been reflecting on her immeasurable influence.

A protagonist of some of the most fantastical fashion editorials ever committed to the pages of Vogue and a prolific cover star, Veruschka helped expand the possibilities of what a model could be. Her body was her artistic medium, her imagination as instrumental to the making of a photograph as that of the person behind the lens. Her creative curiosity would endure long after her heyday in the 1960s and ’70s, finding expression in her experiments with body painting and camouflage, her performance art, and her occasional, much-feted returns to the runway.

For those who knew and worked with Veruschka, though, there was as much to marvel at away from the camera: her generosity of spirit, quiet eccentricities, intellectual curiosity, and her sense of humor. In the tributes shared with Vogue below, fellow models recall their first encounters with a woman whose photographs once adorned their bedroom walls, while designers and photographers reflect on the creative communion they shared with her—and how rare a model like Veruschka is today.

It has been revealed that I am so sad to hear the news of Veruschka’s passing. When I started modeling in 1966, she was one of my idols—she was so beautiful and exotic. I had always wanted to meet her, and then in the 1980s, while I was appearing on Broadway in the musical My One and Only, a knock came on my dressing room door after the performance. I opened it and, to my surprise and huge delight, Veruschka was standing there. It was so lovely to finally meet her, and she was absolutely divine, and we chatted for ages. She certainly is one of the greatest of all models. RIP, beautiful lady.

Veruschka was an extraordinary artist that I was blessed to know. Thank you, Vera….

Recent findings suggest that I remember sitting in the library at Saint Martins, transfixed by the camouflage photographs in Veruschka: Trans-Figurations, the book she made with Holger Trülzsch. Years later, when I had the chance to work with her, I knew I wanted her to close my spring/summer 2011 show. We flew her in from Berlin and made her a bespoke dress for the finale. What I loved about working with her was how open she was to the ideas behind the collection and how wholeheartedly she embraced them. She was 71 and absolutely majestic on the runway. She had a presence unlike anyone else. A creative powerhouse and a true original.

In a recent development, being a model is an art form, and she was one of the people who truly mastered it. She had both creativity and respect for what she was doing. When we worked with her, she was incredibly impressive. There was an energy, a grace, and a lasting presence that you don’t see so often today. The lifespan of a model’s career seems to have become so much shorter. I sometimes wonder if, in the way the industry works today, we’re leaving less room for someone to become truly iconic.

It has been revealed that when I was a young girl, my bedroom walls were covered in photographs of Veruschka. To me, she looked like she had stepped out of another world—a dream I looked up to, one of the incredible women who had paved the way before me. I used to lie in bed, staring at those pictures, wondering what it would be like actually to know someone like her. Years later, that dream literally knocked on my door.

Recent findings suggest that we ended up living together at our agent Zoli’s house on East 63rd Street. For months, after a long day’s work, we would settle in for the evening with our sketchbooks. I can still see her drawing her little cats—curled up, stretching out, or peeking from the corners of the pages—while I sketched beside her. We didn’t need to say much; the quiet between us always felt so full.

Veruschka was always an enigma to me, a woman with a poetic soul and a nature I could never quite put a name to. She had a wicked little smile and a twinkle in her eye when she’d look up from her drawing, as if she knew a secret about the world she might someday share. Her voice was low and sensuous, and she was always kinder than anyone needed to be.

Sometimes, while watching her sketch, I would think back to that little girl staring at the pictures on her wall. I wished I could tell her that one day she would be sitting right beside her icon, and that Veruschka would be her friend. I have always loved Veruschka, and I always will. Knowing she taught me that dreams really do come true. She was mine.

It has been revealed that we’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

Culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the company is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

Sources indicate that the biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

According to recent reports, add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

This Clever Fork Trick Makes Slicing Cheese So Much Easier

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that as much as I love a major, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

Industry observers note that as much as I love a major, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

One of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

Start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

This trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.
