📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Body, Overcompensating, Off Campus… Just when you thought pop culture had reached peak teen drama, the streaming giants release another slew of bingeable shows to capture the hearts of Gen Z and Gen Alpha viewers, and upcoming audiences for their sponsors.

According to recent reports, taking the lion’s share of views at the moment is The Body, a coming-of-age psychodrama set in a Catholic school, which has promptly made its way into fashion fans’ For You pages. Just this week, the Netflix show has amassed 9.5 million views, marking its second week in the platform’s global top 10. It’s also at the moment the number one show in 39 countries.

Costumed by Mirren Gordon-Crozier, the series features iconic ‘00s designs, including the Dior Saddle bag, a Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette, a John Galliano-era “J’adore Dior” T-shirt, and various Juicy Couture accessories.

Industry observers note that fans have responded online, applauding the depth and details of the costuming. “This is why the Y2K clothing in The Body was so accurate,” reads one TikTok with 106,200 views. Another TikTok splices glamorous scenes from the series, showing significant sunglasses, velour tracksuits and flip-flops, soundtracked to Gwen Stefani’s 2004 hit, “Rich Girl” (257,000 views).

Sources indicate that “With a show set in 2004, the pieces had to feel real — not like a costume of the era,” says Gordon-Crozier, recalling that a lot was sourced vintage and last-minute finds in local Toronto thrift shops. “The ‘J’adore Dior’, the Juicy, the City bag, and the Murakami were the status language of those girls.” Since the show aired, Gordon-Crozier has received hundreds of messages on Instagram asking where pieces are from, along with compliments on the styling. “Y2K fashion was loud, optimistic and completely unembarrassed,” she says. “It was pre-Instagram, so there was no algorithm telling you what to wear.”.

True to the period, Gordon-Crozier even recreated tabloid clapback tees, including ‘Team Aniston’ and ‘Team Jolie’ tees for the identical twins Bailey and Britt Bradley. “That generation grew up on upcoming, flashy pop stars like Britney Spears, Paris Hilton and Christina Aguilera, who were all about excess and fun,” she adds. “Today, there’s so much curation. Quiet luxury I’m sure is a response to that in a way.”.

In a recent development, “Teen dramas have become Gen Z’s lookbook,” notes Rick Jackson, marketing agency Pion’s head of B2B content. “Unlike a traditional ad, a show places a product inside a character, and a lifestyle young people already aspire to.” As such, the City bag or the Juicy Couture tracksuit isn’t just shown, but lived, he explains. “Because Gen Z watches with their phone in hand, an outfit can go from screen to TikTok to checkout within hours,” he adds. This is a massive draw for brands, and arguably a far stronger marker of credibility than paid media.

Balenciaga’s City bags were sourced especially for the The Body.

In a recent development, many brands are wise to this already. H&M consistently ties its collections to Netflix youth hits, channeling the mood of each series into capsules: ’80s retro for Stranger Things, romcom prep for To All the Boys and bold retro looks for Sex Education. This consistency is key. Based on Pion’s recent report into Gen Zalpha (16-24-year-olds), cultural relevance needs ongoing presence in youth culture — on screen, through sport, music and movements — instead of a single, one-off moment.

Recent findings suggest that “Placement gives brands cultural relevance with a generation that’s sceptical of traditional advertising,” claims William Weeks, Pion’s chief marketing officer. On the primary market, he explains, interest converts fastest when there’s an accessible entry point. That might mean a discount, a dupe-friendly price point, or a smaller item from the brand. Merch can also fill this gap.

It has been revealed that but resale will reap the rewards first, experts agree. Luxury pieces can generate traction as resale offers young fans a way to tap into the moment at a fraction of the price. “For brands, these series are less about a direct ‘buy this exact item’ moment and more about spotting cultural momentum early,” states Sophy Vanner, a strategy partner at creative agency Amplify. “Often, secondary platforms get the first wave of demand because fans want the hunt and the specific reference point.”.

“The smartest brands play both,” states Weeks. “They win the cultural moment on screen and make it affordable for young fans to buy into straight away.”.

Vanner argues that another way primary brands can still win is by leaning into the codes, lore and IRL spaces around those moments: “Turning on-screen energy into real-world hangouts, collabs and shared rituals rather than just another product push.”.

Euphoria has served as the playbook here, offering everything from pop-ups where guests can have their makeup done, DJ-ed events and talks. In 2022, A24 also released a makeup line with Euphoria's makeup artist Donni Davy called Half Magic. Globally, the number of TikTok videos posted using #EuphoriaMakeup increased by 1,051% year on year between November 2025 and October 2026, TikTok shares with Vogue Business.

The Half Magic brand was founded by A24 and Euphoria makeup artist Donni Davy.

Recent findings suggest that in February next year, Amazon will air the second season of Benito Skinner’s Overcompensating, a comedy about a closeted ex-footballer. The show has swiftly become known for its very 2010s costumes. Already, the first season (aired in 2025) has built a cult following around its preppy fare. Mall prep brands such as J.Crew, Polo Ralph Lauren, and even L.L.Bean have become associated with the male characters.

In a recent development, “We were trying to tap into archetypal ways that people represent themselves — the way that kids try to fit in by overdressing in the version of the thing that they want to be,” says the show’s costume designer Hanna Puley. “For the girls it was a lot of fast fashion. I think we pulled a fair bit from H&M and stuff that was readily accessible and felt familiar. It’s that Forever 21 aesthetic.”.

Recent findings suggest that the costuming tracks with a shift that’s been underway for a while among young consumers. Mall brands are having a comeback, accessible luxury is performing (Ralph Lauren revenues climbed 10% in the last quarter), and nostalgic pre-loved designer accessories continue to captivate. It’s exactly why brands should look to these love-triangle, first-kiss dramas to position themselves in the zeitgeist.

Consider also Amazon’s Off Campus, which launched in May and follows a men’s ice hockey team in their heterosexual dalliances. Aside from the usual plot analyses that flood TikTok, the show has also built a strong online contingent of fans wanting to discuss the outfits. Leading female protagonist Allie Hayes, played by Mika Abdalla, appeared in one episode wearing a recreation of Jennifer Lopez’s Donatella Versace-designed dress for Halloween. The piece went viral on TikTok, with creators sharing behind-the-scenes footage of costume designer Charlene Akuamoah at work and, of course, their own reactions. One video shared generated 258,200 views.

Sources indicate that “I think part of what makes Off Campus resonate so strongly from a fashion perspective is that the clothing strikes a balance between aspiration and relatability,” notes Akuamoah. “I was intentional about mixing contemporary brands, vintage pieces, and different price points to create wardrobes that felt authentic to each character. Younger audiences are increasingly turning to television for fashion inspiration, and social media allows them to immediately identify, share and shop what they see on screen.”.

Off Campus star Ella Bright attends the Miu Miu Womenswear Spring/Summer 2027 show.

According to recent reports, across the board, the teen drama genre remains a well for fashion inspiration. Past contenders include US first-love hit, The Summer I Turned Pretty, Spanish private-school thriller Elite and A24’s Euphoria. With them come merch opportunities for the streaming platform and commercial careers for actors beyond the significant screen. A24 is no stranger to merch, and after Euphoria, starring actresses Zendaya and Sydney Sweeney have both gone on to become style icons in their own right, closely followed for their press tour wardrobes and brand ambassadorships with Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu, respectively.

Industry observers note that “These demonstrates used to be about putting products on screen, but today the real value sits with the cast themselves,” notes Alison Bringé, Launchmetrics’s chief marketing officer. She points to the average media impact value (MIV) of an Instagram post from some of The Summer I Turned Pretty’s leading stars: Lola Tung ($387,000), Christopher Briney ($256,000) and Gavin Casalegno ($354,000). “Their fandoms don’t just watch: they follow, recreate and share, which turns these actors into commercial voices with real staying power,” Bringé adds. “That’s why we’re seeing brands sign them as ambassadors rather than treating them as a one-season moment.”.

Sources indicate that similarly, Ella Bright, an Off Campus star, commands an MIV of $757,000 per Instagram post. Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty also declared Bright as its first-ever brand ambassador in July. The news culminated in a MIV of $4.6 million within a week and lifted the brand’s overall performance by over 138% the same day, with the top post driving $815,000 in MIV alone. In September, Belmont Cameli, another star from the series, generated $943,000 in MIV in one week for Saint Laurent through a single post.

In a recent development, devin Barrett, General Idea’s copy director for social and culture, says that teen dramas offer brands a direct link to vibrant cultural conversations and the opportunity to align with future breakout talent. He points to The Body as a fictional portrait of the affluent 2004 teen consumer, explaining that it proffers a fresh style inspiration source beyond the oversaturated ’00s paparazzi imagery. “Reveals like this bring Gen Z and Gen Alpha into an era they didn’t originally experience, orchestrating a richer world around Y2K aesthetics,” he says. “It unlocks the potential for new brand ambassadors with an authentic connection to products like the Dior Saddle bag.”.

Recent findings suggest that of course, fashion has long been a fan of teen dramas, both on television and in the movies. Millennials and Gen-Xers might remember Grease, The Breakfast Club and Mean Girls as historic style inspirations. Highlights, however, offer a more enduring marketing avenue for brands to tap into throughout a storyline. “These shows freeze a fleeting, perfect moment — the first love, a friendship group that feels like the whole world,” says Katy Lubin, Lyst’s VP of brand and communications. “The characters are flawed and human. For a brand, being part of that feels genuine in a way a campaign shoot just can’t.” As she sees it, specific pieces become associated with specific character traits, much like the Fendi Baguette gave a cool, Fresh York yuppie association through Sex and the City’s Carrie Bradshaw.

Benito Skinner, director and lead in Overcompensating, attends the Burberry Spring/Summer 2027 show.

According to recent reports, ultimately, because viewers follow demonstrates for long periods across seasons, it means the fashion choices can also shift and evolve, presenting latest opportunities for brands. Competitors will need to be agile. Indeed, next season, Overcompensating is leaning into a different vibe, Puley tells Vogue Business. She’s interested to see how viewers react. “We’re not veering so mainstream. There’s a lot more niche stuff,” she indicates.

Is It Rude to Bring Your Own Food to Thanksgiving?

  • Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

For the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host says dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

In a recent development, I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

Sources indicate that the short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

Recent findings suggest that A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:.

In a recent development, I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a big breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

According to recent reports, I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

First, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a massive deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

This is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really notable to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

And I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really important for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

It has been revealed that thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

Sources indicate that if your holiday spread always includes a plate of crispy latkes and a round of dirty martinis, these dirty martini latkes are probably your dream mash-up. This playful party app takes everything you love about the classic Hanukkah potato pancake and gives it a cocktail-inspired twist with buttery green olives, pimento peppers, and a tangy blue cheese and vermouth-spiked sour cream for dipping. The blue cheese isn’t mandatory, but if you love an ice-cold filthy martini with a couple of blue cheese stuffed olives in it, you’ll totally understand my vision. Pair these with other Hanukkah favorites for a festive spread that's equal parts nostalgic and fun.

The latkes:Traditional latkes start with freshly grated potatoes, but frozen shredded hash browns are the secret shortcut here, cutting prep time without sacrificing crispy edges or fluffy centers. The key is squeezing out as much moisture as possible, then fluffing the shreds with a fork so they stay light instead of turning dense. Castelvetrano olives add a rich, buttery flavor, but Spanish queen or manzanilla olives work just as well. If you can find green olives already stuffed with pimento, go ahead and use them—you can skip the extra chopped pimentos altogether.

Recent findings suggest that make ahead & storage:The vermouth-blue cheese dipping sauce can be made up to 7 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, making your day-of party prep that much easier. Leftover latkes can be refrigerated for up to 4 days; just reheat them in a 400° oven or air fryer until hot and crisp again for the best texture.

In a recent development, this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

Industry observers note that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

According to recent reports, most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

According to recent reports, mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

It has been revealed that slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.

According to recent reports, this giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan. The bigger, the better, as they say, but we’re more into its shareable nature and simple-to-make design. Shatteringly crisp puff pastry (store-bought, of course) replaces hard-to-make croissant dough, with extra square footage for both this treat’s iconic croissant fillings: pain au chocolat and almond croissant. Win-win-win. Save this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant for special occasions or holiday mornings.

According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 425°F. On a lightly floured surface, roll out each sheet of puff pastry to a 12×10-inch rectangle. Place one on a parchment-lined 15x10x1-inch baking pan. Top the puff pastry with a second piece of parchment paper and a second 15x10x1-inch baking pan. This keeps the puff pastry from rising too much so it stays flat.

It has been revealed that bake the puff pastry for 15 minutes. Remove the top pan and parchment. Continue baking the puff pastry until it’s golden brown, five to seven minutes longer. Cool the puff pastry on a wire rack. Repeat the same process with the second slice of puff pastry.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, in a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, almond flour and confectioners’ sugar until they’re light and fluffy, two to three minutes. Add the egg and beat well until it’s incorporated.

Industry observers note that place one baked sheet of puff pastry on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread two-thirds of the almond filling over it.

Sprinkle the chocolate chips evenly all over. Carefully place the second sheet of baked puff pastry over top, and pipe or spread the remaining third of the almond filling on top.

Sprinkle the top with sliced almonds.

Reduce the oven setting to 350°. Bake the croissant just until the filling is set, 18 to 20 minutes longer. Cool the croissant completely on a wire rack before serving.

Just as you’re ready to serve, dust the top with confectioners’ sugar and, if desired, drizzle it with warm hot fudge.

Store leftover giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant in an airtight container in the fridge. It can be kept for up to three days. Just know that it is best enjoyed the day of, as the frangipane will make the puff pastry soggy.

Yes, you can make certain aspects of a giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant ahead of time, but wait to assemble and bake it until you’re ready to serve. You can bake the puff pastry sheets one day ahead, let them cool to room temperature, wrap them tightly in storage wrap and store them at room temperature. Make the frangipane up to two days beforehand and keep it covered in the fridge.

Yes, you can make a gluten-free version of this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant. Simply replace the puff pastry with a gluten-free variety. DuFour, Sweet Loren’s and Schar make fantastic gluten-free puff pastry. All other ingredients are naturally gluten free (but do double-check the hot fudge, if you’re using it); just make sure they weren’t processed in a facility that handles wheat.

According to recent reports, serve your giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant with strong coffee or tea. Pair it with other brunch, like egg casseroles, plates of bacon and sausage and a fruit salad. I wouldn’t set out any other sweets—this croissant is plenty!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is rich in striking, darkly memorable imagery: Margot Robbie shimmying in a sunshine-yellow two-piece at the Playboy Mansion; the sunbaked menace of Brad Pitt’s visit to the Manson ranch; the audaciously bloody denouement, all pit bulls and flamethrowers, playing out high in the Hollywood Hills, with the glittering carpet of nighttime Los Angeles extending endlessly beyond.

But for some—this writer included—the film’s most indelible legacy is its costumes. And, more specifically, those of Pitt’s laid-back (and possibly wife-murdering) stuntman Cliff Booth. Double-denim layers, gold-rimmed aviators, scuffed moccasins—and, of course, those Hawaiian shirts—the character’s late-’60s California cool burnt up the screen and almost certainly played a part in the Americana wave that plenty of menswear fanatics are still riding.

So, when David Fincher stepped into the director’s chair for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth—the Netflix film picks up the story of Pitt’s character nearly a decade later—the task of evolving those indelible looks fell to one of the director’s most trusted creative collaborators: costume designer Trish Summerville. Indeed, the trust ran so deep (the pair had previously worked together on The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, Gone Girl, and Mank) that Summerville didn’t even know what the project was when she said yes. “I’m always in for whatever he’s doing,” she tells Vogue. “I don’t know anyone else I would do that with.”.

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth, Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby, Scott Caan as Charlie Peters, and Carla Gugino as Toni Becka.

According to recent reports, across the eight-year gap between the two films, a lot has changed in Hollywood—not least in its style. By the late ’70s, it’s the heady era of Studio 54 excess, punk-rock rebellion, and Halston halter necks. Still, rather than leaning into disco-fever, polyester-everything clichés, Summerville looked to the real-world period artifacts she could get her hands on locally, scouring the vintage mail-order catalogs and archival racks at Los Angeles’s legendary Western Costume, among other places. Under Fincher’s famously exacting eye, every garment had to serve the story without ever feeling like, well, a costume—and it was a challenge that required building nearly every piece from the ground up. (Though with a little inspiration from some select vintage garments along the way.).

In a recent development, arguably most seductive of all are the costumes worn by Elizabeth Debicki: in Cliff Booth, the six-foot-three Australian actor plays Karen Crosby, an enigmatic, glamorous Hollywood studio executive whose crisp wardrobe practically gleams within the seedy underbelly of 1970s Los Angeles conjured by the film’s production designer, Donald Graham Burt. Dressed exclusively in varying shades of white—a strict mandate from Fincher that required extensive color-testing with cinematographer Eric Messerschmidt—Debicki’s looks deliberately stand out, but never feel disconnected from the world around her.

It has been revealed that “Unless it’s something in the script that really wants the clothing and the costumes to jump off the screen, I never want it to distract,” Summerville indicates, a sentiment that could apply to the lived-in textures of her costuming work on Cliff Booth as a whole. “It should just help you watch this story.”.

Below, Summerville talks figuring out exactly the right cut of 1970s denim for Pitt, looking to Lauren Hutton and Cher as muses for Debicki, and why the decade’s unstudied sex appeal continues to shape fashion today.

Vogue: Obviously, you’ve worked with David a number of times before—but how did this project end up in your lap?

Trish Summerville: It came up through Ceán Chaffin, who’s Dave’s producer. We met at a coffee shop, which was very formal for us, and she didn’t really say what it was—she just said that they had a project coming up, a film, and they’d like me to do it, but she couldn’t tell me what it was because it was quite secretive at that time.

In a recent development, I had to say I was in without knowing what it was. Because of my history with Dave and really liking working with him a lot, I’m always in for whatever he’s doing. I always hope I’m available when he has a project; I hope I’m asked to do it. The only thing I knew was it was a film and it would be in LA, and that was all I knew until I agreed. And then I got an explanation of what it was, and a text from Dave afterwards saying, “Yay, I’m glad you’re in.”.

In a recent development, I presume you had seen the first film. Did you revisit it before starting work?

Yeah, I definitely had seen the first film, and after they did call me, I did rewatch it so I could get refamiliarized with the characters, but then I got the script, and realized there’s not a lot of overlap in the characters—it’s pretty much just Brad, so it’s a whole new story about him.

Recent findings suggest that when we last saw Cliff Booth, it was 1969, and this film is set 1977. How did you first start thinking about the ways in which his look—and the look of the city generally—was going to feel distinct from the first film?

According to recent reports, I did a lot of research. We have a couple of rental houses here that have pretty extensive research materials, and Western Costume is always a great place to start. They have a search library of periodicals, photographs from sets, behind-the-scenes stuff, and every kind of catalog you could imagine. So it was really important for me to look at everything from films in Hollywood that were happening, behind the scenes, the actors, and then also looking at everyday catalogs like JCPenney or Sears catalogs, looking at Vogue magazine, Ebony magazine—just so I could have a range. It needed to cover what’s depicted on screen as the movie within the movie, then also, how people dressed every day.

According to recent reports, even though there wasn’t fast fashion like there is now, in that amount of time you did see a shift in silhouettes across both men’s and women’s clothing—shapes of jeans, shapes of jackets, the jewelry. But with Brad’s character, it was really about keeping the integrity of who his character is, and the ease—Cliff Booth is really just a fucking cool guy. It was about shifting him a little bit: changing the silhouette of his jeans, giving him Roper suede boots instead of moccasins, not doing as many layers this time, having his shirts buttoned a little bit lower. He’s really, really comfortable with who he is.

Oh, and we definitely wanted to start the film off with the Hawaiian shirt from the first film, so the audience has something to immediately recognize and feel a kinship with.

Industry observers note that tarantino is known for having quite detailed descriptions in his scripts about costumes. Was that the case here?

Yeah, in some instances there were. Some of the descriptions of Cliff, it would say he’s wearing Billy Jack boots, or that he puts on puka shells for when he tends bar. But it wasn’t excessive. We stuck pretty much to anything that was a key story point, or that seemed really integral to the character—he’d maybe describe that he’s wearing sunglasses here, or a leather jacket. With Hot Rod, it would describe the style of clothing he would wear, but nothing as specific as a color or anything like that.

How much of the costumes were sourced, recreated, or made from scratch?

Sources indicate that pretty much most of it was made, at least for our principals. When it’s a period film, and you have stunts, and a really long shoot—we shot, I think it was 105 or 107 days—you really have to have at least doubles of things. It’s too scary. We kind of have a saying in the costume world: “If you have one, you have none.” For Elizabeth, we made her costumes, especially because Dave was very specific that he just wanted her always in a tone of white, and white is very scary in general.

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth and Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby.

And with Brad’s character, even the shirts that we found for him—like the Hawaiian shirt and the tiki shirts and the liquor bottle shirt—we bought rayon fabric and printed all those ourselves. For the liquor bottle shirt, one of my shoppers found a vintage one and sent me a picture, and I was like, “Oh my God, that shirt is amazing.” Then I found another one, and then one of the guys in our department said, “Wait, I think I have this shirt at home—I’ve had it for 20 or 30 years.” So we found three different versions of that shirt from the mid-to-late ’40s to the ’70s. I selected all the bottles I liked from the different shirts and changed the colors a bit, and the illustrator I work with drew up a pattern, and then we had a printer here in Los Angeles print up the fabric. We even built jeans for him—we found a Levi’s shape that was great on him, and then we built multiples of them. His barong—the shirt he wears at the end—we ended up making 68 of that particular shirt. It’s all embroidered, all natural fibers, because of how the shirt is used for him and his stunt guy.

Brad knows a lot about fashion—he has his own cashmere line, for one. Was dressing him quite a collaborative process?

It is. He does have opinions, and he’ll bring in inspiration pieces or things that he likes. Then it’s just trying a bunch of shapes, and retrying things once we build them. He really liked the idea of having T-shirts that leaned into an automotive inspiration for Cliff, which makes sense, and we chose to use that at the speedway in the figure-eight races. Working with the Evel Knievel logo, because Evel Knievel was so major at that time, and being a stuntman, he would really have an affinity for that. And then Brad was like, “Oh, I want a red, white, and blue helmet.” So we went to the props guy and said, “We’re going to have this Evel Knievel vibe for him for the T-shirts—could you have a helmet painted for him?”.

Industry observers note that brad’s great about little details, like keeping on these native beaded bracelets that he wears always, which wears them in and gives them a lot of life. And he took some of the jeans and his bracelets home at the end, which is nice.

Tell me about working with Elizabeth. Was there anyone specific from Hollywood history or otherwise that you were looking to when figuring out her wardrobe?

I was really inspired a lot by Lauren Hutton for Crosby, because you can’t deny that if you saw Crosby, she could be a fashion model. Even though her character is rooted in reality, she’s very glamorous. Lauren Hutton had this really classic look to her, but very sexy, and with this edge—she would wear very drapey tops and really fitted high-waisted pants with silk blouses. There was also a little Cher vibe too, with the drapey halters. And Elizabeth was a lot of fun to dress. She’s really great about exploring character—with her, it was more talking about who Crosby is and what her day-to-day is like. I always try to work very closely with the production designer and the director of photography. Debicki’s going to be wearing white: how white can I be? Can it be optic white? Does it have to be a toned-down white? For some of her costumes, we had to do two different versions for when she was outside versus inside, because the tones read so differently.

Like Brad, Elizabeth looks amazing in those high-waisted trousers and flares.

Industry observers note that she really does. It was so fun. In that figure-eight racing scene when she’s walking through between the bleachers up that little alleyway, it was quite nice to see other people in the cinema take a gasp—because she stands out so much there in this all-white look, so elegant and beautiful. And right before that, when she’s walking down the street at the premiere—so elegant and chic and regal.

Were there any other moments that, when you saw the film on the massive screen, you were especially satisfied with?

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to choose, because I really loved the Manila stills that you see as flash-cut stills—that was several days of shooting, having this whole Filipino vibe, and these brothels, and a Filipino rock band to dress with significant platforms and crazy makeup. I also love the scene when Hot Rod is leaving the movie set, and he’s in the velour one-piece Bordeaux jumper with the saddlebags, walking out and talking to Scott Caan. And seeing the tennis scenes—for us, the tennis section was such a big thing because we had to make so many multiples, again all in white, with body-makeup tanner getting on the clothing. And the Verdusco brothers! They would always come together to do their fittings—they never showed up solo—and after we took individual photos, they would always do a back-to-back pose or a karate pose.

As someone who immersed themself so deeply in ’70s fashion for this—an era that’s been cropping up all over the runways recently—what do you think it is about that decade’s aesthetic that remains so aspirational today?

I think it just was cool. People were very sexy without trying to be sexy. You didn’t have to have all your skin exposed—it was something about the silhouette and the drape of the fabrics and the ease. Silk blouses that are just a little bit open, thin gold chains, and the nice drape of the pants. People were so much more carefree then; music was major and fun, and you were out and dancing. I keep joking, “Oh my God, can we please just have jeans with no stretch in them?” Because it’s such a better fit, and the weight of that denim was really nice. Plus you had disco, punk rock, rock and roll: it lent itself to individuality.

Did any of that rub off on your own wardrobe after wrapping the film?

In a recent development, yeah, actually! For the premiere, I wore the jeans worn by Lauren Glazier, who plays Raquel, Brad’s bartending partner. At the speedway, she’s wearing a pair of ’70s Levi’s with a good boot-cut flare to them, and I borrowed those and wore them to the premiere with a Tom Ford dinner jacket. I definitely had to wear six-and-a-half-inch heels to accommodate the length, because she’s quite tall and I’m not!

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Whether you're hosting a small gathering this year or simply craving the comforting flavors of Thanksgiving any time of year, this sheet-pan dinner is the way to go. It’s a feast that’s as cozy as it is convenient, bringing together the classics with a few flavorful twists. The beauty of this meal lies in its simplicity—everything roasts together on a single pan, making cleanup a breeze.

According to recent reports, the turkey:Using a bone-in split turkey breast helps ensure juicy, flavorful meat with rich, golden skin, slathered with butter and seasoned with poultry seasoning. This nod to tradition is enhanced with a touch of smoky paprika and garlic to amp up the flavors. For the stuffing, I went the classic route, using store-bought seasoned cubes for a bit of nostalgia, along with onions, celery, and soy sauce to boost the savory notes, and cranberries for a hint of sweetness. The stuffing offers the best of both worlds, with crispy edges and an irresistibly savory center soaked in turkey drippings.

According to recent reports, the sweet potatoes:The sweet potatoes strike a perfect balance, spiced with warm and aromatic garam masala—a perfect pairing with the sweet yet earthy tuber. A splash of orange juice adds a tart-sweet touch, while pecans provide a satisfying crunch. If garam masala isn’t your thing, a dash of pumpkin pie spice works beautifully.

The green beans:The green beans, a nod to the iconic casserole, are streamlined for the sheet pan, tossed with mushrooms, Parmesan, and thyme-infused butter, and finished with crispy fried onions for that quintessential touch.

In a recent development, make-ahead & storage:If the idea of making a whole Thanksgiving dinner on a sheet pan in one day feels daunting, here’s a tip—prep some components ahead of time. Most, if not all, of the ingredient chopping, grating, toasting, etc., can be done 2 to 3 days in advance. The stuffing can be made a day ahead; just be sure to cool it completely before refrigerating. Even the turkey can be buttered and seasoned the day before, leaving you with just the assembly and roasting on the day of.

I've broken down the differences between the lines below, and the defining details about specific models in each line that are on sale right now. Introduced in 2014, Nespresso’s Vertuoline modernized the brand’s original pressure brew method and marked the true beginning of Nespresso espresso and coffee machines. Most Vertuo machines feature just one button and brew both coffee and espresso-style shots using a centrifugal method. Once you choose your preferred pod based on style, roast, and cup size, the machine takes care of the rest. Vertuo Next Coffee with Aeroccino Milk Frother.

Like the Next and Pop machines, the Vertuo Up is Wi-Fi enabled and you can use the companion app for maintenance alerts and to customize how the machine brews your favorite pods, if you'd like tweaks to the pod-specific presets.

The newest Vertuo machine, the Vertuo Lattissima is a one-touch machine that makes coffee, espresso, cappuccinos, and latte macchiatos at the push of a button.

I Tried Ina Garten’s Ranch Dressing, and It Changed My Mind About Ranch

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing.
  • I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing.
  • I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing. Then I made Ina's version.

I have a confession to make. I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing. I realize this puts me at odds with a substantial portion of the American population, but I’ve always preferred a good balsamic vinaigrette or a creamy Caesar. And despite making countless salad dressings over the years, I’ve never once felt compelled to make ranch.

I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch. I found the whole business unappealing, an opinion that has apparently skipped a generation seeing as both of my children now do exactly the same thing. There’s always a bottle of ranch in our refrigerator that was purchased specifically for pizza night, and it has absolutely nothing to do with me.

Then I came across an Instagram reel of Ina Garten making her buttermilk ranch dressing for a wedge salad. I’ve trusted Ina with everything from roast chicken to panna cotta, and if anyone could persuade me to reconsider my longstanding position on ranch, I figured it would be her. So, after decades of avoiding it, I finally made a batch of ranch dressing.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, ina’s recipe makes about 3 cups of dressing, which initially struck me as an ambitious quantity for someone with my history of distatte. Fortunately, it comes together in just a few minutes, and the ingredients are far more fresh and interesting than anything I’d previously associated with ranch.

Industry observers note that combine the scallions, basil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, olive oil, garlic, salt and pepper in a food processor fitted with a steel blade. Puree them for 15 to 20 seconds, until the mixture is smooth.

Add the mayonnaise, Greek yogurt and buttermilk, then blend the dressing again until everything is thoroughly combined. Transfer the dressing to a covered container and refrigerate it for an hour to let the flavors develop.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that that’s really all there is to it. No complicated technique or careful emulsifying, and very little cleanup. The hour in the refrigerator is crucial, though, since it gives the garlic, herbs and other seasonings time to mingle with the creamy ingredients.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Of course, I expected Ina’s ranch to be better than the bottled varieties I’ve tried. What I didn’t expect was for it to taste like an entirely different dressing.

The first thing that struck me was how fresh it was. The basil and scallions give it a wonderful, almost garden-like quality, while the garlic and Dijon add savory sharpness that keeps all that creaminess interesting. There’s plenty of richness from the mayonnaise, but the buttermilk, Greek yogurt and lemon juice provide enough acidity to balance it. It’s tangy, herbaceous and wonderfully flavorful—without the heavy, slightly cloying quality I’ve always associated with ranch.

And the basil! It’s not an herb I would have thought to put in ranch dressing, but it works beautifully. Its flavor comes through clearly without overwhelming the other ingredients, giving the dressing a character all its own.

According to recent reports, in her video, Ina serves the dressing over a wedge salad topped with tomatoes and onion. Having already entrusted her with the dressing, I figured I might as well follow her lead with the salad, too. I made my own wedge with Flavor Bombs tomatoes (my favorites), pepitas and crispy pieces of bacon, then spooned a generous amount of ranch over the whole thing. The cold, crunchy lettuce was the perfect backdrop for the dressing, while the sweet tomatoes, salty bacon and nutty pepitas made the whole thing particularly satisfying. I’ve always loved a good wedge salad, but this was easily one of the best I’ve had.

By the time I’d finished testing and photographing the recipe, nearly half the dressing was gone, and I was already making plans for the rest. I have to admit, I’m even curious to see how it tastes with pizza, which is not something I ever expected to say about ranch dressing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving leftovers are a thing of beauty, but it’s time to move beyond the classic Thanksgiving sandwich. When we want to turn our holiday leftovers into a satisfying appetizer, these egg rolls are what we turn to. They have a perfectly crunchy exterior and are filled with all of our favorite Thanksgiving dishes: leftover turkey, mashed potatoes, cranberries, and stuffing. It’s the perfect way to use up every last bite of those beloved leftovers—here’s how to make them:.

According to recent reports, making Thanksgiving egg rolls:The key to keeping your egg rolls together when frying? Don’t overstuff them. If you add too much filling, you run the risk of your egg rolls exploding when fried. Plus, when it comes to fillings, you don’t have to limit yourself to what we included here. If you have any leftover veggies, or want to switch up your mashed potatoes (garlic mashed potatoes, anyone?), feel free to adapt these to what you have in your fridge.

Industry observers note that variations:Prefer to leave your oven off? Follow our air fryer egg rolls method and adapt for this filling.

Make-ahead & storage: If you want to freeze these egg rolls, fill and prepare them, then space them out on a lined freezer-safe tray to avoid any sticking. Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

No ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

Industry observers note that my kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

Tech Report: Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • Recent findings suggest that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Fresh York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

Recent findings suggest that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

In a recent development, while there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Sources indicate that originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, noted that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

In a recent development, wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit Newly introduced York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she notes. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

It has been revealed that A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Industry observers note that spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, states that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to fresh takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Who states peanut butter doesn’t deserve a spot in your dinner rotation?

Jif, the beloved peanut butter brand that’s been a staple in American pantries for decades, has ventured into some unexpected territory. If you’re a frequent Costco shopper, you might want to take a closer look the next time you’re browsing the instant noodles.

Some locations of the warehouse retailer are now carrying a six-pack of Jif stir-fry-style instant ramen noodles, giving shoppers an entirely different way to enjoy the taste of peanut butter.

But so far, the reviews among shoppers are mixed.

Recent findings suggest that “Anyone who thinks this sounds gross has never had Thai food and it highlights. Peanut butter noodles are kinda awesome,” one fan wrote in a video making the rounds on Instagram.

“Prolly fire w some chili oil,” another claimed.

According to recent reports, “I had this last month. Pretty good for instant noodles,” another said.

A fourth wrote, “As a peanut butter [connoisseur] I don’t approve this.”.

“Diabolical waste of resources,” a fifth claimed.

Peanuts have long been incorporated into savory noodle dishes, particularly in Asian-inspired cooking. Still, seeing the recognizable Jif logo on a package of instant noodles might have you raising your eyebrows. Rather than replicating the sweet, creamy taste of a spoonful of peanut butter, the noodles take a more savory approach. The seasoning contains peanut flour alongside ingredients like soy sauce, garlic and artificial beef flavor.

Jif has another product worth keeping an eye out for at Costco. The brand’s peanut butter and chocolate pretzel Snappers hit shelves in October and offer a sweet-and-salty alternative for those who aren’t quite sold on the noodles.

As always, product availability can vary by warehouse, so it’s worth checking your warehouse’s stock online before making a special trip. You can also buy the Jif instant ramen at Walmart or Amazon.

But the real question is, would you give peanut butter ramen a try, or is this one food crossover you’ll happily sit out?

In a recent development, never in your life have you had such an exemplary vegetable as these boiled potatoes, inspired by the version featured in the 2005 film adaptation of Pride and Prejudice. While the moment is not part of Jane Austen’s classic novel, the simple dish has developed a bit of a cult following. Our interpretation has a little garlic and lemon zest in addition to plenty of butter and parsley; we think Mr. Collins would approve—dare we say, he may even declare them excellent. Don your finest Regency-style garb and place a pot of water on the hearth: We have potatoes to boil.

Even more excellent potato recipes this way.

Combine ¼ cup Diamond Crystal or 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Morton kosher salt and 10 cups water in a large pot.

Peel 1½ lb. Yukon Gold potatoes (about 3 large or 4 medium). Quarter if potatoes are large, halve if medium, adding to pot as you go. Potatoes should be covered by at least 2" water when finished; add more if needed.

Place pot over high heat and bring water to a boil. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer until potatoes are cooked through (a fork should slide easily into flesh), 15–20 minutes. Drain in a colander.

Set pot over medium-low heat to cook off any excess water, then add 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter and cook until melted. Stir in 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper. Remove from heat; mix in ¼ cup finely chopped parsley and 1 tsp. finely grated lemon zest. Add drained potatoes and toss to coat. Taste and season with more salt if needed. Transfer potatoes to a large shallow bowl to serve.

Store in refrigerator until ready to use for up to 2 weeks or in the freezer for 3 months.

According to recent reports, even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Suqaar Digaag (Chicken and Vegetable Sauté)

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s no exaggeration to say that xawaash is at the heart of Somali cuisine. It is Somali history on a plate—a culinary reminder of Somalia’s centuries of global trade, particularly along the Indian Ocean. Xawaash is what makes many Somali dishes taste distinctly Somali. While every household’s xawaash recipe is its own, typically seven core spices—cumin, coriander, black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and turmeric—are toasted until their fragrance blooms, then blended into an earthy golden-brown powder. Xawaash stores very well and for a long time in an airtight container, though it’s at its peak shortly after it’s made. If you use it often, you can double or triple the recipe for a big batch.

Like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar. It has a hint of heat thanks to the black pepper and optional jalapeño. Suqaar is cooked covered to keep the meat juicy and moist. Serve with the flatbread of your choice (canjeero, muufo, or sabaayad) for a light lunch or over plenty of rice for a more filling dinner.

More tasty chicken thigh recipes here.

Toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp. green cardamom pods, and 1½ tsp. whole cloves in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly so the spices don’t burn. The spices are toasted when they have a slightly darker color and become fragrant, 1–2 minutes. Transfer the toasted spices to a blender or spice grinder and blend until they become a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and mix in ¼ cup (30 g) ground turmeric until it’s fully incorporated and the spice mix is golden brown. Allow to cool completely, then store in an airtight container.

Sources indicate that in a medium bowl, combine the juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp. xawaash, 1 tsp. fine sea salt, ½ tsp. paprika, and ⅛ tsp. ground black pepper. Add 1 lb. (450 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-sized pieces, and mix everything together to coat the chicken. Set aside.

Sources indicate that in a large skillet over medium-high heat, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil until loose. Add 1 large yellow onion, halved and sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes, or until the onion is softened. Add 6 garlic cloves, minced, and 1 medium jalapeño, halved, and stir for another minute, then add the chicken in a single layer. Allow it to cook undisturbed for 5 minutes, then turn the pieces over and cook for 3 minutes more, until fully cooked through.

Recent findings suggest that add the remaining 1½ tsp. xawaash, ¾ cup (12 g) coarsely chopped cilantro leaves, 1 medium red bell pepper, sliced, and 1 medium yellow bell pepper, sliced, and stir to combine. Cover the skillet and turn the heat down to medium-low; cook until the peppers have softened, 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The biggest difference with this potential menu overhaul is how the chicken would be prepared.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mcDonald’s has been paying close attention to its chicken menu lately. Between the return of the Snack Wrap, the introduction of McCrispy Strips, and several new dipping sauces, it’s clear the chain is looking to become a bigger player in the fast-food chicken game. If the latest reports are true, some of its biggest changes might still be ahead.

Recent findings suggest that mcDonald’s is reportedly testing five hand-breaded chicken menu items in select U.S. markets, including Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and the Tucson, Arizona, area. The information comes from McFranchisee, an account on X that regularly shares details about the chain’s operations and upcoming menu changes.

The biggest difference with this potential menu overhaul is how the chicken would be prepared. Rather than simply introducing new flavors or sauces, McDonald’s is reportedly experimenting with having employees bread the chicken by hand inside its restaurants.

According to recent reports, among the alleged test items is a fresh McSpicy chicken sandwich. According to the report, all five items are also available as meals, with prices ranging from $8.19 to $9.99 at the location pictured in the social media post.

A similar test is also taking place in Ireland.

I’m particularly interested in how hand-breading could change the texture of McDonald’s chicken. Having taste-tested plenty of fast-food chicken sandwiches and tenders, I’ve found that the breading can make or break the entire experience. A crispier, more substantial coating could make McDonald’s a much stronger competitor to chains like Popeyes and Chick-fil-A.

Rolling out hand-breaded chicken across thousands of restaurants, however, is easier said than done.

The reported tests are designed to evaluate customer demand, preparation costs, and how the additional steps could affect kitchen operations. Some franchisees have reportedly expressed concerns about increased labor requirements and potential kitchen renovations.

According to recent reports, while McDonald’s hasn’t officially confirmed the five-item lineup or specific U.S. test locations, the idea of hand-breaded chicken isn’t entirely out of left field.

Sources indicate that during its November earnings call, the company confirmed that it had begun setting up operational pilots for hand-breaded chicken in the U.S. and Ireland. It also confirmed intends for larger U.S. sales tests at roughly 100 restaurants in early 2027.

It has been revealed that for now, there’s no confirmed nationwide U.S. release date or guarantee that all five reported items will make it onto the permanent menu.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon.
  • Sources indicate that whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • It has been revealed that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, these homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 concern of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Sources indicate that whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

It has been revealed that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Recent findings suggest that absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

Sources indicate that IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

In a recent development, IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

If that sounds familiar, you’re in excellent firm. As it turns out, the night before the big feast is one of the busiest times of the year for pizza orders, and our collective craving for a good slice is practically a holiday tradition of its own.

Ridiculously popular. According to DoorDash’s latest trends report, pizza was the No. 1 pick this time last year, with orders jumping more than 50% compared with other Wednesdays in November. And the ‘za of choice? Plain cheese, up a whopping 70%.

It has been revealed that the craze isn’t limited to the couch, either. Toast data indicates that pizza orders at sit-down restaurants and bars spiked 48% that evening. Salads, meanwhile, dipped 5%, which sounds about right.

National chains feel the rush, too. “Across the industry, it consistently lands in the top handful alongside Halloween and the Super Bowl,” Greg Hamilton, chief marketing officer at Little Caesars, said in a statement.

In a recent development, there’s a certain satisfaction in wiping down the counters the day before, knowing the casseroles are assembled and you’re as ready for tomorrow as you’ll ever be. The last thing anyone wants to do is pull another pan out of the cupboard.

Sources indicate that “Thanksgiving Eve is about making life easier,” Hamilton said. “The kitchen is already prepped for Thursday, the house is filling up and nobody wants to cook twice.”.

But there’s more to it than giving the dishwasher a break. College kids are back in their hometowns, and childhood friends are making aims to reunite. Even siblings who usually communicate via memes in the family group chat are finally in the same room.

Industry observers note that with AAA expecting 81.5 million Americans to travel this week, plenty of those reunions kick off a day before anyone carves anything. Order pizza, and whoever’s hosting actually hears the surprise engagement announcement instead of yelling “Wait, WHAT?” over a sizzling skillet.

Most customers “tend to go with the classics,” Hamilton noted, but if you’re looking to shake up your usual order (or feed a small army without spending a fortune), several pizza chains have specials running right now:.

Prices and participation vary by location, and given how busy tonight is shaping up to be, ordering ahead isn’t a bad idea.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that A grease fire is one kitchen emergency in which instinct can work against you. Here's how to handle one safely.

Industry observers note that one of the most valuable things I learned in culinary school was how to work with fire without losing control of it. So much of cooking depends on knowing how far we can push the heat—getting a pan hot enough to sear steak or bringing oil just to the right temperature for a batch of fried chicken. I’ve yet to lose the little thrill of flambéing a steak au poivre or a rum-laced bananas Foster, but after years in kitchens, I have a healthy respect for high heat.

That respect is particularly warranted around the holidays, when every burner on the stove seems to be occupied, and our attention is divided between the cooking and the guests milling about in the kitchen. According to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and Christmas Eve are the three peak days of the year for home cooking fires.

Recent findings suggest that what makes a grease fire especially dangerous is that many of the things we’d instinctively do to put out a fire can actually cause it to spread. Fortunately, handling a grease fire safely is a fairly simple matter of knowing what to reach for and what to leave alone.

Industry observers note that whether you’re sauteing vegetables in a little olive oil or frying chicken in a Dutch oven, it’s notable to recognize when your cooking fat is getting too hot. Different oils have different smoke points (the temperatures at which they begin to smoke) but if an oil continues to heat well beyond that point, it can eventually ignite without ever coming into direct contact with a flame. Overheating isn’t the only culprit, though. Oil that splashes onto a hot burner or an open flame can also catch fire, as can grease that has accumulated around the burners.

Industry observers note that I find a thermometer invaluable when I’m deep-frying, but it’s key to keep an eye on the pan even when sauteing. It’s frighteningly easy to get distracted chopping the next ingredient or chatting with your dinner guests. If you notice smoke rising from your pan, turn off the burner immediately.

Should the oil catch fire, leave the pan where it is. As instinctive as it may be to move it to the sink, carrying burning oil through the kitchen is a serious burn hazard, and risks spreading the fire.

Industry observers note that the most crucial thing to remember about a grease fire is that water will only make it worse. Most of us are familiar with the rather unpleasant sensation of hot oil spattering onto our hands when moisture finds its way into a sizzling pan. The science behind that reaction is the same here: Water sinks and turns rapidly to steam, agitating the oil. When the oil is burning, that sudden expansion can send flames and droplets of burning oil well beyond the stovetop.

According to recent reports, A fire extinguisher may seem like the obvious thing to reach for, but not all extinguishers are suited for grease fires. Class K extinguishers are designed specifically for fires involving cooking oils and fats, and they can be useful if you have one and know how to use it safely. For a small grease fire contained within a pan, though, there’s a simpler (and considerably less expensive) piece of kitchen equipment that can do the job: a metal lid.

Industry observers note that both the NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration recommend keeping one nearby when cooking. A small, contained grease fire can often be extinguished simply by depriving it of oxygen. Provided the flames haven’t spread beyond the pan, and you can approach it safely, here’s what to do:.

If covering the pan doesn’t extinguish the flames, it’s crucial to recognize that the situation is beyond your control. Get everyone outside and call 911.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

It has been revealed that whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Recent findings suggest that stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

💡 Key Takeaways
