America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.
  • As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension.
  • Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

In a recent development, lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

Industry observers note that determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

It has been revealed that the pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

According to recent reports, the estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

To understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” says Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”.

It has been revealed that the researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

Of the approximately 650 premature deaths estimated for 2023, 513 were attributed to fine particulate matter and 137 to smog. Together, they represented about 5.3 percent of all estimated electricity-related premature deaths nationwide.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin states.

As companies continue to expand their computing infrastructure, the findings suggest that decisions about where to build data centers and how to power them need to account for public health well beyond the immediate surroundings.

Recent findings suggest that “When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” Chen says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers hope to investigate the air quality consequences of a growing industry trend in which data centers incorporate their own on-site power plants. They could also examine whether adjusting when these facilities consume electricity could reduce their impact on air quality.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States” by Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin, 19 November 2026, Environmental Research Letters. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4.

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that on top of all that, there are plans to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today. Beyond NASA and China's looks to send crewed missions to the Moon by the end of the decade and create permanent infrastructure there, both space agencies hope to put boots on the surface of Mars by the 2030s or 40s. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency (ESA) is active in the Artemis Program and plans to send the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover to the Red Planet in 2028. India aims to send the first "gaganauts" to space next year (as part of its Gaganyaan program).

Sources indicate that on top of all that, there are plans to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars. All of this begs the question of how humans intend to live in extraterrestrial environments and among the stars. What is needed to ensure that humans can not only survive the hazards of being off-world, but also flourish? As Mars City Design CEO Vera Mulyani would say, "How can we thrive, and not just survive?".

This is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences. In addition to questions related to engineering and astronaut health and safety, astrosociology takes a more holistic outlook and examines the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of humans related to outer space. Consider Abraham Maslow's "Hierarchy of Needs," which begins with the basics (physiological and security needs) and extends upwards to include the immaterial, such as love, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

This challenge motivated Dr. Jim Pass to found the Astrosociology Research Institute (ARI) in 2008, a California-based nonprofit educational organization dedicated to developing astrosociology as a multidisciplinary academic field. As Pass describes on the organization's website, astrosociology is both a subdiscipline of sociology and a multidisciplinary field that includes (but is not limited to) "psychology, anthropology, economics, social psychology, political science, space history, space law, space policy, philosophy, as well as the arts.".

At its core, the ARI's mission comes down to a simple but highly relevant question: "How can social and behavioral scientists collaborate with physical and natural scientists to further the success of space exploration and settlement in the future?" In their latest newsletter, titled "Analog Space Missions: The Astrosociological Factors That Affect Analog Space Missions - Part 1," Pass and his colleagues share the perspectives of analog astronauts who participated in their call for papers and expert commentary by educators, space medics, and systems engineers.

As Mia Belle Parkinson, a postdoctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and ARI's editor-in-chief, wrote in the issue:.

Sources indicate that when we talk about preparing for space exploration and settlement, we too often default to the technical: propulsion systems, life support, radiation shielding. These things matter enormously. But so do the quieter, harder-to-quantify questions â how do people build trust in isolated environments? How do cultural backgrounds shape group dynamics? What does it mean, psychologically and socially, to live on the edge of the unknown?

It has been revealed that while analog astronaut training may seem like a relatively new idea, it's actually part of a long-standing tradition almost as old as the "Space Race" itself. Before astronauts landed on the Moon, NASA conducted a series of training missions known as the "Apollo Geology Field Trips" between 1964 and 1972. The first field trip saw the first two astronaut groups travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, for a two-day mission to Meteor Crater and other locations that resembled volcanic features on the Moon.

In a recent development, other locations included the Grand Canyon, the volcanic fields in Hawaii, the Nevada National Security Site, and mountain formations in the Sonoran Desert, New Mexico, Oregon, Alaska, west Texas, and Sudbury, Ontario. Additionally, the Soviets conducted the BIOS-3 experiment within the closed ecosystem built at the Institute of Biophysics in Krasnoyarsk in 1965. This was followed by Tektite I and II in 1969 and 1971, which studied human behavior in a confined, isolated, pressurized habitat on the ocean floor near the U.S. Virgin Islands.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Satoshi Furukawa pedals on the upgraded CEVIS system, keeping muscle and bone density levels during spaceflight. (Credit: NASA).

Recent findings suggest that since that time, research aboard space stations such as Mir, the International Space Station (ISS), and the Chinese Tiangong space station has provided invaluable knowledge about living in space and the effects of microgravity on humans' mental and physical well-being. However, these studies are not directly relevant to proposed missions that will send astronauts to the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. As Parry writes:.

While extremely valuable for zero-gravity spaceflights, living and working at the bottom of a gravity well presents altogether different conditions, including an inability to manufacture drugs or lift heavy objects. Planning for bases and settlements on the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and eventually beyond can only be simulated on the surface of the Earth to humankind's best approximation even in 2026, because gravity matters!

Recent findings suggest that the first analog astronaut (hereafter AA) profiled was former NASA Advisor, science communicator, and space exploration expert Beth Mund. Mund is an especially experienced AA, having participated in the HI-SEAS (Hawai'i Space Exploration Analog and Simulation) program on the summit of Mauna Loa, Hawai'i, the LunAres Research Station, and the Jules Undersea Lodge. The first involved an all-female crew working together during the height of COVID in an uninsulated temporary habitat with minimal privacy and tough conditions.

According to recent reports, the second took place in a converted World War II bunker in Poland located inside an old hangar. The hangar itself was filled with sand to simulate lunar regolith, and steel doors sealed the habitat and its six-person crew inside a rather confined space. At the Jules Undersea Lodge, located in Key Largo off the southern tip of Florida, Mund and her colleagues entered a submerged habitat with no escape hatches, accessible only through a "wet room" portal.

Looking back at these three missions, Mund noticed patterns that transcended any single environment. While each had its own geography and logistics, confinement was the common theme. From her experiences, Mund identified four universal human responses that were consistent throughout. The first, she wrote, was the importance of improvisation:.

In a recent development, no matter how carefully equipment is designed or schedules are drawn, something always fails... each failure forces us to understand the problem and formulate a response to it in the context of very tight resource constraints. And in adapting, we discover more about ourselves than about the broken machines... These small acts of invention prove that ingenuity is not a luxury in confinement. It is a decisive factor in survival.

Photo of analog astronaut Beth Mund sitting outside the HI-SEAS habitat on the summit of Mauna Kea, Hawai'i. Credit: Beth Mund.

In a recent development, the second lesson was the importance of ritual: "At HI-SEAS, our crew naturally gathered each evening for what I came to think of as our 'campfire,' a circle of debriefing, storytelling, and laughter, even in the cold dome with no flame. In Poland, games became our escape valve, a way to puncture the heaviness of the surveys and the claustrophobic walls. Underwater, simply gazing out the porthole together felt like a ceremony. In every analog, the crew instinctively created moments of reconnection that grounded us, even in places designed to isolate.".

The third lesson for Mund was continuity, as she and her colleagues inherited experiments started by crews they never met and which would be handled by future analog crews. "It gave weight to our confinement, transforming it from a private trial into a communal contribution," she said. "That continuity across crew "generations" is perhaps the most powerful sociological insight of analog missions. We are practicing not only how to live together, but how to build across time, leaving work - and maybe even some data/ insights - for crews who serve next.".

Lastly, there was the inevitability of testing. While every mission includes tests of equipment, plants, and methods for living in space, the experience also tests the limits of human endurance, creativity, and cohesion. This, she wrote, is the true essence of analog astronaut training:.

From Mars-like lava fields to a Polish bunker to the ocean floor, I have learned that analog missions are not about pretending to be astronauts. They are about practicing human endurance in places that strip away comfort and certainty. In that practice, in all the different shapes it takes across environments, facilities, missions, and crews, lies the real preparation for humanity to endure no matter the circumstances.

According to recent reports, mund is merely one of many analog astronauts profiled in the Astrosociological Insights Forum's newsletter. To include as many testimonials and experiences as possible, the glitch was released in two parts, incorporating perspectives not only from AAs but also from several experts in the burgeoning field of Astrosociology. More to follow, so stay tuned! In the meantime, check out some other articles we have about organizations committed to analog astronaut training:.

Further Reading: Astrosociological Insights Forum, vol. 10, problem 1.

  • Industry observers note that in addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Try as we might, there’s just no changing the hearts and minds of some people, even our dearest loved ones, by presenting them with inconvenient truths. I’m talking, of course, about people who prefer coffee from pods. But based on the popularity of coffee pod machines, it seems those of us who haven’t been assimilated into pod people are outnumbered. And, to be fair, even if the quality of their coffee is all over the place, we can’t deny their convenience. My goal here is to find single-serve coffee makers that can blend that convenience with coffee I actually want to drink.

Industry observers note that in addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing. So if you’re interested in the ease of pod machines, low-volume coffee brewing for one, or just can’t avoid K-cups, here are the machines that brewed the best.

Thanks to the revival of pour-over and French press coffee making and the proliferation of chic matte-finish electric kettles, there are plenty of ways to brew a single cup of coffee without a dedicated machine and, in general, they give you better results. We will also note that many fancier drip coffee makers (like our favorites from Fellow and Oxo) can now be programmed to brew just one cup of coffee at a time—and do so without the plastic waste of pods. If you want true versatility and have the counter space, we’d advise you to consider a machine that will let you brew for yourself or a crowd, if needed. But we understand the convenience factor of capsule machines, which is why, if you must pop a pod for your daily cup, we’ve made our recommendations below, plus suggested some non-pod options too.

Updated 11/25/26: Nespresso is phasing out it's old Vertuo Plus machines but never fear, the newly introduced Vertuo Up is an even better version of the original and it's our new top pick. And in other news, Keurig released its first completely K-Cup-free machine, and the new Alta platform is really quite good. That makes it the first Keurig machine we've ever recommended.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 5” x 18" x 10.5”Water reservoir capacity: 47 oz.Colors: 4Coffee sizes: 1.3 oz., 2.7 oz., 5 oz., 8 oz., 12 oz., 18 oz.

What we love: Everything we loved about the original Nespresso Vertuo machine is present in the Vertuo Up. The centrifugal brewing method patented for Vertuo machines makes more balanced, better extracted coffee than most typical pod and capsule methods that just shower the grounds with water. And Nespresso continues to expand the world of capsules you can use, now featuring a number of single origin pods for those who prefer flavor profiles from different growing regions around the world, as well as flavored pods for folks whose regular Starbucks order is 13 words long.

And the Vertuo system also reads whatever capsule you insert and automatically brews at the proper volume, so it really does have one-button operation.

The rotating water tank is a nice touch because it allows the machine to fit in any configuration of kitchen and it's very easy to refill.

But the biggest upgrade is the addition of what Nespresso calls “Coffee Creation” mode, which is particularly good for iced coffee lovers. The extra button tells the machine to brew a more concentrated, smaller dose of coffee. That means it can melt the ice without diluting the flavor of the drink. It also lets you add a healthy pour of milk to hot coffee with the same results.

Industry observers note that what we'd leave: Nespresso pods tend towards darker, roastier coffees. So if you have a thing for fruitier, more acidic coffee, you may be better off with either something that uses whole beans or Keurig's Alta.

Size: 10.84" W × 11.77" H × 19.0" DWater reservoir capacity: 72 ouncesColors: 3Coffee sizes: 1.5 oz. to 12 oz.

For a brand that’s name is pretty much synonymous with plastic pods, Keurig threw us for a loop in 2026 when it unveiled Alta, its first plastic pod-free system. Alta is still a single-serve machine and it still uses a capsule of sorts, swapping those little cups for AltaRounds, tablets of ground coffee held together by a compostable vegetable-based coating. Each AltaRound is printed with a QR code that tells the machine what drink styles it should offer up on the touchscreen display from said coffee, whether it is a smaller espresso tablet or a larger flavor coffee round.

Industry observers note that what we love: In my experience, this is the first machine with any association to Keurig that I’ve actively enjoyed the coffee from and kept returning to. For contrast, the whole time I tested the Alta, I had my usual DeLonghi machine set up but a few feet away and for weeks I didn’t touch it because the coffee I really liked the coffee I got from the Alta. There were nuances between the different roasts, from light to medium to dark, and detectably different intensities in the espresso rounds. (Keurig’s announcement states that Peet’s coffee is already on board for future AltaRounds offerings and more partnerships are on the way.).

It has been revealed that customization, while usually limited to three dots indicating temperature and brew strength, was also effective, if a bit. When selecting a milk-based drink, the frother did an impressive job of adjusting to various temperatures and thicknesses, though I did find I usually had to scoop a good bit of any super airy cold foam or cappuccino foam from the pitcher with a spoon.

Navigating the menu was clear and easy. And once I got the hang of it, I found many aspects of the Alta, like the generous 72-ounce water tank and easy to empty drip and used coffee trays, or the simple swaps from hot to iced, to be seamless and a pleasure to use.

According to recent reports, what we’d leave: First, it’s a large machine at 19 inches deep, occupying significant counter space, and while part of that has to do with the milk frothing apparatus, it’s also because the AltaRounds and separate K-cup slots are side-by-side, meaning if and when the brand just made the leap to an AltaRounds-only machine, it could probably be a good bit smaller. The automatic nature of the frother is handy, but pouring my own milk in a world of automatic dispensers on super-automatic espresso machines, left it up to me to set up the milk and do the pouring which may be more work than most Keurig converted coffee drinkers are used to. The generous water tank I called out above is slightly limiting in terms of where it allows you to set the machine up. It slides in or out from the side and if you don’t have space next to your Alta to do that, this could pose a problem. I also found the pours a bit splashy, and constantly had little droplets of coffee on the machine and on the counter nearby.

The touchscreen placement is a little wonky. It’s flat on top of the machine making it a little hard to read, and it’s actually housed in the lid for the AltaRounds slot, something that a new user (or houseguest) might not realize, as the K-cup slot is more readily discoverable with no screen and a lip for lifting it up. I fully put an AltaRound into the K-cup slot on the first go around before I more carefully read the instructions. This machine connects to WiFi, which is probably vital for downloading new coffee brand specs as more AltaRounds become available, but my software updates were sometimes sticky and required unplugging the machine to unfreeze it.

Lastly, just to harp on the elephant plastic pod in the room, the Alta as it stands feels like a bridge machine to something better, but because of the sheer magnitude of the K-cup world Keurig has created, we’re stuck with a hybrid that feels part past and part future.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 12.6"H x 4.5" W x 14" DWater reservoir capacity: 48 oz.Colors: Concrete, MidnightCoffee sizes: 4 oz., 6 oz., 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz.

In a recent development, what we love: If you’re looking for a streamlined, smart-looking machine to brew your K-cups, Chefman’s Caffeinator wraps its pod machine in a chic shell. There’s a snazzy drip tray that slides up and down for differently sized cups, and backlit touch buttons that disappear into the satin finish exterior (in Concrete or Midnight) when not selected. In addition to looking good, it also produced a pretty good cup of coffee, both from pods and grounds thanks to three simultaneous streams of water.

It offers a lot of customization possibilities, with three hot temperature options from “warm” to “piping hot” (the latter of which raised the temp about 20 degrees from default “hot”), plus a lower temp iced coffee mode, and three brew strengths in addition to multiple cup size selections. It's also compatible with both K-cups and ground coffee. All that gave me the ability to get my coffee a little closer to the way I want it, even if it comes from a plastic pod.

Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: Clearance for larger cups and tumblers is pretty low, unless you remove the drip tray entirely, which gives you 8.25" of height. But doing that leaves a ring and fixed “divot” about the width of a cupholder that some bigger travel mugs still may not fit into. I wish the water tank was a bit bigger, wasn’t rear-mounted, and had a sturdier lid, however it requires only a slight lift to remove it from the base so it’s easy to manage, even if you can’t see behind the machine. I would have also liked a place to store the K-cup/grounds adapter inserts when not using one or the other.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 15.71" H x 7.99" W x 11.47" DWater reservoir capacity: 58 oz.Color: Black Stainless (only one option)Coffee sizes: 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz., 16 oz., 20 oz., 24 oz.

According to recent reports, what we love: Why settle for stale pods when you can have freshly ground coffee at the touch of a button? This single-serve machine from Cuisinart has a built-in stainless-steel conical burr grinder that grinds beans only when you’re ready for a cup of coffee. The bean hopper holds up to half a pound of coffee beans and has a gasket-sealed lid to keep them relatively fresh (a seemingly simple feature that my fancy grinder-equipped espresso machine lacks).

I was also impressed with the fineness of the sediment that was left in the bottom of my cup using the mesh filter. You should expect anything that uses only a mesh filter to leave at least a little bit of ground coffee sediment, but in this case it wasn’t unappealing during the last sips. If that is the sort of thing that bothers you, the basket is also paper filter compatible. Grinding and brewing are relatively quiet operations that probably won’t wake anyone up, and gentle beeps let you know your coffee is ready. Also, while you’ll need to find a carafe or container that fits under the machine, the fact that the Cuisinart can brew up to 24 oz. of hot coffee means you could, in a pinch, use this for a few guests over for brunch.

What we’d leave: Cleaning the filter after every use is a chore (and some people choose single-serve machines specifically to avoid that chore by using pods) That remarked, there are more gentle beeps to remind you the filter access door hasn’t been opened since the last brew, so at least you won’t forget. Clearance for cups, even with the drip tray completely removed, is still rather low for travel cups at just seven inches. Also, when brewing at the 24 oz. setting, the coffee was noticeably weaker than smaller cup sizes.

Size: 11.5" H x 7.5" W x 10.6" D (plus positionable water tank)Water reservoir capacity: 20-plus oz.Colors: Black, Linen (white)Coffee sizes: 5 oz.–20 oz.

Sources indicate that what we love: Portland, Oregon–based Ratio takes its coffee maker design seriously, including its smallest entry, the Ratio Four, so named because it brews a maximum of four 5-oz. cups of coffee in a single batch. The machine couldn’t be simpler; it uses one button that brews however much water is in the reservoir and a filter basket with flat bottom paper filters. Turn it on, and the first of three lights illuminates to let you know it’s in Bloom mode, followed by Brew and Ready when your coffee is done. The Ratio heats brewing water to an average of 200º F and has a wide stainless-steel showerhead that evenly wets the coffee grounds, producing a full 20-oz. brew that was robust, strong, and exactly what I like to wake up to.

It has been revealed that but we’re here to talk about single-serve coffee, and while using it for one cup is a little trickier (you’ll have to measure smaller quantities of water and coffee), the Four delivered the same bold, balanced brew in a 5-oz. cup, it did in a 20-oz. carafe. I found the recommended 9 grams of coffee lacking, but the instructions advise customizing the ratio a bit, and sure enough a few more grams in the filter did the trick. I found I got the tastiest results brewing two cups (10 oz.), as I think the longer siphoning and heating process with more water flowing through the system was key to a more satisfying extraction. Plus, I like a substantial cup of coffee.

The Ratio Four comes with a handblown 20-oz. glass carafe that also has a sealed lid and a silicone padded bottom. But what I appreciated is the ability to brew directly into any container; there is no hidden button or latch that the carafe needs to activate to brew or let water through. I could use a mug or travel tumbler if I wanted to. And, surprisingly, the same goes for the filter basket, with the Ratio website and instruction booklet explaining that they’d be just fine with you using it with a Kalita Wave or Origami pour-over dripper if you want. A long-press of the brew button also lets you choose between the default (4 oz. of water) bloom and a shorter (2 oz.) bloom, which is preferable if you are brewing a single cup.

It has been revealed that all of the removable parts are hand-wash-only, but I never found them needing more than a rinse between uses. The instructions recommend occasional cleaning and descaling with an approved solution to keep the lines clean, though, which is important maintenance for any coffee maker.

It has an external, detached water tank that takes up more counter space than it would if it were flush with the machine, but that cuts both ways. I actually love that it’s connected via a sturdy yet flexible hose, allowing you to position it on either side of the machine in a variety of ways depending on your specific needs.

Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: Ratio is a brand known for machines with parts that feel very high quality, as senior editor Noah Kaufman has pointed out in his reviews of its other two machines. Some of the Ratio Four’s parts are definitely in line with that reputation, like the heavy braided hose between the brewer and water tank. But there are exterior parts of the brewer that do feel less substantial than you might expect for something that costs $279. I also found myself double-checking that the filter basket was installed correctly, because it doesn’t click or snap to signal it’s on right.

“Set it and forget it” coffee drinkers should take note that the water reservoir isn’t “smart,” meaning it will brew whatever water is inside, so a full reservoir with a coffee mug underneath will overflow. If that’s something you don’t want to think about, the Cuisinart Custom Grind and Brew might serve you better as it requires less frequent refills.

Size: 19" x 6" x 16"Water reservoir capacity: 80 oz.Colors: 2Coffee sizes: 2 oz., 10 oz.

Industry observers note that what we love: We have an in-depth review of the Cumulus cold-brew machine for more details, but here’s the gist: You could, in some ways, consider this the Nespresso of cold coffee with its recyclable aluminum capsules that are filled an even more concentrated cold-brew concentrate. The machine does the job of chilling water via an onboard compressor, meaning you don’t need ice in your cup. For texture, the Cumulus offers three settings—still, nitro, and espresso—making it one of the best machines we’ve tried for cold coffee connoisseurs. (Oh, and it achieves that “nitro” coffee without any gas canisters by using ambient air.) It vacuums out the capsules, leaving them empty and ready to recycle after you’re done brewing. And at just 6", wide it’s got a relatively small footprint and front-loading water reservoir, making it easy to use and keep on the countertop.

What we’d leave: At its current nearly $700 price tag, this is a luxury item—though, if you’re dropping $5 on cold brew every day, maybe it isn’t?

With so many brands and varieties of pods out there, I did my best to compare apples to apples by using Starbucks pods and beans of the same roast for every machine (Bruvi being the only exception that doesn’t sell Starbucks pods). That’s not because the global corporate coffee giant is my favorite coffee roaster, but because it is the most cross-pollinated among all types of machines and formats. For Keurig machines, I also tested using K-cups from Illy coffee, which I’ve found produce stronger coffee (an attribute testers often flag as missing from Keurigs). I used fresh grounds for any machines that offered a refillable pod and whole beans of the same roast were used on machines with grinding capabilities. I also tested the different brew size, strength, and style options on any machine with multiple settings.

Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of subpar single-cup coffee makers out there, and life is short, so we don’t think bad coffee needs to be a part of it. We looked for coffee pod machines that delivered balanced flavor and a smooth finish with consistency.

In a recent development, are the pods simple to load and is the interface (buttons or screens) intuitive and simple? Does the water reservoir require constant refill oversight, and is it easy to access? Does the machine require regular cleaning or maintenance to keep working? The ease of use should extend to pod collection and disposal as well. Some machines require emptying the coffee pod chamber after each use. Others collect them for occasional disposal or recycling.

Pod coffee makers don’t need to take up too much space, but they can also be too small, relying on heating and brewing elements that sacrifice on quality. And because most regular coffee drinkers won’t be putting their machine away every day, it should look good on your countertop too.

According to recent reports, pods are a problem. There’s no way around it. No coffee brewing option will be as ecologically sound as simply pouring water over grounds (and then composting those grounds if you can). Yes, technically you can tear apart Keurig pods, empty their spent coffee into your compost bin and the filter into the trash, and then recycle the plastic cup portion. But overall, we can’t get behind any machine that requires plastic pods that aren’t easily recyclable. Machines that operate using a reusable pod were also given some bonus points.

It has been revealed that you’d be hard-pressed to find a better looking coffee machine than the Terra Kaffe Demi. It’s stylish, it comes in four colors, and it’s relatively small for something with a built-in grinder at just over 7" wide—however, it’s nearly 16" deep, and you’ll need access to both sides of the machine, plus the reservoir housed on the back. (If you opt for the milk-frothing TK-02 option, it’ll be wider and deeper still.) Aside from brewing great espresso and pretty great coffee, the most impressive aspect of the Terra Kaffe is how quiet it is. Compared to the cacophony my similarly priced grind-and-brew automatic espresso machine makes, the Demi barely produced a sound.

Generally, I liked the espresso results I got from the Terra Kaffee more than I liked the drip coffee. Once I dialed in my preferred drip settings—which you can adjust for any of the machine’s four drink presets after navigating a maze of menus and submenus—I was impressed with the rich flavor and texture of the coffee with no hint of sediment at the bottom of the cup. For what’s essentially a super-automatic espresso machine with no milk frothing, it’s expensive (commitment-phobes can rent it for $40 a month), so it wouldn’t be my first choice to simply fill a mug in the morning. But if you toggle back and forth between coffee and espresso, it’s comparably priced with other super automatic machines, and it offers a sleek and almost silent option.

This touchscreen pod machine is everything we wish most K-cup machines could be. It offers rich, balanced, and nuanced coffee, plus eight brewing sizes, one-touch presets for low-acid, americano, iced coffee (which brews hot over ice), and cold brew (which uses cooler water), as well as simple customizations to any of these like temperature control and brew strength. And it does all this using its own proprietary pods made with specially treated polypropylene, which will (mostly) break down in a landfill. So other than you need to use its proprietary coffee pods, Bruvi offers all of the convenience of capsules and the fancy-pants settings of high-end coffee makers and good coffee with little downside.

In a recent development, an espresso machine but make it Nespresso. That’s the idea behind the Creatista series from Nespresso, which adds the automatic milk steaming perfected by Breville, bootstraps it on to a Nespresso Vertuo machine, and wraps the whole thing in handsome stainless steel. It’s great for someone looking for a cappuccino hack. Ultimately we picked the Keurig Alta over the Creatista for this genre of machine because it’s a little less expensive and offers a little more versatility in the form of cold foam options.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville.

The Vertuo Plus does everything the Vertuo Up does sans the iced coffee and full carafe brewing features. The major knock on it is that it's being phased out to make way for several other Vertuo machines. But it's still available from third party retailers like Williams Sonoma and Amazon right, often for pretty affordable prices.

According to recent reports, the Essenza Mini comes from Nespresso’s Original line, which uses smaller capsules and only brews 1.35-oz. espresso shots or 3.7-oz. Lungo cups of coffee. And it does so using 19 bars of pressure for extraction, as opposed to the VertuoLine’s centrifugal extraction method. It doesn’t make plain old cups of coffee, however, but we’ve included it here as a good option for pod coffee drinkers who prefer espresso drinks and want a simple way to make beverages like cappuccinos and macchiatos.

It has been revealed that like its larger Moccamaster brethren, Cup-One has a timeless, old-school design and a single, tactile glowing “on” switch would make it look at home in a truck stop diner or a trendy modern apartment. And speaking of diners, the coffee, even in a 10-oz. default brew, was diner quality (I mean that affectionately), with robust flavor and texture—though that may have had something to do with the fact that I used the recommended four tablespoons of grounds, twice what other machines suggest for eight oz. Considering its higher price tag, it appears to be pretty low-tech. Okay, okay, it’s just an automatic pour-over machine. But it brewed one of the best single cups from grounds I’ve had from any drip machine. And it’s quiet with no bubbling or burping. What can I say? The small footprint and retro vibes also won me over. It’s a small luxury. It’s a vibe. As the kids say, it’s aesthetic.

In a recent development, now for the minuses: Yes, you could get a (really nice) gooseneck kettle and pour-over system for, like, half the cost. Give and take. Low clearance under the drip spout means you’re stuck with brewing into mugs and low-profile tumblers. The included measuring scoop and a needle-like poking tool for clearing the filter holder have no home onboard the machine, adding to your “things we need to keep but don’t know where else to put” drawer.

Sources indicate that of all the podless machines, this one is the most podlike in its convenience while producing pod-beating coffee. The eponymous Scoop is a small mesh filter that doubles as a measuring spoon. Just scoop up (or in) your grounds to the maximum fill line, and you’re good to go. The Scoop sits in a second “grounds catching” mesh filter which, in my tests, reduced silt in my cup compared to similar single-filter systems, but didn’t eliminate it. Using the two size settings, you can brew either 8 oz. or 14 oz. per cup. The coffee it produced on normal brew mode was fine, but tapping the BOLD setting did actually produce much more robust results. However, each cup I made was on the oily side.

A flip-down drip tray holds standard mugs, while the lower drip tray has a clearance of 7", so lots of travel tumblers stand a chance. The 40-oz. water reservoir is on the small side, but is easy to access and lift off from either side with a molded-in handle.

Sources indicate that when you’re done, simple empty and rinse The Scoop (filter) and, if necessary, the secondary filter, and you can brew another cup right away. That’s as long as your Scoop filter is dry, anyway. If it’s still damp from the last cup, you’re going to need to scoop into The Scoop, which basically just makes this like any other small filter machine.

4-in-1 Single-Serve Latte, Iced, and Hot Coffee Maker.

When you think of Mr. Coffee, you probably think of a basic, no-frills drip machine sitting on your grandparents’ countertop. And, for the most part, this multifunction machine is still just a small, simple rain-shower-style drip coffee maker designed for one-cup-at-a-time brewing. The reservoir and reusable mesh filter sit under the lid and feature graduated measurements for water levels from 4 oz. up to 16 oz. You can fill the removable filter with grounds using a double-ended measuring scoop that nests on the side of the machine and has guidelines for different sizes and styles of coffee, whether you’re brewing a “shot” for milk-based drinks or a tumbler full of iced coffee. The bonus of this machine is that, while still retaining a small footprint, it also includes a decent self-contained, stainless-steel milk frother cup with presets for hot milk and cold foam that can be used completely independently from the coffee-making portion.

As for taste and texture, everything was like middle-of-the-road drip coffee. However, I found that following the instructions for the weakest iced coffee (one large scoop) actually gave me decent results that weren’t as watered down as other machines on this list. It also comes with a 22-oz. plastic tumbler just for iced coffee—and enough brewing clearance to fit such a large cup—so if you’re someone who flip-flops between iced and hot coffee and aren’t too finicky about dialing in precise strength, it’s a practical option.

System Coffee and Espresso Machine.

Sources indicate that if, for whatever reason, you want to brew Nespresso pods but don’t want to actually get a Nespresso machine, the L’or is your choice. It brews Original Nespresso pods along with its own proprietary pods (which are cross-compatible with classic Nespresso machines). L’or’s brewer offers three brewing sizes and extracts coffee from the pod at 19 bars of pressure through two spouts, similar to the way coffee comes out of a semiautomatic espresso machine. This produces a delicious layer of crema that’s as good as Nespresso’s. It was only in a head-to-head matchup that we slightly preferred Nespresso.

Industry observers note that if you like the idea of Nespresso but not the idea of being stuck with one-cup-at-at-time brewing, the Vertuo Next has brew sizes ranging from a single shot of espresso up to 18 oz. of coffee with the proper pods (an optional carafe is available for the biggest brews). This smart machine also has Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, so you can track your favorite pods and get firmware updates. However, the Next is a smaller machine than the Vertuo Plus, and with that comes a smaller water tank. And like the Vertuo Pop+ below, the closing and locking mechanism is a bit clunkier than we’d like. But for all out versatility, it’s probably your best Nespresso brewing option.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for a K-cup-compatible coffee machine that can do a little more, this is a good option. It comes with a reusable filter capsule that, while a little finicky getting it to work properly, does, indeed, work. It also has a 72-oz. water tank for less-frequent refills, as well as settings for five cup sizes and two brewing temperatures. The biggest boost we’ll give this machine is that it produced superior tasting coffee using K-cups than any Keurig machine we’ve tried.

In a recent development, we like almost all Nespresso machines, but we think the three recommended above are better than the Vertuo Pop+ for a few reasons. On the Pop+, the actual snapping down of the lid to puncture the pod inside was the clunkiest of the bunch and a lot of effort in a pre-coffee morning fog. And this low-profile machine was so low to the counter, we couldn’t fit a pint glass or similarly sized tumbler underneath, which was a problem considering that Nespresso offers Iced Leggero pods that brew 7.7 oz., overflowing our smaller ice-filled cups. Lastly, the water reservoir on the standard version of this machine (which comes in at 25.4 oz. or 32 oz. on the Deluxe model) is pretty small compared to the Vertuo Plus, and it’s set in a fixed side-mounted position, so you’re stuck with the orientation as is. In other words, it’s still a solid Nespresso coffee brewer but less versatile than what you get for a few dollars more.

According to recent reports, you might consider this machine Lavazza’s attempt to answer the classic Nespresso; its plastic coffee pods and presets brew in espresso or lungo sizes. It beats the Keurig and K-cup machines when it comes to robust and flavorful coffee, but it didn’t live up to the high bar set by Nespresso. The Ristretto capsules we tried were a bit bitter and the texture was thin, though we actually liked the medium-roast decaf capsules enough as after dinner/dessert coffee. Considering Lavazza makes capsules for both Nespresso classic machines and K-cup machines, along with other espresso products, we just don’t think it’s necessary to buy into the Lavazza tech—as sleek and compact as it is—to enjoy its coffee.

Recent findings suggest that the dual on this machine refers to both drip coffee and coffee pods. It offers multiple brew sizes and strengths, and, being a drip machine first, comes with a glass carafe. It accepts pods with an adapter that fits into the filter basket. Some of its handier features are an adjustable 60-oz. water reservoir, dedicated hot water dispenser, fold-away milk frother, and an adjustable drip tray that allows you to brew directly into a cup or tumbler. But we don’t think it’s the best drip coffee maker out there, and it’s too substantial and complex for just making capsule coffee.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot to like about the exterior design of this slimmed down version a Ninja single-serve system, from its pleasing colorways like stone, sage green, and glacier blue (in addition to black), its handy fold-away frothing wand that easily whipped some pre-warmed milk into a mug full of foam, or its storage nooks for the pod/grounds adapters and measuring spoon. The generous water tank, while rear-mounted, has a pressure fit lid that actually stays put between the faucet and counter. And all of its detachable parts and pieces are dishwasher-safe. But whether you’ll crave the actual coffee from this machine is another story. Pods tasted weak, even at the lower 6-oz. brewing size, and grounds were better but not by very much. The Specialty Brew setting, which brews a 4-oz. shot of coffee for use with the frother, isn’t quite an espresso experience, either. And while you can choose multiple cup sizes, you can’t select anything but the preset temperature.

Despite its 4.4 stars from over 100,000 ratings on Amazon, we can’t imagine using this machine for coffee every day. Our experience with Keurig coffee pods, regardless of the brand of coffee we tried, was watery or bitter coffee (or, at worst, somehow both). That, plus the fact that this machine’s reservoir is only large enough for one cup at a time makes this one tedious for regular use.

Unfortunately, the “smart” features of this machine add more frustration than anything. The machine is supposed to recognize which K-cup you put inside and adjust its brew settings accordingly. It also allows you to select and save brew sizes and temperatures as presets. But in our tests, the machine frequently froze and had to be unplugged to get it going again. Being “smart,” this machine also offers app-enabled remote brewing, something we can’t imagine using since you have to put K-cups in (and take used cups out) one at a time. One plus was the generous 66-oz. water reservoir with a convenient pitcher handle. But in the end, this fancy Keurig didn’t improve our pod coffee experience whatsoever.

In a recent development, as iced coffee rivals hot coffee consumption these days, it’s no wonder Keurig would offer a machine that specializes in cold drinks. One aspect of this machine that’s well thought-out is its dispensing spout, which is high enough off the counter to accommodate a pint glass or tumbler. We found the iced coffee setting only reduced the brew temperature by less than 10°, so our ice still had to do most of the work while also watering the coffee down, which was already diluted with 12 oz. of water during brewing. Even on the smallest of three preprogramed hot coffee brew sizes, it mirrored our other Keurig experiences with weak or just not tasty coffee output.

Oxo 8-cup Coffee Maker with Podless Single Serve Function.

Sources indicate that even though this is an 8-cup coffee maker, I tested this machine because it proudly advertises on the box that it’s also a single-serve machine. Let me get one thing out of the way immediately: This is a great little drip coffee maker if you’re brewing by the carafe. It has the option to brew full and half carafes, and a heated warming plate that keeps the coffee pleasantly hot for hours. But it fell short on a few functional aspects, as well as that single-serve option. First, the water tank is not “smart”—as in, it uses all the water you put in it every time. So if you want a full carafe, you fill it all the way up with water, and if you want a single cup, you put in just enough for… two cups. No, it doesn’t actually brew a single serving of coffee. For a $200-plus machine purporting to do single-serve brewing that can go toe-to-toe with Keurig, that’s a little disappointing.

Additional testing and reporting by Emily Farris.

The Gifts Chefs and Bartenders Actually Want This Year

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streetwear cooking shoes, a perfect pepper mill, and more.
  • If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission.
  • This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streetwear cooking shoes, a perfect pepper mill, and more.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up. We know that you’ve probably been given a few too many wine glasses and cookbooks. “As a professional, I don’t want to be gifted introductory-level items that will ultimately go unused,” says Storm Brunni, private dining director at Barolo Grill in Denver. That’s why, for our guide, we’ve consulted you, the hospitality pros, about what you actually would like to receive this year.

New shoes for service. “I’m getting all of my favorite people the new high-top kitchen shoes by Chuck Taylor in leather anti-slip. They’re cool enough to complete your streetwear look, functional enough to wear in the dining room, kitchen, or work, and comfy enough to wear as a commuter.” —Jonathon Sawyer, chef at Kindling in Chicago.

According to recent reports, an industry-favorite hand cream. “Between constant handwashing, citrus, chiles, and hot pans, hospitality hands take a beating. Add a heated neck massager to use on the couch after a midnight close, and you’ve basically given someone a spa day.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef at Casa Oaxaca in Newly introduced York City.

Something for the coffee nerds. “It’s definitely a splurge, but I buy myself the Onyx Coffee Advent Calendar every year. A lot of hospitality pros nerd out about coffee, and Onyx is one of the best roasters. They fill the calendar with individual portions of beans (enough for two people) with different origins, roasts, and processes every day. Everything is roasted on a schedule so that when you’re brewing each one, the coffee is at its peak that day. The calendar has some of their signature coffees, alongside one-offs that you’ll never be able to get again, and I’ve tried some of the best coffees of my life in past calendars.” —Katie Renshaw, owner of Bar Bambi in Chicago.

An upgrade for kitchen organization. “I love this automatic tape dispenser. Gift it with a nice fresh box of Sharpies.” —Kevin Beary, beverage director of Gus’ Sip & Dip, Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, Three Dots and a Dash in Chicago.

In a recent development, the gift of longer-lasting produce. “Vejibag is a family-owned business, run by a small team of women who create 100 percent organic cotton bags designed to keep produce fresher for longer at home. They genuinely work and are an amazing addition to any kitchen.” —Lauren DeSteno, executive chef at Ai Fiori in New York City.

Industry observers note that A tool for operators who know there’s always something that needs fixing. “I was given a precision screwdriver from HOTO Tools and now I’m obsessed with the brand and their design aesthetic. So many things in the restaurants need little fixes all the time and the 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro has all the bits you could need. I also love their rotary drill for polishing plateware with chips/scratches for work.” —Zach Engel, chef at Galit and Cafe Yaya in Chicago.

Gifts with a personal touch. “As a general manager some of the top staff requests I’ve received are for nice wine keys (it’s an even nicer touch if they’re engraved) and custom server books.” —John Schneekloth, general manager at Toro in Chicago.

Nice dishware is worthwhile at home, too. “I’d love to receive items from Ivo Angel, a beautiful ceramics firm out of Italy. I am a huge fan of the splatter design and always want a pinch bowl; I can’t have too many. Also the olive bowl with an attached vessel for pits is perfect for hosting.” —Julia Jaksoc, chef and owner of Bar Roza, Cafe Roze and Roze Pony in Nashville.

The pepper mill that chefs swear by. “It’s one of those tools that gets used constantly, makes a real difference, and is something every cook or bartender would appreciate having.” —Marco Torres, Chef at Brass and The Tusk Bar in Latest York City.

Industry observers note that fun socks. “Being locked down in heavy black pants, unforgiving non-slip shoe leathers, and a stiff chef coat means you have to find your personality somewhere. A pair of loud, ridiculous socks underneath always makes me feel a little more human. I’ll never forget getting this pair of bright yellow Spam socks as a Christmas gift one year. Honestly, it’s one of the best presents I’ve ever unwrapped, and it brings a little joy each time I slip them on.” —Soo Ahn, chef/partner at Adalina Prime, Arla and Adalina Italian in Chicago.

Something to take the edge off. “For the industry pro who enjoys a little puff puff and a good nap (especially after a Saturday morning shift with lines out the door), you can’t go wrong with Tokin’ Jew rolling papers. We sell them at the deli because, come on, but they’re also a fantastic gift. And for the pipe people, their pickle pipes are another way to keep it kosher.” —Jake Schneider, chef and co-owner of Schneider Deli in Chicago.

Recent findings suggest that A beautiful book for recipe writing. “I would gift this brown leather journal cover from Shinola along with this 12-pack of pens. I think the notebook is a worthwhile splurge, and while I know the idea of a more expensive and elegant pen is both compelling and sexy, it is also impractical for when you’re on the go or as prone to losing nice pens as I am. These ones write fluidly and beautifully.” —Róbert LeBlanc, creative director and founder of LeBlanc + Smith in New Orleans.

Industry observers note that the kitchen fit of your dreams. “I could wear this jumpsuit 24/7! It’s comfortable, easy to move around in, and perfect for those long days in the kitchen when I’m constantly running around and want something that looks as good as it feels.” —Andrea Belfiore, chef and founder of EVÈNTO in New York City.

Sources indicate that A tool for foraging. “I love my ARS pruning shears. I take them pretty much everywhere when I’m out foraging, and they’re great for everything from cutting herbs to collecting branches and other ingredients for drinks. They’re one of those tools I use all the time.” —Danny Childs, co-owner of Field Day in Philadelphia.

It has been revealed that A trio of pastry chef staples. “On any given day, a pastry professional will produce dozens of recipes, and we need tools to measure mass/weight, time, and temperature. Even when we have our own, backups or better ones are always welcome! My top picks include: this scale, which has a pull-out screen when you’re scaling on to sheet trays or large bowls; this kitchen timer has four color-coded channels for timing multiple projects at once; and this thermometer, which is fast-reading, accurate, and has a magnet on the back for easy access on any magnetic surface.” —Orlando Soto, executive pastry chef of Le Bernardin in Fresh York City.

It has been revealed that the perfect vessel for an industry-favorite amaro (or 50/50 shot). “Some of the best hospitality happens in an ounce and a half: a pour of Cynar for a regular who had a long week, a welcome taste for someone newly introduced at the bar. I’d recommend these little ceramic artichoke shot glasses to make that moment feel even more considered.” —Steven Waters, owner and operator of Fino in Denver.

Sources indicate that many knife options. Patrick Dooley of Harry’s Bar in Paris recommends Le Grand Tradi, which is sized between a paring and chef’s knife, making it a great workhorse option, while Nancy Santiago, beverage director at NYC’s IGC Hospitality, recommends a Japanese petty knife “for precise citrus work and garnish prep.” Amir Babayoff of Ophelia Lounge in NYC is partial to Tojiro’s chef knives.

And knife storage and upkeep options. Schneekloth of Toro recommends a knife backpack, while Devin Denzer, chef at Atsumeru in Chicago, recommends a whetstone and ceramic sharpening rod, especially for newer line cooks.

In a recent development, A thoughtful gift card. “Here are a few gifts that I have received that stood out to me: a hefty gift card to a sought-after restaurant with guaranteed reservations on a night off, which is such a good way to give someone a night out; a gift card to a shoe store that carries high-quality work shoes, like Red Wings, Dansko, or Blundstones; and a gift card to something wellness-related—my business partner Jesse got me three sessions at a body-stretching spa downtown.” —Phila Lorn, chef and co-owner of Mawn and Sao in Philadelphia.

#134696. Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (648 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.
  • Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption.
  • It has been revealed that the characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A newly introduced study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

It has been revealed that the characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

It has been revealed that A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

In a recent development, “This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang remarked.

Industry observers note that aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

According to recent reports, water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

To put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

Recent findings suggest that “This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”.

Industry News: A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that highly-evolved stars spread the material for upcoming planets and stars into space with their stellar winds.
  • It has been revealed that the material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind.
  • Researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that highly-evolved stars spread the material for upcoming planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

It has been revealed that the material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are key parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

Researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The research is "A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

Industry observers note that "Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe.".

It has been revealed that since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

According to recent reports, âFor decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the starâs outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release.

This schematic indicates the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics.

Sources indicate that astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

Recent findings suggest that recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Industry observers note that both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

Recent findings suggest that this time-lapse shows ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

Sources indicate that âWe were astonished to see how the starâs surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," remarked study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

In a recent development, but the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

Industry observers note that âIn 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the starâs surface, but it didnât stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadnât seen anything like that before," mentioned co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

Masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

Recent findings suggest that âIn the loop, thereâs a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the starâs wind. That showed us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," noted Vlemmings.

Recent findings suggest that this figure from the research demonstrates a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

Industry observers note that for now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

Sources indicate that the flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a newly introduced element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections, where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

âNow we see that magnetic storms on Miraâs surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the starâs outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,â said Andriantsaralaza.

This research demonstrates that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

Industry observers note that "The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae, the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

"Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

âOur study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxyâs ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldnât be here if it wasnât for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," mentioned Vlemmings.
