📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have narrowed down when three massive collisions reshaped the Moon, bringing them closer to understanding why its Earth-facing side looks so different from its far side.

According to recent reports, billions of years ago, a collision powerful enough to melt enormous quantities of lunar rock created the Moon’s largest impact basin. Subsequent collisions broke apart and scattered some of that ancient material across the surface, leaving behind a geological record that scientists are now piecing together.

Located on the Moon’s far side, the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the oldest and largest impact structures in the solar system. Understanding its history could help explain why the Moon’s near and far sides are so different, what lies beneath its surface, and when major collisions occurred during its early evolution.

An international research team led by Professor Guochun Zhao, Mok Sau-King, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), and Dr. Yuqi Qian, the study’s first author, has identified two types of magnesium-rich rocks with remarkably different origins. Published in Science Advances, the research also establishes a clearer timeline of the major impacts that shaped the region.

Industry observers note that for decades, the basin remained largely unexplored. That changed in 2019, when Chang’e-4 completed the first successful landing on the Moon’s far side, followed in 2024 by Chang’e-6, which brought the first rock samples from this largely unexplored region back to Earth.

Using Chang’e-6 samples allocated to HKU DEPS and surface measurements from both missions, the researchers obtained the first direct geological evidence from the two landing sites for reconstructing the basin’s impact history. Satellite observations and numerical simulations helped them trace the origins of rocks across the wider basin.

It has been revealed that one group of rocks, known as moderately magnesium-rich norites, formed in the aftermath of the original SPA collision. The impact generated a thick sheet of molten rock that gradually cooled, with different minerals crystallizing at different stages. Later collisions exposed these ancient rocks at the central peaks of large craters. Some were eventually blasted toward the Chang’e-4 landing site in Von Kármán crater by the impact that formed Finsen crater.

The second group contained considerably more magnesium and likely formed through a separate process called magnesium-suite magmatism, a type of magma activity associated with the original SPA impact. These rocks were exposed along the western ring of mountain peaks within the Apollo basin before the Chaffee S impact scattered some of them toward the Chang’e-6 landing site.

Earlier research by the HKU-led team had already uncovered evidence of prolonged volcanic activity and previously unrecognized magma activity in the region. Those studies also suggested that underground accumulations of titanium-rich minerals, known as ilmenite-bearing cumulates, helped account for the contrasting volcanic histories of the Moon’s two sides.

In a recent development, the latest findings suggest that the South Pole-Aitken basin formed approximately 4.34 billion years ago. Another major collision created the Apollo basin around 4.2 billion years ago, followed by the formation of the Orientale basin approximately 3.87 billion years ago. Together, these three events reveal how successive collisions reshaped the Moon’s largest impact basin over hundreds of millions of years.

It has been revealed that reference: “Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6” by Yuqi Qian, Wenlei Song, James Head, Mingyu Tian, Zhuang Guo, Harald Hiesinger, Carolyn H. van der Bogert, Le Zhang, Jingyou Chen, Wanfeng Zhang, Ziqing Li, Lingzhi Sun, Xiangsong Wang, Wei-Ran Li, Jiacheng Liu, Nicolas Dauphas, Yi-Gang Xu and Guochun Zhao, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh9798.

Viking has taken delivery of the Viking Libra, its newest ocean ship, at Fincantieri’s shipyard in Ancona, Italy.

The 998-guest ship will sail itineraries in the Mediterranean and Northern Europe in her inaugural season.

She is a sister to the rest of Viking’s ocean fleet, but unlike the others she has a hybrid propulsion system designed to run on liquefied hydrogen and fuel cells.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer’s next ocean ship, the Viking Astrea, is under construction and will have the same system. Viking expects both ships to be operating on hydrogen in 2027.

“The delivery of the Viking Libra is a proud moment for Viking and an important milestone in our growing ocean fleet,” said Leah Talactac, president and CEO of Viking.

“Together with the Viking Astrea, she will set a new standard for innovation as we bring this technology into operation in 2027 and will allow us to welcome even more curious travelers to explore the world in Viking comfort,” she added.

Under its committed orderbook, Viking expects to take delivery of 25 more river ships by 2030, 10 more ocean ships by 2032 and two more expedition ships by 2031.

Those deliveries would bring the company’s fleet to 123 river ships in 2030 and 28 ocean and expedition ships in 2032.

Recently China has been busily sending landers and rovers to the site, and a newly introduced paper, published in Science Advances, details the actual samples returned to Earth by the Changâe-6 mission and combines them with the in-situ data from the Changâe-4 mission and rover. Those details combine to form a complete geological history of the major impacts that formed the basin, and some insight into the age of other impact craters scattered throughout the solar system.

Industry observers note that A sense of scale and time helps in understanding the SPA. Itâs roughly 2,200 kilometers across, making it similar in length to the north-south axis of mainland China. And it runs up to 10 kilometers deep, much deeper than any comparable land-based feature on Earth. For a long time, astronomers and planetary scientists have been debating how old it is, with dates ranging from 4.35 billion years ago to around 4.2 billion. That discrepancy is part of what the fresh paper hopes to solve, but thereâs another larger discrepancy it hopes to solve as well.

According to recent reports, the two halves of the Moon - the one that faces us and the one facing away - appear very different in terms of their features. The nearside is covered in smooth, dark plains called âmariaâ, whereas the far side has many more craters, with almost no volcanic plains and a thick layer of crust sitting on top. This difference, known as the âlunar dichotomy,â has stumped scientists for years. To solve it, many have turned to the SPA.

Fraser talks about collecting the Chang'e-6 moon rocks.

Sources indicate that SPA was formed during a gigantic ancient collision that broke through the crust on the far side and exposed underground rock that had been buried since the Moonâs formation. But the main crater isnât the only one in the area. Various smaller craters have formed overlapping the main one, including the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater (where Changâe-4 landed with its Yutu-2 rover) and the 490-kilometer-wide Apollo basin, where Changâe-6 landed and that was created by a separate impact.

According to recent reports, crucially, those impacts created different types of magnesium-rich igneous rocks. One type, found by Changâe-4 in the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater, is known as moderately magnesium-rich norite. It crystallized directly from the vast sea of molten rock generated when the SPA-forming asteroid slammed into the Moon. Over millions of years, the lava lake this created cooled, and the minerals separated out into layers. Later impacts then pushed the solid rocks up to the peaks of newly formed craters, and eventually another impact known as the Finsen impact blasted pieces of that cooled lava lake into Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater for Changâe-4 to find.

According to recent reports, another type of rock held even higher levels of magnesium. It was created via a process called magnesium-suite magmatism. When the SPA impact broke the Moonâs crust, the magma from its then liquid interior broke into the crust, cooling underneath its top layer. Later, the impact that created the Apollo basin pushed those now cooled materials up into its western peak ring, and then another impact that created whatâs now known as the Chaffee S crater blasted pieces of rock directly into the path of plains where Changâe-6 collected them billions of years later.

Fraser talks about the Chang'e-6 mission collecting lunar samples.

Itâs kind of cool to think that those fragments have been waiting billions of years for us to find and study them.

Experimental Drug Shrinks Tumors in Two of the Hardest-To-Treat Cancers

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.
  • According to recent reports, when pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options.
  • The drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.

According to recent reports, when pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options. In some patients, the difficulty lies in genetic mutations that keep cancer cells growing and have historically been difficult to target with drugs. An experimental cancer drug called ERAS-0015 has shown promising results in an early clinical trial, shrinking tumors in patients who had already undergone other forms of treatment.

The drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division. In healthy cells, RAS proteins act like molecular switches, turning on when cells receive signals to grow and turning off when those signals are no longer needed. Certain genetic mutations can leave these switches stuck in the “on” position, continuously instructing cells to grow and helping sustain cancer.

For years, scientists struggled to develop drugs capable of interfering with these faulty proteins. ERAS-0015 takes an approach known as a pan-RAS molecular glue. It works by bringing proteins together at the molecular level and is designed to bind to RAS while the switch is active, blocking growth signals associated with several different cancer-driving RAS mutations.

“The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient’s mutation, or the ‘Achilles Heel’ of a specific individual’s cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations,” said Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute in Sarasota, Florida.

Wang presented findings from 148 patients participating in the phase I AURORAS-1 clinical trial on November 19, 2026, at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

The trial began in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 both alone and in combination with other anticancer therapies. Participants include people with pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread beyond the original tumor site, and other solid tumors driven by RAS mutations. The results presented at the symposium included 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC. The trial is continuing to enroll patients.

It has been revealed that “AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients that have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer. A ‘response’ means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer. In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects,” Wang told the symposium.

These response rates came from relatively small groups of patients receiving a 32 mg dose of the drug. Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer who had previously received chemotherapy and in three of five patients with lung cancer who had previously been treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer, or platinum-based chemotherapy.

Industry observers note that researchers gradually increased doses of ERAS-0015 from 2 mg to 40 mg to evaluate how well patients tolerated the drug. After a median follow-up of just over four months, there was no indication that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

Recent findings suggest that at doses of 16 to 32 mg, the most common side effects, affecting at least 10% of patients, were rash, diarrhea, nausea, and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) experienced severe treatment-related side effects, classified as grade 3 or higher. No dose-limiting side effects were reported.

“We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients that have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer,” said Wang.

Sources indicate that “Our goal is to give clinicians upcoming, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options.”.

It has been revealed that phase I clinical trials involve relatively small numbers of patients and are primarily designed to evaluate safety and determine appropriate doses. Although the tumor shrinkage observed in this trial provides an early indication of the drug’s potential, larger phase II and phase III clinical trials will be necessary to confirm its safety and effectiveness.

Recent findings suggest that “If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1,” Wang concluded.

Professor Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology’s clinical research program, was not involved in the study. She commented: “This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging anti-tumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

“This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently.”.

Meeting: 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR SYMPOSIUM.

Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space.
  • According to recent reports, modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem.
  • Sources indicate that unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space. JPl physicist Dr. Slava Turyshev, who wrote the paper at the center of that article, also published a follow-up study in August, available in preprint on arXiv, about how getting the hardware off the ground is only half the battle. Once all that equipment is up there, someone, or something, is going to have to maintain it.

According to recent reports, modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem. The computer chips and memory that power AI data centers become obsolete every 3-5 years. If a company builds an orbital data center, its processing power is effectively useless for training the latest AI models in less than half a decade. So, in their business plans, the solution is to build intentionally disposable satellites.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware. Given that those bulkier pieces of equipment pose their own challenge for launches, as we saw yesterday, that seems a bit of a waste. So, Dr. Turyshev suggests that orbital data centers must be designed with hardware replacement in mind.

Fraser talks about a NASA project designed to assemble large-scale structures in space.

Sources indicate that on Earth, replacement of data server racks involves a human technician walking down an air-conditioned aisle, pulling some cables, and pressing pins before replacing a standardized blade. In orbit, that would require a pressurized housing with airlocks, life support and fire suppression systems, while still having the problem of cooling all of those heat-producing microchips in the vacuum of space. According to Dr. Turyshev, that means the entire data center architecture should be based around plug-and-play âorbital replacement unitsâ (ORUs).

Sources indicate that he assigns each of those ORUs into one of three main replaceable component tiers (alongside replacing an entire 100 kW satellite node if it suffers catastrophic damage). One is a 5 kW âcomputeâ module that holds the memory, storage and optical transceivers necessary to actually perform calculations. These are designed to be rapidly swappable, and are intended to be the most replaced part of the whole satellite.

Recent findings suggest that another ORU category is the âsubsystemsâ â the power converters, batteries, pumps, and manifolds meant to keep the whole system running but that are settled enough technologically to not require regular replacement. In the paperâs architecture, these can be swapped out by specialized 6 or 7 degree-of-freedom robotic arms, as compared to the automated cartridge changers that handle replacing the compute modules.

Fraser talks about the difficulties repairing missions at L2, like JWST.

The third group of ORUs consists of the solar arrays and radiator panels themselves. Making them modular has the added advantage of not needing to replace the entire cooling or power generation system if one part happens to be struck by a micrometeoroid, which will undoubtedly happen often even in Low Earth Orbit. Despite the fact these modules make up the bulk of the weight and surface area of the spacecraft, they will not have to be repaired as frequently as the compute modules, as random failures caused by cosmic rays will brick compute modules fairly frequently..

Unfortunately, replacing these systems isnât as easy as it would be on Earth. Each 5 kW processor will heat up nearly half a degree Celsius every second, triggering a thermal overload in a little less than a minute if left uncooled. And the power capacitors riding along to maintain power to the system have the capability of producing an arc strong enough to weld a robotic gripper to a maintenance touch point, so they must be bled off before a robot can start interacting with the satelliteâs hardware.

Recent findings suggest that and then, there is once again the sense of scale. For a standardized 1 MW cluster, comprising ten 100 kW sized systems, a collection of 3-4 robots specialized assigned to each 1MW cluster would have to perform around four hundred standardized swaps per year â more than one a day. This would include replacing broken or damaged parts, as well as upgrading to the server hardware itself.

It has been revealed that hubble has already been repaired by a crewed mission. NASA wants to do it again, Great Space expliains. Credit - Great Space YouTube Channel.

Scaling that up once again to a 1 GW computer cluster, comparable to a major modern AI campus here on Earth, the number becomes staggering. There would have to be 400,000 automated replacement tasks every year. And supplying the parts to do that would require launching up to 25 metric tons of replacement cargo every day.

To put it bluntly, we donât have that kind of launch capacity yet. Nor would sending humans up help manage such a drastic workload. The paper estimates that housing and feeding a crew of 4-6 technicians to actively manage a data center constellation would require $500 million to $1.5 billion per year. Until we get to the scale of several hundred megawatts to a gigawatt-level system, that is not economically feasible.

Sources indicate that thatâs not to say we couldnât launch specialized crewed repair missions occasionally. But at the scales needed to make a dent in the AI infrastructure we have down here on Earth, it would be hard to keep up with the overall maintenance workload using humans. And unfortunately, the entire concept of maintenance is another area that the back-of-the-envelope calculations of the companies that want to build orbital data centers seem to ignore.

Sources indicate that their solution is simply to add some extra hardware to account for the inevitable damage/failure that comes with operating in space. While that might work for a little while, if the proposal is to have a long-term data center presence in orbit, it's better to design for at least the possibility of continual operation rather than burning up tens of thousands of satellites in fireballs across the world every year. It remains to be seen if that message will get across to the people designing these systems, though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that astronomers have detected titanium oxide in gas form for the first time around a young, massive star. The detection offers a rare glimpse into the very earliest stages of solar system formation, before the formation of planets and asteroids.

Sources indicate that the detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth. Orion Source I has not yet reached the main sequence phase of a starâs life cycle â it continues to accrete material from its surrounding molecular cloud.

Recent findings suggest that models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars. This includes elements like calcium, aluminum, and titanium. Only later do materials that vaporize easily â volatiles like water, for example â accrete to young solar system objects.

But itâs not exactly clear where these seeds form. Samples collected from our own solar system suggest that they form under high-temperature conditions. They are, as far as we can tell, the oldest solids ever formed in our solar system.

Now, for the first time, this detection of titanium oxide around Orion Source I is providing astronomers more direct evidence of vaporized rock at the dawn of a upcoming star system.

In a recent development, âWe're in a unique situation with this object, Orion Source I,â said Adam Ginsburg, Associate Professor at the University of Florida and a co-author on the paper announcing the discovery. âThis object has a luminous enough star that it's evaporating the rock. We're seeing the rock evaporate from solid into gas, and so we can do the spectroscopy now and figure out what the rock is made of.â.

Ginsberg and his coauthors are getting the first real glimpses at the formation environments of these rocky dust-seeding materials, which complements knowledge gathered from our own solar system.

Recent findings suggest that âThe exciting thing is we're seeing the titanium oxide; we can measure how much there is, and we can start comparing our measurements to how our own solar system formed,â Ginsburg remarked. âIn our solar system, we can measure the ratios between different types of rocks, different elements, because we can grab those rocks and bring them into a lab.â.

This isnât the first time Orion Source I has provided valuable insights into solar system formation. In 2019, salty compounds were similarly detected in the protoplanetary disk.

It has been revealed that while the salt was found mainly in the outer disk around the star, the titanium oxide was found closer in, at the base of the starâs outflow of material: a hotter, more extreme region where the material could be vaporized. Understanding the origin of this material is an crucial discovery for researchers trying to piece together exactly how a latest solar system comes together, and offers a glimpse into the past of our own star and rocky neighbourhood.

The detection was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2026.

An Overlooked Metabolic Byproduct Could Help Repair a Damaged Heart

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A substance often treated as waste may be vital to the heart during a crisis, offering a potential target for treating heart failure and heart attacks.
  • The heart has to keep beating whether the body has plenty of energy available or is running low.
  • Scientists previously knew that the heart could draw energy from two carbohydrate sources at once: glucose, a sugar, and lactate, a substance produced when cells break down glucose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A substance often treated as waste may be vital to the heart during a crisis, offering a potential target for treating heart failure and heart attacks.

The heart has to keep beating whether the body has plenty of energy available or is running low. Maintaining that constant supply of energy is a complicated process, and when it breaks down, it can contribute to serious cardiovascular conditions such as heart failure. Researchers at University of Utah Health have now uncovered an unusual feature of heart muscle cells that helps them stay fueled during periods of stress and could point toward upcoming ways to treat a damaged heart.

Scientists previously knew that the heart could draw energy from two carbohydrate sources at once: glucose, a sugar, and lactate, a substance produced when cells break down glucose. In most human tissues, increasing the use of one fuel makes it harder to use the other. Heart muscle somehow avoids this competition.

In a recent development, in a study published in Nature, researchers discovered that heart muscle cells process these fuels in separate parts of the cell. Glucose is broken down in the cytosol, the fluid that surrounds structures inside the cell, while lactate is used inside mitochondria, which produce much of the cell’s usable energy. Keeping these processes separate allows the heart to draw energy from both sources simultaneously.

Recent findings suggest that the system depends on a molecule called MCT1, which transports lactate into the mitochondria. The researchers found that genetic mutations affecting MCT1 prevented lactate from entering the mitochondria and disrupted the heart’s energy balance. Although the heart could largely function without this pathway under everyday conditions, losing it when the heart was under stress led to heart failure.

Recent findings suggest that “This appears to be a critical backup system for heart function,” notes Gregory Ducker, PhD, assistant professor of biochemistry at University of Utah Health and senior author of the study. “In an emergency, we would really, really rely on this.”.

The discovery identifies a previously unrecognized role for lactate in sustaining injured heart muscle and gives researchers a potential target for developing treatments that restore its energy supply.

Sources indicate that “Our findings help point to new areas in which we could target the heart muscle to benefit and repair itself by allowing it to use lactate better,” Ducker notes. “That’s the long-term goal: to help the heart muscle heal.”.

Whether enhancing this energy pathway can improve heart function in patients remains to be established, though the researchers see potential applications beyond heart failure.

Recent findings suggest that “Rather than simply releasing lactate into the bloodstream as a waste product, we may be able to enhance the heart’s ability to use it as a valuable source of energy,” says Stavros Drakos, MD, PhD, professor of medicine at University of Utah Health and co-senior author of the study. “By optimizing this process, we could potentially improve heart muscle function in patients suffering from heart failure or heart attacks.”.

We’re constantly testing and writing about pocket knives here at Popular Mechanics, and Benchmade is a brand that always tops our list of favorites. Its folders, automatics, flippers, and fixed blades are beautifully designed using all high-quality materials, and all are U.S.-made in its Oregon headquarters. But there’s no denying they’re pricey, costing upward of $200, and they rarely go on sale for much of a discount.

But right now, ahead of Black Friday, Benchmade is knocking 20 percent off three of its most popular knives on Amazon—the Osborne, the Bugout, and the Bailout—for a savings of roughly $70 each.

When the Osborne debuted in 2000, it was Benchmade’s first blade to sport the Axis lock, which been replicated in some form by nearly every major knife manufacturer since its patent expired in 2019. It’s designed for ambidextrous operation and fast, one-handed deployment, plus it keeps your fingers clear of the blade while you open and close the knife.

This seasonal version uses CPM-S90V stainless super steel, which offers great edge retention and reliable toughness for everyday tasks like opening boxes. It’s coated with a protective distressed finish to make the reverse tanto-style blade look rustic and has a rich-looking dark-green aluminum handle, with copper accents. It feels good in hand—a durable yet lightweight EDC knife.

The Bugout is the knife our resident expert Justin Park grabs first for backpacking, camping and hunting and indicates it’s “arguably the defining pocket knife of the explosion of modern EDC blades.” It’s strong, but ultra lightweight and hardly registers in your pocket or pack.

Like the Osborne above, the Bugout uses S90V stainless super steel, featuring a shorter drop-point blade, copper accents, and handle that combines the same dark-green aluminum with a grippy and rugged-looking canvas micarta.

It has been revealed that the Bailout is lightweight and tough. It has a longer drop-point tanto-style S90V stainless steel blade covered in the same stonewashed protective finish as the Bugout and Osborne, along with the same dark-green aluminum handle and copper accents. While it’s another great choice for EDC, the Bailout is outfitted with tactical-style elements, like the lanyard slot at the rear and the deep-carry clip.

Industry News: Hidden Viruses in the Human Gut Offer Fresh Clues to a Disorder Affecting Millions

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many gut viruses were found at lower levels in people with irritable bowel syndrome, offering newly introduced clues to a poorly understood condition that affects roughly one in ten people.
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists have identified more than 116,000 groups of viruses living in the human gut, over 99% of which had no close match in the largest existing catalog of gut viruses.
  • Recent findings suggest that research into the gut microbiome has traditionally focused on bacteria, leaving much less understood about bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many gut viruses were found at lower levels in people with irritable bowel syndrome, offering newly introduced clues to a poorly understood condition that affects roughly one in ten people.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have identified more than 116,000 groups of viruses living in the human gut, over 99% of which had no close match in the largest existing catalog of gut viruses. These largely unexplored microbes could offer newly introduced clues to how the digestive system functions and why it changes in people with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Recent findings suggest that research into the gut microbiome has traditionally focused on bacteria, leaving much less understood about bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. Scientists from King’s College London, Helmholtz Munich, and the University of Nottingham are now filling that gap with two studies published on November 17, 2026, in Nature Communications and Gut.

Professor Ana Valdes and Dr. Afroditi Kouraki from the University of Nottingham stated, “For a long time the viral part of the gut microbiome has been a kind of dark matter: we knew it was there but couldn’t see it. Advances in sequencing and computational methods mean we can now start to map it properly, and this study highlights just how much has been hidden.”.

For the Nature Communications study, researchers analyzed genetic material from stool samples collected from more than 1,000 participants in TwinsUK, the largest twin registry in the United Kingdom. Using data on gut bacteria, health measurements, and diet, they examined how populations of viruses and bacteria varied together. Certain viruses were consistently more abundant alongside particular bacteria, while others demonstrated the opposite pattern.

According to recent reports, dr. Panayiotis Louca, a research associate at King’s College London who led the study, said, “Gut viruses are difficult to study, so most of what we found simply isn’t in existing catalogs. What stands out is how closely they track with gut bacteria and with the chemicals those bacteria produce. We can’t yet say whether the viruses are driving that, and testing it is our next step.”.

According to recent reports, studying twins also allowed researchers to estimate how much genetics and the environment shape the gut’s viral community. Genetic factors accounted for an estimated 47% of the variation in overall viral diversity, although most individual viral populations appeared to be influenced primarily by environmental factors.

According to recent reports, the researchers also discovered a small group of viruses carrying genes linked to harmful bacterial behavior. These viruses were more commonly found alongside bacteria that can sometimes cause infections and less commonly alongside bacteria that break down dietary fiber.

In a recent development, such relationships could be relevant to IBS, a condition that affects around 10% of the population and can significantly disrupt daily life. Its underlying causes remain poorly understood.

It has been revealed that in the second study, published in Gut, researchers used TwinsUK data to identify 50 viral groups associated with IBS, most of which were less abundant in people with the condition. Relationships between bacteria and viruses also differed, with many viruses infecting bacteria previously linked to IBS. This suggests that the condition may involve changes across the wider microbial community rather than in bacteria alone.

Recent findings suggest that senior author Dr. Cristina Menni, who leads the metabolomics research group at the Department of Twin Research, Ageing and Genomic Epidemiology at King’s College London, noted, “Our research highlights that to fully understand the gut microbiome and its links to health and disease, we need to look beyond bacteria and consider the viruses that live alongside them. We reveal a fascinating and largely unexplored dimension of the gut microbiome—discovering that viruses are not only closely associated with bacterial communities, but also with the metabolites that connect the microbiome to our health. This opens exciting new avenues for understanding how the gut ecosystem works.”.

According to recent reports, future research will examine whether gut viruses actively influence bacterial metabolism and how these interactions change in health and disease. Understanding these relationships could eventually help researchers develop better biological markers and treatments for IBS, as well as more personalized approaches to gut health.

It has been revealed that dr. Louca added: “The study is observational, so it cannot show that the viruses cause these effects, but it provides greater understanding of a largely unexplored area of the human gut. It would also be beneficial to replicate the study on a more diverse cohort, as participants were mostly older women of European ancestry.”.

“Population-level characterization of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites” by Panayiotis Louca, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Afroditi Kouraki, Erfan Khamespanah, Yu Lin, Xue Peng, Robert Pope, Alessia Visconti, Francesco Asnicar, Daniel Kirk, Ricardo Costeira, Nicola Segata, Mario Falchi, Jordana T. Bell, Tim D. Spector, Lindsey A. Edwards, Li Deng, Ana M. Valdes and Cristina Menni, 17 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79230-0.

According to recent reports, “Large-scale shotgun metagenomic analysis of gut bacteria–phage interactions in IBS” by Daniel Kirk, Erfan Khamespanah, Panayiotis Louca, Alessia Visconti, Robert Pope, Francesco Asnicar, Sarah E Berry, Jonathan Wolf, Nicola Segata, Tim D Spector, Mario Falchi, Frances M K Williams, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Li Deng and Cristina Menni, 16 November 2026, Gut. DOI: 10.1136/gutjnl-2026-338807.

AI Helps Three Powerful Supercomputers Simulate The Milky Way In Extraordinary Detail

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the early days, astronomers kept sketchbooks close at hand when they looked through their telescopes.
  • In a recent development, in an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved.
  • These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the early days, astronomers kept sketchbooks close at hand when they looked through their telescopes. They drew what they saw and shared their drawings. Modern astronomy, with its enormous segmented lenses, gigabyte cameras, and cryogenically-cooled infrared space observatories, makes those days seem more distant than they really are. But one of the latest efforts in astronomy makes astronomy's sketch-pad days seem so far in the past, they're almost red-shifted.

In a recent development, in an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved. They used the supercomputers and AI together to simulate the Milky Way down to the level of individual stars. Up until now, the smallest level of detail in simulations, called particles, was clusters of stars with the mass of about 100 Suns. The behaviour of individual stars was averaged out in those simulations (Auriga, FIRE, etc.).

These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis. The lead author is Keiya Hirashima, from RIKEN in Japan.

In simulations, achieving a level of individual stars means that individually simulated particles have one solar mass. So it's like a proxy for the population of stars. But regardless of that important distinction, the fresh simulations are extraordinary.

"Our highest-resolution Milky Way simulation used 5.4 trillion particles, â¼ 10, 000Ã those in the state-of-the-art simulations," the authors write.

Sources indicate that âWe expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way-sized galaxy, itâs not straightforward,â stated Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo. âWhen we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required.".

This figure from the paper demonstrates different structures of disk galaxies at different scales, emphasizing the complexity necessary for accurate simulations. Top left and middle: NGC 4414, a disk galaxy similar to the Milky Way Galaxy, taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. Top right: NGC628, a disk galaxy with spiral arms and bubble structures taken with the JWST. Bottom left: Carina star forming region taken with the JWST. Bottom middle: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant taken with the JWST. Bottom right: turbulent innterstellar gas around Cassiopeia A taken with Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. Image Credit: Hirashima et al. 2026. SC2026.

Recent findings suggest that to achieve this fine particle resolution, simulations need ever shorter time steps, and time steps are like simulation currency; the shorter they are, the more computing resources they demand. To supply the resources for that, the researchers harnessed the power of three exascale supercomputers together: Aurora, Frontier, and JUPITER. Each one ran the same software on different hardware: Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD graphic processing units (GPUs) and central processing units (CPUs).

But linking three supercomputers was only part of the solution.

Industry observers note that "We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves," mentioned Fujii. "This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented.".

According to recent reports, by using this model, the larger simulation was able to skip over many small timesteps. It's called PHEASANT, and it was developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. Supernovae are complex and require their own detailed simulations with very small timesteps. By plugging PHEASANT into the larger simulation, it relieved that simulation of a lot of work.

It has been revealed that "With trillions of particles, we resolve individual stars and model their SN feedback self-consistently within a galactic-scale simulation," the authors write. "Such a simulation reveals how individual stars, such as the Sun, contribute to the overall structure of the MW through multiple physical processes.".

This image from PHEASANT demonstrates the Milky Way's disk. Galaxies are complex structures, with different types of structures at different scales. They have thin and thick disks, bulges, halos, spiral arms, star clusters, nebulae, and individual stars and gas clouds. In this work, the researchers divided the galaxy into smaller regions that could be processed by different parts of a supercomputer. Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND.

Industry observers note that âOne of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years,â noted Hirashima. âMy model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation. Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel, or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations.â.

These panels are snapshots from PHEASANT. The panel on the left demonstrates the distribution and temperature of gas across a model galaxy. The panel on the right is a close-up view, where individual stars are visible as dots. Image Credit: Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND.

Sources indicate that we can't understand the Milky Way, or galaxies in general, without a detailed understanding of how its gas and stars behave. Stars are born, drift away from their clusters, and evolve. Depending on their masses, they can remain on the main sequence for trillions of years, leave the main sequence after a few billion years and then linger as white dwarf cinders, or exhaust their fuel rapidly and explode as supernovae.

It has been revealed that gas is also complex. It collects in clouds where stars form, can be funnelled into the galactic center and "recycled" by supermassive black holes, or blasted away by explosions. Stars and gas are linked, and there's an extraordinary amount of detail involved.

Supernovae are among the most complicated events. In some regions, the massive young stars that eventually explode as supernova are born in the same region. When they exhaust their fuel, they explode and carve massive bubbles in the interstellar medium. That can drive gas away to form more new stars elsewhere. They can even propel gas outside of the galaxy. It's all part of the life of the Milky Way, and simulations that struggle to recreate all of the detail in supernova explosions can lead astronomers astray.

This is LHA 120-N44 (N44) in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the ESO's Very Large Telescope. It features a massive bubble excavated in the interstellar medium by exploding young stars in its center. Some of the stars are still there, and they're still expanding the bubble with their powerful winds. Simulating all of the complexity involved is an enormous challenge. Image Credit: ESO/Manu Mejias.

âSomething we want to understand is how events on the scale of individual stars connect to the larger structure of the Milky Way,â noted Fujii. âWith this simulation, we can investigate how individual supernovae affect the number of stars that form, the size of these giant gas bubbles and the material that flows out of the galaxy. We can also study how groups of stars form and how they may eventually develop into star clusters.â.

The PHEASANT AI surrogate model plays a critical role in this work, and that's part of a broader trend in science.

"The surrogate modeling approach can also be generalized beyond astrophysical problems to other research fields," the authors write.

"AI surrogate modeling accelerates simulations and bridges wider physical scales, opening new pathways in various real-world applications, including climate modeling, space forecasting, and low-temperature plasma," the authors conclude.
